News.title: Cops share CCTV of dog walkers & other passers-by they want to speak to after woman ‘raped’ on cycle path
News.content:
HELP US Cops share CCTV of dog walkers & other passers-by they want to speak to after woman ‘raped’ on cycle path







Next

POLICE have shared CCTV of seven potential witnesses they want to speak to after a woman was allegedly raped on a cycle path.

The horror incident unfolded on a path running parallel to a set of train tracks at around 3pm on November 18 in Newark, Nottinghamshire.



Cops have now shared still images of seven people they believe may have seen something while walking past the Clay Lane entrance to the path where the alleged assault occurred.

Five passersby were filmed either walking or cycling past Barnby Road Academy, in John Gold Avenue, between 2.35pm and 2.53pm on the day.



Due to the location being so close to the Clay Lane entrance, officers believe they may have vital information.

One woman was seen walking her dog while wearing a pink hat and beige coat, while another was carrying a purple umbrella and wearing a polka dot coat.

The other three are a cyclist wearing a navy blue coat and bobble hat, a walker in a black puffer jacket and grey tracksuit bottoms and a hooded pedestrian with a light blue backpack.

Two more potential witnesses were pictured near the NSK sports and social club, off Elm Avenue, heading towards Clay Lane, around 2.40pm.



They are a cyclist in a yellow coat and a dog walker in a red jacket.

Police have stressed that none of the seven people are suspects, but are potential witnesses they would like to speak to urgently.



Detectives are also appealing for any head-cam or dashcam footage filmed by motorists or cyclists nearby.

They have asked specifically for footage filmed while travelling along Clay Lane, London Road, Beacon Hill Road or Barnby Road between 12pm and 4pm on November 18.

Officers are also keen to hear from anyone in the vicinity of the cycle track who may have seen or heard something.

Detective Inspector Daniel Buckle, of Nottinghamshire Police, said: “Our officers are continuing to support the victim in this case, who has been updated at each stage of our investigation as it has progressed.



“We are now in a position to release this short video featuring seven people, who we want to speak to urgently as part of our ongoing inquiries.

“I want to make it absolutely clear that none of these people are in trouble, or are viewed as suspects, but are instead important potential witnesses.

“Any piece of information, however small or insignificant it might seem, could make the difference in helping us establish who was responsible for this horrible offence.

“We completely appreciate how much shock and concern this incident has caused within the community, so officers will continue to provide visible patrols of the area.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

To report any information, including any relevant footage, directly to the police, call 101, quoting incident 508 of 26 November 2026.



Crimestoppers can also be contacted anonymously on 0800 555 111.

WHO CAN HELP? Doctor Who-style Tardis pops up in town centre to offer direct line to police

A DOCTOR Who-style Tardis aims to nail local crime lords after materialising in a town.

The £42,000 police public call box is sited where 512 offences were reported last year.



Its functioning phone lets shoppers connect to cops in a control room.

Just like The Doctor’s time machine, a blue light on the roof flashes when in use.



Inside is far bigger than it looks — with space for a desk and chairs, and officers regularly available.

The 18-month trial began in Watford on Thursday.

Lib Dem Mayor Peter Taylor said: “The police box is a distinctive addition and will provide reassurance to everyone visiting the town.”

Hertfordshire Constabulary secured Home Office funding.



A Tardis in Boscombe, Dorset, installed in 2014 led to a 35 per cent reduction in crime and anti-social behaviour.

This month police there confirmed it no longer had an operational use so will be donated to a local youth group.

Doctor Who’s Tardis was based on a 1929 Met Police box design.

Doctors such as David Tennant and companions including Billie Piper’s Rose Tyler have used it since the show’s 1963 debut.

News.title: Married prison maths tutor, 52, avoids jail after sending naked snaps to inmate and snogging him
News.content:

JAIL LET-OFF Married prison maths tutor, 52, avoids jail after sending naked snaps to inmate and snogging him







Next

A PRISON maths tutor who smuggled naked snaps of herself to a lag and snogged him has avoided jail.

Married Oksana Antanaitiene, 52, fell for the prisoner while teaching inmates at HMP Chelmsford and young offender institution in Essex.



Colleagues found the mum of one locked in a staff office with the inmate and emerging “looking flushed”.

Jail bosses found naked photos of her that she had sent him in his cell.



Prosecutor Ian Cain said their communication was “often of a sexual nature”.

A letter at her house “suggested the relationship had been physical and sexual”.

Antanaitiene, of Grays, Essex, admitted misconduct in public office.

She was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for two years, at Chelmsford crown court yesterday.

HMP Chelmsford is a Category B men’s prison and young offender institution.

A previous scheme at the jail saw specialist maths courses developed after prison bosses revealed a high proportion of inmates arrived with poor numeracy skills.

News.title: Andy Burnham faces Labour civil war as nearly 100 MPs demand North Sea oil drilling is blocked
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham is facing a Labour civil war over North Sea oil drilling as rival camps of MPs pile pressure on the PM.

Nearly 100 Labour MPs have written to him demanding he blocks drilling at Rosebank – Britain’s biggest untapped oil field.



Some ministerial aides are considering quitting if the project gets the green light.

But around 80 Labour MPs have privately urged the Government to approve drilling and are weighing up publishing their own letter of support.



Pro-drilling rebels are also reportedly considering an amendment to Labour’s energy legislation next week to overturn the ban on new North Sea oil and gas licences.

Both the Tories and Reform have vowed to back any amendment to scrap the ban.

Anti-drilling Labour MPs warned approving Rosebank would “permanently damage our climate credentials as a party and as a country”.

The row has also exposed divisions at the top of Government, with Chancellor John Healey said to be backing the project.

But the final decision rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who is legally required to remain impartial.

One MP said she is “like Icarus – flying too close to the sun” and accused her of trying to stir up a revolt over the proposal despite being a Cabinet minister.



Ms Fahnbulleh – a protege of Ed Miliband – is pro Net Zero and against oil and gas drilling.

She is under pressure from Scottish MPs and the Chancellor to give the greenlight to the project.

One Labour MP said: “She sat on the frontbench when she was organising the revolt against welfare under Keir Starmer.

“Rosebank is rebellion number two for her. But she is like Icarus – flying too close to the sun.”

In Greek mythology, Icarus made himself wings of feathers and wax.



But crashed into the sea and drowned after flying too close to the sun.

News.title: Fury as Labour admits empty private homes could be seized to house asylum seekers without owners’ permission
News.content:
Next

ASYLUM seekers could be housed in empty ­private homes without the owners’ permission under Labour rules.

Town halls were handed wider powers this month to take control of properties vacant for six months — down from two years.



Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook has now confirmed the homes can be used to house asylum seekers and refugees.

He told Tory MP Katie Lam councils could use the properties for “providing private rental and temporary accommodation to house refugees and asylum seekers through dispersal arrangements”.



Yet last year, his department had dismissed suggestions the powers would be used that way as “pure speculation”.

The Tories insisted available homes should be used to house Brits first. It comes as Labour seeks to shut migrant hotels but faces opposition to plans to house them in town centres and closed military sites.



Villagers near Piddington, Oxfordshire, have protested against plans for an asylum camp housing 1,256 migrants.

The number of asylum ­seekers in hotels fell to 13,185 by the end of September, Home Office figures released on Thursday showed.



But nearly 76,000 were being housed outside hotels — up six per cent in a year.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “It’s outrageous they have admitted empty properties they seize could be used for asylum seekers.

“They should be for British ­citizens and especially for homeless veterans first.”

Reform’s Sarah Pochin also said: “Instead of stopping the boats, Burnham is plotting how to put more migrants on people’s streets.”

Town halls must first secure tribunal approval to take over the management of eligible empty homes.



“They can then rent out the properties without the owners’ permission under a final management order.

News.title: Death defying moment schoolboy dives out of oncoming train’s way moments before being hit
News.content:
Next

THIS is the unbelievable moment that a schoolboy dives out of the way of an oncoming train and is missed by inches.

CCTV footage shows the unidentified boy take a leap of faith across the tracks of Imanta station in Riga, Latvia.



At the start of the video, can be sauntering up to a railway crossing before quickening his step as he notices something speeding towards him out of shot.

A train than steps into view as the boy makes a dramatic lunge for the opposite side of the tracks.



In a desperate bid to make the distance, the boy grabs onto the end a metal railing to pull himself to safety.

The massive city-link train continues to steam pass at speed, missing him by inches.

The boy lands heavily on the opposite tracks, lying there for a moment as another train waits to pull out of the station.

After a few seconds of reflecting, he gets up still holding a cardboard box he was carrying before making his way out of shot.

The train involved in the near-death incident was heading from Riga, the Latvian capital, to Tukums, a town around 40 miles west.

The footage was released as part of a rail safety campaign urging Latvians to stay safe around the tracks.



“About to miss your train? No matter how important it seems to make it in time, nothing is worth your life!” a post on X read

It continued: “Remember – a train cannot stop immediately!

“We encourage parents to discuss the rules of safe behaviour near railway tracks with their children, stressing that their safety is far more important than catching a train!”



A protest demanding safer crossing took place at the same station in June.

Demonstrators armed with signs criticised Riga city council for its failure to improve traffic safety at the station.

The demanded that robust barriers be built to prevent the exact incident that occured today.

It came after two tragic accidents claimed tha lives of three people at the Imanta crossing in the eight months priot.

On October 1 last year, two underage girls were hit by a train while crossing on an electric scooter.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

And another man was killed while crossing the tracks nine months later.

Latvian Railways reportedly rejected the demand, considering the installed pedestrian mazes to be a sufficient safety measure.

News.title: At least 14 tragically found dead in Canary Islands migrant boat as thousands reach isles in ‘invasion’
News.content:
Next

AT LEAST 14 migrants have been found dead on a boat rescued near the Canary Islands amid a surge in undocumented arrivals.

Around 100 people on a single boat were rescued off the archipelago’s smallest island on Friday, with six airlifted to hospital in a serious condition.



Rescuers discovered 14 bodies onboard the stricken vessel around 39 miles south of El Hierro.

The health chief said the boat had been at sea for ten days with many people close to dying of thirst.



Several migrants onboard were suffering from hypothermia and burns.

The remaining 84 people including three women and three children disembarked pier with clear signs of fatigue.



One officer was injured during the operation and was evacuated by aircraft to Tenerife.

In a separate incident on Friday, a 111 migrants were rescued, including 10 women and 10 children.



Some of the arrivals were carried to the port on stretchers, unable to walk, while others were wrapped in red thermal blankets as they reached the port.

President of the Canary Islands, Fernando Clavijo slammed the Spanish government for not doing enough.



He said: “Canarians do not have to bear all this pressure alone.”

The two operations came as arrivals at the Canaries have skyrocketed since October with a record 2,100 people arriving on Tuesday.

Most migrants head to El Hierro, an island of 11,400 residents that declared a state of emergency earlier this month.

Around 15,000 migrants – largely from Senegal and Gambia – have arrived at the port in November alone.

The Atlantic route from west Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings.



Despite this, thousands continue to attempt the journey in overcrowded boats unfit for the rough seas and long distances.

With the Spanish election in a matter of days, the recent boom has become a central issue on the ticket.

Far-right Vox party leader Santiago Abascal denounced what he called the “abandonment of parts” of Spain, including Ceuta and El Hierro, by the current prime minister.

The party accuses Pedro Sanchez’s government of failing to control the country’s borders, saying his open migration policy encourages people to make the perilous journey.

Leader of the opposition party – the Popular Party (PP) – Alberto Nunez Feijoo echoed this and said: “People losing their lives at sea is the worst consequence of this government’s irresponsibility.”



Following Friday’s arrivals, he warned that Spain urgently needs an “orderly” migration policy.

Most polls are suggesting the PP will win the most seats but just fall short of a majority.

Demanding action from the government and European Commission, regional leader Fernando Clavijo said: “A lot of pain and feeling of impotence over this new tragedy.

“The humanitarian emergency doesn’t start on El Hierro, but on the shores of Senegal and Gambia, where we have to act.”

According to Clavijo, around 100 children arrived at the Spanish border on Tuesday including a four-day-old baby who was born on the crossing.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tuesday’s surge shattered the previous record set just ten days earlier on November 14, when 1,580 migrants landed on El Hierro, Gran Canaria, and Tenerife.

It marked the highest number in a single day since records began in Spain, emergency services operating in the port of La Restinga confirmed.

News.title: Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'
News.content:
Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".

Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.

But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.

The UK's former Chief Technology Officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the incident was an attack.

"They've taken down some of the citizen-facing services which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door," he said.

Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC the technological disruption meant she was missing Â£1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday.

"I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."

Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.

"I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."

Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.

Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.

She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.

"With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.

The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.

There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.

A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.

News.title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.

Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.

The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip.

This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.

It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before.

"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything.

"But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.

News.title: 'Calculating predator' who blackmailed girls into self-harm jailed for 14 and a half years
News.content:
This aticle contains distressing details

A "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others has been detained for 14 and a half years.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was 17 when he began forcing vulnerable girls to send sexual images, hurt animals and carve his assumed name into their bodies, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

One of the girls' mothers said he used the internet to breach the safety of his victims' homes and minds, causing lifelong devastation.

Mensforth, 20 and from Sunderland, admitted 17 offences. They included crimes against nine victims, the youngest of whom was aged 12, and having indecent images of children as young as five.

Mensforth was in online groups who made content for their "com", short for community, by victimising "vulnerable young girls", prosecutor Charlotte Hole said.

They often targeted girls in self-harm support groups and used apps including Telegram and Discord to befriend them.

Abusers convinced the girls they were in romantic relationships and coaxed them into sending indecent images of themselves, then threatened to publish the pictures unless they committed more "extreme" acts, the court heard.

If you are affected by any issues raised, help can be found through BBC Action Line

The girls would be forced to carve the names of their abusers into their flesh and write messages and logos in blood promoting the "com" groups.

They were also ordered to "sacrifice" animals under the threat their personal information would be released online or false reports would be made to trigger armed police raids of their homes.

Under the username Yuri, Mensforth targeted girls in the UK, USA and Australia, making them write "I worship Yuri" in blood among a litany of other abuses.

When one of his victims asked him why he was doing it, Mensforth replied "for content", the court heard, with the abuser seeking to rise to the top of the group's hierarchy.

News.title: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
News.content:
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.

Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".

This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.

Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (Â£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.

News.title: Charity founded in Captain Tom's name bids to be struck off
News.content:
A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.

The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Sir Tom's name at the request of his family last year.

An application to have it struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.

The World War Two veteran became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising Â£39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire.

However, the charity founded in his name became mired in controversy after the charities watchdog found misconduct and mismanagement on the part of his daughter and her husband in their running of it.

The Charity Commission's report uncovered a "repeated pattern of behaviour" through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling "misled".

A Â£1.4m book deal and an Â£18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores were found to have enjoyed through the Captain Tom Foundation.

They have already been banned from being charity trustees and earlier resigned from the foundation.

The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.

The father-of-two died aged 100 in February 2021 with coronavirus.

News.title: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'
News.content:
Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early".

"From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.

McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."

Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans.

"There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure.

"AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."

He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".

McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."

News.title: Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?
News.content:
For better or worse, everyone recalls their first date. But how will the last one be remembered?

After more than a decade of serving up her awkward, off-the-wall questions, Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date is no longer looking for love, with the YouTuber calling time on her hit series.

From a youth club project to a full-blown media empire with A-listers asking her out, the series has influenced the interview landscape and carved a new path for the next generation of content creators.

"To start my next chapter, I have to close this one," Dimoldenberg told the BBC earlier this month.

"I'm focussing on making sure I say goodbye in the perfect way so I feel ready to do my next thing."

This article contains spoilers for the final episode of Chicken Shop Date.

After much speculation as to who would be the final date, fans were never going to be able to agree as to whether the farewell was indeed perfect.

Names like Harry Styles and BeyoncÃ© had been floated around, but it was Drake who was the favourite with some bookies after Dimoldenberg previously described the Canadian rapper as her dream date.

So when the camera panned to psychotherapist Esther Perel, "everyone was a bit surprised", says fan Sarah Almond, who watched an early cinema screening on Tuesday.

News.title: 'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped train attacker
News.content:
Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

News.title: Police look for more than 100 gig-goers to help Co-op Live probe
News.content:
Police have said they are trying to contact more than 100 gig-goers to help their investigation after an unknown substance was released at a concert at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.

Detectives believe a "small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night".

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

No arrests have been made and the substance has not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We're working to identify those [robbery] suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents.

"All of this work is ongoing at pace.

He said there had been "similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries".

Fans reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.

News.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
News.content:
Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

News.title: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says
News.content:
The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.

"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.

"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."

The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp â including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC, external it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

"That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."

Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

News.title: Body found in woodland confirmed as missing Kelsey Hunter
News.content:
Police have confirmed that a body found in woodland in southern Scotland has been identified as missing 20-year-old Kelsey Hunter.

She had last been seen in Castle Douglas at 17:00 on Saturday and a major search was carried out around the nearby village of Springholm where she lived.

On Tuesday, Daniel McKnight, 21, appeared on petition at Dumfries Sheriff Court charged with murder and two other charges, including defeating the ends of justice. Kelsey's body was found at about 19:15 on Wednesday.

McKnight made no plea and was remanded in custody.

News.title: NHS Grampian publishes leaked report at centre of hospital scandal
News.content:
NHS Grampian has published the internal report which revealed there had been 19 avoidable deaths of patients who had undergone liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

It was leaked last week by surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide probe after the report said some patients bled to death on the operating table.

NHS Grampian has now released the report from September 2022, along with a redacted version of a follow-up from November the same year.

The health board said they were being published, external now "in the interests of absolute transparency".

Meanwhile, written submissions have also been published from witnesses who will appear at the Scottish Parliament's health committee next week.

These include two whistleblowers and Prof Caroline Hiscox, former chief executive NHS Grampian.

News.title: Ex-council leader jailed for fraud and tax evasion
News.content:
A former council leader accused of inventing a fake heritage society to scam a local authority out of thousands of pounds has been jailed for 27 months.

Jason Zadrozny set up the Ashfield Heritage Society before applying for council funding, which he then transferred into his personal account.

He claimed the cash was "to support heritage projects", but pocketed the money for himself. He was convicted of fraud and tax evasion on 21 September following a trial.

At Northampton Crown Court on Friday, the 46-year-old, of Stanton Hill, sobbed in the dock as Judge David Herbert KC told him he had "failed the electorate and harmed public confidence in the district council by your fraudulent conduct".

The six-week trial heard Ashfield District Council leader and county councillor Zadrozny - of the Ashfield Independents - set up the heritage society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council.

This, the trial heard, included Â£7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield".

The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March.

Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends.

Jurors were also told Zadrozny was a landlord who did not pay tax on income from four of his properties, estimated in court to be "less than Â£15,000".

Zadrozny told the jury he did not keep the money for himself, and gave cash from the heritage society to Tony Brewer, a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020, to repair war memorials.

News.title: Fury cleared to fight Joshua after wife retracts schizophrenia claim
News.content:
Tyson Fury has been medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in December after the bout was put in jeopardy by claims of a schizophrenia diagnosis.

Fury, 38, spoke of his mental health struggles in a Netflix documentary which was released on Friday, with his wife, Paris, saying he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

But Paris has since retracted that statement, saying he "doesn't have this condition" and Netflix have edited the remarks out of their film.

The British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) told BBC Sport: "Tyson Fury has been cleared to box on 11 December."

Fury faces Joshua, 37, in a long overdue all-British heavyweight contest at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in the early hours of 12 December.

Originally, the Netflix documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.

Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion as it sees fit".

On Thursday, the BBBoC general secretary Robert Smith told BBC Sport that it was "in the process of dealing with the matter" and that it was "confident he [Tyson Fury] will be absolutely fine".

News.title: Maura Higgins splashes $10K on extravagant gift for DWTS partner Mark Ballas
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Maura Higgins has bought her Dancing with the Stars partner Mark Ballas a $10,000 Rolex Submariner watch as a thank-you present, despite the pair failing to win the show.

The duo reached the final of the ABC Latin and ballroom dance competition, but missed out on lifting the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy after finishing in fifth place on Tuesday night (24.11.26).

Nevertheless, Higgins was full of appreciation for Ballas and demonstrated this by purchasing the lavish gift for him.

The reality TV star previously received a luxurious gift herself when TV personality Rob Rausch, 28, gave her a $17,000 burgundy Hermès Birkin bag in March, following his betrayal of her in the finale of the US version of The Traitors.

Higgins had promised to purchase Ballas a Birkin bag if they won the contest.

And while there was "no Birkin for Ballas", Higgins joked that he had not done too badly with his new Rolex.

Taking to her Instagram Stories, the former Love Island star shared a photo of a surprised Ballas holding the watch in a presentation box, with the caption: "But I think he'll survive. A massive thank you for all your time, patience and belief in me.

open image in gallery Higgins with her dance partner Mark Ballas ( Disney )

"Something I'll forever be grateful for."

The Dancing with the Stars finale saw Higgins and Ballas score a perfect 30 for each of their three routines from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, 58, Derek Hough, 41, and 71-year-old Bruno Tonioli.

They performed a tango to Gallo Ciego in the Judges' Choice round, a quickstep to Tutti Frutti in the Instant Dance Challenge, and a freestyle routine to Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend, alongside the Irish folk songs The Parting Glass and Flowers of the Red Hill.

Higgins was left stunned after she and Ballas achieved a perfect total of 90 points across their three performances, saying: "I never thought I'd be this close to winning."

However, once the judges' scores and viewers' votes were combined, the pair finished fifth, with Paralympian Ezra Frech, 21, and his professional dance partner Daniella Karagach, 33, winning after they also received a total score of 90 for their routines.

News.title: France falls into recession as it struggles to contain deficit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

France has technically dipped into recession, official data has shown.

The country’s economy contracted more ⁠than initially thought in the third quarter of 2026, underscoring the difficulty of reducing the deficit and putting the ‌government's growth ​goal for this year of 0.5% all but ‌out of reach.

It comes as S&P revised France's credit rating outlook to "negative" from "stable" on Friday, citing growing budget pressures as weak economic growth and higher interest costs make it harder to reduce the deficit.

The ratings agency affirmed the country's sovereign rating at "A+/A-1", but said it expected larger fiscal deficits this year and next than previously forecast.

"Continued political polarization, including beyond the 2027 presidential election, could continue constraining the implementation of deficit-reducing measures and growth-enhancing reforms," S&P said in a statement.

The minority government in France is seeking to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to cut the fiscal deficit from 5.4% of output this year to 5.0% next year ( AFP/Getty )

France's benchmark 10-year borrowing ⁠costs rose to more than 5.14% last month, their highest since ​2002, ⁠and climbed more sharply than those ‌of most peers.

The rise reflected concerns about the country's ability to rein in its deficit, secure passage of the 2027 ‌budget and contain social unrest linked to ‌the cost of living.

The minority government is seeking to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to cut the fiscal deficit from 5.4% of output this year to 5.0% next year, in France's deeply divided parliament five months from a presidential election.

"(S&P's) this assessment underscores the urgent need to give the country a responsible budget without delay, that restores our public finances by bringing the deficit down to no more than 5%," Finance Minister Roland Lescure said in a statement.

"The French Government remains fully committed to pursuing along a path of fiscal consolidation," he added.

Earlier on Friday, it was revealed that French authorities were investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information about judicial investigations to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez summoned Hugues Moutouh, a former general secretary in the ministry, for a meeting Friday. Moutouh now serves as prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region, representing the central government there.

Nuñez confirmed that a judiciary investigation has been opened, a day after Le Monde newspaper reported that the Paris prosecutor’s office was investigating the suspected leaks.

News.title: How the opening night of Nations Championship finals weekend fell flat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It had been billed as a three-day Super Bowl of rugby but the grand opening of the Nations Championship finals weekend fell short of such lofty comparisons. Sparsely attended, bitterly cold, a few television technical gremlins – one always feared this Friday night would be a tough sell and so it proved.

Not many more than 30,000 spectators made it in to watch Ireland complete a November clean sweep with victory over Australia, and far fewer for Italy’s narrow win over Fiji that preceded it.

open image in gallery Ireland overcame Australia at a sparsely-attended Twickenham ( AP )

With those results came a 2-0 lead for the north in the race for the “Hemisphere Shield”, though that the organisers spent much of the night clarifying that these were not placing play-offs said plenty about a competition still yet to truly cut through. Colossal contests await over the weekend as the southern hemisphere powers seek revenge on their northern foes, but neither England vs New Zealand nor the grand final between France and South Africa is expected to draw a full house.

There was an admirable effort at razzmatazz wrapped around the logistical challenges that a double-header poses – but this first of three consecutive rugby-laden days suggested an imperfect idea that requires some refinement. A neutral site detracted from, rather than enhanced, the occasion.

open image in gallery Myles Smith provided entertainment before kick-off of Ireland against Australia ( Getty )

Credit to the hardy few who ventured in on a chilly winter’s night; particularly those who managed to make it in time for the Italy vs Fiji curtain-raiser. Twickenham was not exactly bouncing or buzzing pre-match – one rather felt for DJ Char Stape, who had drawn a wretched 2.30 slot in the “Fan Village”. The use of the singular was appropriate... At least the string band in the Jubel tent had a couple of heaters and canvas roof for company. Myles Smith, a Brit Award winner, was the centrepiece of the entertainment offering, with a no-doubt-pricey but enjoyable two-song set hurried in after Ireland and Australia finished their warm-ups.

It is thought that future editions of this weekend, provided the six-game format is maintained, may use smaller venues for the Friday night particularly. With just a week’s notice on the actual fixtures, and a mighty number of tickets to shift, organisers should be commended for their ambition – and have a useful test case now as to what works and doesn’t. Sadly, though, the early knockings of the first helping of the double-header felt a lot like being here during the dark pandemic times.

open image in gallery The start of the finals weekend was watched by plenty of empty seats ( PA )

To take a more glass – or stadium – half full approach, there was at least a spirit of conviviality. Scottish fans were sighted two days before they take on Argentina and flags of all nations waved, with even a Portuguese supporter or two among the throng. Ticket sales north of 150,000 over the whole weekend in a saturated November market probably should not be sniffed at, either.

The bulk of the match-goers on this Friday night were clad in Irish green. They could enjoy a solid enough showing, particularly in defence, and a convincing 38-14 win. Australia dominated the bulk of the opening exchanges, and should probably have earned more from the first 20 minutes than Jeremy Williams’ short-range score. Ireland soon showed their error, striking via Robbie Henshaw at the first opportunity, before a maul score from Nick Timoney gave them a seven-point advantage. Fly half Sam Prendergast had enjoyed a good half, and had the last kick of it, knocking over a penalty.

open image in gallery Rob Baloucoune continued his breakthrough year with a try ( Getty )

He was soon back amongst things, too, lifting a cross-kick delicately over the head of debutant James Ramm to set up Rob Baloucoune. Kalani Thomas slid over to give the Wallabies hope but a double from replacement back row James McNabney, emerging as a real Irish find, dashed that for good. Andy Farrell may consider success in this meeting of third-place pool finishers as meagre reward for a campaign in which they’ve beaten the world champions.

“We had no field position, no ball,” the Ireland head coach. “But we found a way to be clinical when we had an opportunity in the 22. We’ve seen a shift in our appetite to want to grow and get better. We’ve seen a step up as far as that is concerned. It’s been a very successful campaign, but we’ve got to keep going now.

“I don’t know whether the Friday night thing works at the same venue. If we played at the Aviva, it would have been full tonight. I love what they are trying to do, the razzmatazz, it felt different and like it was trying to be an event. It was just a shame we couldn’t get the people through the door. It’s not our jobs to make sense of it; it’s our job to just play what is in front of our face.”

Beforehand, Italy and Fiji served up a captivating clash of contrasts, with the Pacific Islanders left to rue some late profligacy. A sensational score from Kitione Salawa – a 13-phase blur of offloading limbs and bad decisions turned good – was the highlight of a Fijian second-half surge that took them in front having been 17-0 down, only for Tommaso Allan to slot a third penalty 13 minutes from time as Italy earned a hard-fought win. It was the first for Gonzalo Quesada’s side since a historic victory over England in the Six Nations; injuries have hit the Azzurri hard in this campaign.

open image in gallery Italy ended their losing run with a win over Fiji ( Getty )

Fiji, though, could take the positives from a first real chance to test themselves consistently against the world’s top teams – it should be noted, too, that they played not a single game on home soil.

“This is exactly what the Fijian team needs,” head coach Jake White said. “I’ve read a lot about teams being fatigued, but we’ll play as many Tests as we can. If you look at how we’ve grown, we are definitely going to be much better when we get to the World Cup.”

News.title: ACLU seeks court order blocking Trump administration's efforts to unmask ICE critics on social media
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticizing its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights attorneys claim in a federal court filing Friday.

A federal class action, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a court order enjoining the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals' First Amendment free speech rights.

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators.

ACLU attorneys sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case's unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a Jan. 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until Dec. 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office in Washington didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU's lawsuit.

ACLU lawyers say Pirro's office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.

"The investigation," the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” ACLU attorney Laura Moraff said in a statement.

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organization says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit's plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.

News.title: Southampton beat Middlesbrough to claim Spygate bragging rights as Finn Azaz taunts former club
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Goals from Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz earned Southampton a 2-0 win against Middlesbrough, securing the bragging rights in the first match between the clubs since last season's Spygate controversy.

Manning, making his 300th Championship appearance, broke the deadlock in the second half before former Boro forward Azaz punished a defensive error to double the lead. The result extended Saints’ unbeaten home run to 19 matches and moved them within four points of the league leaders.

The fixture carried significant context after Saints were removed from last term’s play-offs and hit with a four-point deduction this campaign for illegally observing training sessions carried out by Boro, Ipswich and Oxford.

Middlesbrough were restored to the play-offs as a consequence, though they ultimately missed out on Premier League promotion following a final defeat to Hull at Wembley.

While both managers sought to dismiss any lingering animosity beforehand, the contest carried clear competitive weight between two key promotion contenders.

open image in gallery Southampton came away with the three points in a tense clash with Middlesbrough ( Getty )

Middlesbrough dominated the opening period, registering 11 attempts without finding a breakthrough. Leading scorer Will Lankshear squandered the best opportunities to add to his 15 league goals, firing straight at Daniel Peretz when put clean through in the 16th minute before directing a free header into the goalkeeper's midriff.

Callum Brittain also skimmed the crossbar with a cross, contributing to a frustrating run that saw Boro reach 49 away shots without scoring across their past three fixtures on the road.

Southampton had threatened earlier in the match, with Azaz striking the bar following a loose touch from Luke Ayling, while Radek Vitek produced impressive saves to deny Cyle Larin and Lewis Dobbin.

The home side eventually broke the deadlock after the break when James Bree lashed a low cross into the penalty area for Manning to divert into the net. The full-back celebrated by running directly to his manager.

Azaz, who moved to St Mary’s from Boro in the summer of 2025 following two seasons at the Riverside, sealed the victory in the 79th minute. Capitalising on a slip by Aidan Morris, the forward placed a cool finish into the bottom corner before running the length of the pitch to celebrate in front of his former fans while making a crying gesture.

The action sparked a late confrontation between the two sets of players, but Saints comfortably managed the remaining minutes to secure the points.

News.title: Alonso crisis deepens as chaotic Chelsea lose and fans taunt own player
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea.

The City Ground hosts the Premier League clash tonight, with two sides who are both falling short of expectations.

Forest head coach Oliver Glasner brought with him a sense of optimism after he left Crystal Palace, but the club are just outside the bottom three, sitting in 17th position with only nine points. As things stand, they are only clear of 18th-placed Sunderland because of superior goal difference.

Beneath them, Glasner’s former club Palace are bottom, two points away from them, and then Manchester United come in 19th, a single point behind. With Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino now installed at Selhurst Park and Old Trafford, respectively, the pressure could soon be felt yet more keenly.

There have been flashes of encouragement, with a 3-1 win over Manchester City in early November, spearheaded by a brace from Liam Delap, who left Chelsea in the summer. However, last Saturday they lost 2-0 at Bournemouth to dent any nascent momentum, and the match was the sixth in 11 league games where the club have failed to score. Forest have scored nine times this season, with only Sunderland having a worse record in attack.

Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also endured a tough time of late. They were trounced 4-1 against Leeds United at home on Saturday, despite taking the lead in the first half.

That worrying collapse was the fourth loss in five league matches, and it followed a 1-0 defeat against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light before the recent international break.

There is speculation that Chelsea will move for a central defender in January, with 20 goals conceded in the Premier League so far.

Chelsea are currently in eighth place in the league with 16 points, five points behind Liverpool in fourth. Tonight, they could leapfrog Bournemouth, who are in fifth, two points ahead of them. Another loss, though, could see them in the bottom half once the weekend’s fixtures are completed.

News.title: Dominant Ireland down Australia in Nations Championship
News.content:
Ireland claimed fifth place in the Nations Championship, overcoming a slow start to run out 38-14 winners over Australia and make it two out of two for the northern hemisphere on finals weekend.

It was a stuttering start to a rugby marathon that will feature six matches across three days at Allianz Stadium.

This new Nations Championship format is clearly going to take a little getting used to. All the pyrotechnics in the world – and the organisers provided as much smoke as they could – could not mask the sight of 50,000 empty seats at Twickenham.

The fact that no one knew who was playing who and on which day until last Sunday would not have helped ticket sales. But given the size of the Irish diaspora in London alone, organisers might have hoped for a larger green army in south west London. But there is definitely merit in it, too. Ireland were always going to find it hard to top their win over South Africa last weekend, but they can be pleased with their month’s work.

Even Australia grew into the autumn. Their running game is let down by a lack of control from the boot but Les Kiss had demanded a performance of which Australia could be proud and they were markedly improved from their shellacking here against England a few weeks ago.

News.title: Italy edge out Fiji in Nations Championship at sparse Twickenham
News.content:
Italy clung on against Fiji to put the first point on the board for the northern hemisphere in Nations Championship finals weekend, although their entertaining 23-21 victory was played out to a quarter-full Allianz Stadium.

Perhaps that was no surprise given the timing of the kick-off: 4.40pm on a Friday.

But with only 32,000 tickets sold for Friday’s double-header – Ireland vs Australia takes place later in the evening – the sparse nature of the crowd has raised questions about the new format.

It was a shame there were so few fans packed in for this game, because it was a fun match to watch, as Fiji’s games often are.

Gonzalo Quesada’s Italy had lost to the same opposition 16-21 in Rome last weekend, and they entered this game the only team from either hemisphere not to have won a single Nations Championship match. But their 17-7 half-time lead thanks to tries from Federico Mori and Giacomo Nicotera was no more than they deserved. Fiji only made one entry into Italy’s 22m in the first half, although it did yield a try from Sale’s 6ft5in Ponepati Loganimasi, who was allowed to race home from the halfway line.

Fiji scored their second try from their second entry into Italy’s 22m, and it was another beauty, Jiuta Wainiqolo sucking in two defenders before offloading to Peniasi Dakuwaqa, who stepped inside Stephen Varney to score.

Fiji’s third was the best of the lot, 13 phases of wonderful offloading rugby before a Dakuwaqa grubber kick released Wainiqolo., who in turn managed to offload to Sawala to score.

That nudged Fiji 21-20 in front. But a late Tommaso Allan penalty put Italy back ahead, as Fiji opted to kick for the corner with a minute remaining rather than go for the posts.

Italy held on, Andrea Bocelli blasting out over the public address at full-time in front of 60,000 empty seats. First blood to the northern hemisphere.

News.title: Vaccine gaps fuelling global measles resurgence, WHO warns
News.content:
Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to humans and requires 95 per cent of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. Children under-five, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk.

According to the WHO, it can cause pneumonia, brain infection, deafness and blindness, death and “immune amnesia”, where the virus can weaken the immune system for months or even years.

The measles vaccine, which used a weakened (live attenuated) virus in two doses, is safe and highly effective.

Dr O’Brien said: “Some of the more recent graduates have never seen a case of measles, but it is back”.

Diana Chang Blanc, unit head of the essential programme on immunisation at the WHO, said the spread of cases across income levels showed that even in places with strong health systems, small drops in coverage can leave pockets of unvaccinated people that can spread risks far beyond those areas.

In 2025, 59 countries had “large or disruptive outbreaks”, defined as more than 20 cases per million people over 12 months. Of them, 11 were previously declared measles-free. The US was not among them, as its outbreaks didn’t reach the threshold.

“It can take years to regain elimination status, whereas it takes only a 12-month period to lose elimination status,” said Dr O’Brien. “These are hard-fought gains that countries have made, and protecting them now is more important than ever”.

News.title: Australia embarrassed by remarkable Overton spell
News.content:
So often English cricketers have left the “Gabbatoir” looking dazed and confused after yet another horror show. This time, it was an insipid Australian side’s turn to be embarrassed and overawed by a remarkable showing from Jamie Overton. It was a batting display as ugly as anything Australian cricket has served up in the sandpaper civil war, which rumbles on.

As Australia were bowled for a meagre 108, Overton recorded figures of five for 12, the second-best in T20 by an Englishman and the best by any man in T20 fixtures between these old rivals. That was Australia’s lowest T20 total against England since the sides’ first meeting, ahead of the 2005 Ashes, when they were bundled out for 79 chasing 180. Back then, T20 was a bit of fun, now it is big business, and this was altogether more chastening.

A combination of rain, which delayed play three times and led to a DLS-reduced target, and Riley Meredith, who was gifted three wickets, meant that England’s batting lacked the freewheeling fun of their bowling performance.

But the chase was a formality, and England won by seven wickets. The Gabba was just a third full, with some hardy Barmy Army types in fine voice as England celebrated their win. With England leading the five-match series 2-1, it is hard to imagine too many Aussies racing to buy tickets for the final two games in Sydney and Canberra. England are flying out Rehan Ahmed and the uncapped Glamorgan batsman Asa Tribe as they manage a long list of absentees, which will include the South Africa-bound captain Harry Brook and keeper Jordan Cox by Canberra.

News.title: Colombia earthquake triggers surge in malaria cases
News.content:
Cases of malaria in rural Colombia have surged after a devastating earthquake left towns and villages in ruins, according to local charities.

Colombia has recorded over 74,360 cases of malaria this year, 40 per cent of which have been concentrated in Chocó – the epicentre of the earthquake which struck in August, killing at least 335 people and injuring 4,500 more.

The region has seen a 46 per cent surge in cases of the mosquito-borne disease compared to last year, up from 23,757 cases in 2025 to 34,759 cases so far in 2026.

Malaria can be very serious at any age, but it is the most dangerous for young children under five. If left untreated, it can become a medical emergency in as little as 24 hours and result in death.

While Africa accounts for around 94 per cent of global malaria cases, an estimated half a million infections occur in South America every year, mostly in the countries surrounding the Amazon basin – Colombia, Brazil, and Venezuela.

The earthquake hit at 7.4 on the Richter scale and was the strongest Colombia has seen in a decade, destroying roads and buildings. It hit during the rainy season, and water has collected in and around destroyed buildings, allowing mosquitoes, which breed in stagnant water, to survive and multiply, according to Save the Children.

Following the earthquake, thousands of people in Chocó have moved into overcrowded and unsanitary shelters after their homes were destroyed, increasing the spread of infectious diseases including malaria – which is carried between people via infected mosquitoes.

“The earthquake has worsened the conditions that favour the transmission of malaria,” Maria Mercedes Liévano, Save the Children’s Country Director in Colombia, told The Telegraph.

“Because we’re now seeing collapsed and damaged homes, families that are sleeping in overcrowded conditions out in the open, and are dealing with a health network that is overwhelmed,” Ms Liévano added.

News.title: Milk of human kindness: Brazil exports its donor breastfeeding programme worldwide
News.content:
When baby Luis Miguel was born in Guarapuava, Brazil, in February, he was unresponsive.

He had inhaled meconium, a newborn’s first stool, during delivery. It then entered his lungs and blocked his airways. Doctors at Hospital de Caridade São Vicente de Paulo resuscitated and intubated the baby boy, saving his life. He spent the next three weeks in the hospital’s neonatal unit.

His mother, 25-year-old sales assistant Luany Thainara Machado, could not produce enough breast milk and so hers was supplemented with that of a woman she had never met.

“While it might not make much sense for a mother to do this under normal circumstances it becomes very important when the need arises,” she said.

Nine months later, Luis Miguel is healthy and Machado is grateful that donor milk was able to support her son when he needed it most; so much so that today she donates 2.5 litres of her now plentiful supply every week. “Being able to help other mothers and other babies today, it feels really good,” she told The Telegraph, bouncing Luis Miguel on her knee as she spoke.

Sports.title: Frank Lampard reveals he was ‘within an inch’ of joining Leeds before £11m Chelsea move changed football history
Sports.content:
Next

FRANK LAMPARD admits he was ‘an inch’ away from signing for Leeds United 25 years ago.

The Coventry boss expects a hostile reception from home fans when he takes his side to Elland Road on Saturday.



But it could have been so different as there was a time when he might have become a Leeds legend when David O’Leary had taken them into the Champions League.

Lampard was hot property at West Ham — and a wanted man around the turn of the century. He had already seen pal Rio Ferdinand leave Upton Park in 2000 and join Leeds for £18million.



And midfielder Lamps was set to follow a few months later — until Chelsea offered him the chance to stay in London.

Instead he moved to Stamford Bridge in an £11m deal when Claudio Ranieri was in charge — and went on to etch his name into the Blues’ history.



But on his second anniversary as Coventry boss, Lampard knows there will be anything but a warm welcome for him in West Yorkshire.

In recent years, that has come from the ‘Spygate’ controversy in 2019 when Leeds boss Marcelo Bielsa admitted snooping on the Derby training ground when Lampard was Rams manager.

The incident even sparked a fans’ chant of ‘Stop Crying Frank Lampard’ after his accusations that the practice was ‘unethical’.

But now Lampard sees signs of Leeds boss Daniel Farke taking the Whites back to that level — especially after they beat Chelsea 4-1 away last weekend.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Asked why he did not sign for Leeds, the Sky Blues boss said: “Because it was Chelsea! I was within an inch of signing for Leeds at that point.

“There were different factors involved, and no disrespect to Leeds as they were a really good team then, they were quite exciting.

“But I was a London boy and it felt right when I sat with Claudio.

“I felt that I made the right decision in the end. But back then, there was a real feeling, momentum and personality that Leeds had. And the team they have now is creating its own personality and story.

“They are in a really good position, watching them play. It’s an impressive model. They’ve been up, down, back up and they’ve been able to build.



“It’s a good standard for us to look at. It doesn’t always work right away when you come up, but they’re a strong unit.”

Despite Lampard’s respect for Farke’s squad, he knows what to expect from Leeds supporters.

Asked if there is no love lost between manager and fans, Lampard said: “That’s safe to say! Chelsea and Leeds have a very strong rivalry — that’s always there for me as a Chelsea man.



“And at Derby, it was quite public. It’s all history for me. It’s the fans’ prerogative to be passionate and it’s mine to be passionate in my own way.

“They have a strong fanbase. But it’s a difficult stadium to go to because of that and especially now as the way they are playing is great.”

But although Lampard took Coventry to the Premier League last season — the semi-final play-off game at Elland Road remains one of the highlights of his managerial career.

Derby were 1-0 down from the first leg — and went behind in the second — but stormed back to reach Wembley with a stunning 4-2 win.

Mason Mount and Harry Wilson were among the goalscorers and Lampard was captured afterwards singing ‘Stop Crying’ with his celebrating players.



The Sky Blues boss agrees it was a standout moment, adding: “It didn’t win us promotion, we were always aware we had Aston Villa in the final.

“But Leeds were way ahead of us throughout that season. Bielsa had done great work and beaten us quite comfortably in both league games.

“Everybody expected us to lose in the second leg. I wasn’t sure we’d win.

“But to go up against a team that strong in that atmosphere and manage to get the result we did meant it was a special night.

“You’re allowed to enjoy those ones. Some games don’t go your way and you have to take it on the chin, but that was a good night.”
