Sports.title: Parrott fires Republic of Ireland into Nations League play-offs
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott fired the Republic of Ireland into a Nations League play-off berth with two penalties in their 3-0 victory over 10-man Kosovo at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The result ensured the Republic finished runners-up in group B3, and also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month's qualifying draw for that competition.

Tuesday night's contest turned on its head in the 26th minute, when Kreshnik Hajrizi was sent off for handling the ball off the line, and Parrott took advantage with a top-corner finish.

The Real Betis striker doubled the Republic's lead from the spot five minutes after the restart, and Jack Moylan added a 75th-minute cushion to keep alive the hosts' hopes of booking a place in League A for the first time through the March play-off.

Image: Parrot struck twice from the penalty spot

Heimir Hallgrimsson's lone change from Saturday's defeat to group winners Austria was the insertion of John Egan into the line-up, replacing injured captain Nathan Collins.

How Ireland finished as group runners-up...

It was a contest that lacked fluidity in the opening 10 minutes, before the Republic found a foothold and Finn Azaz looked to pick out Parrott, but was blocked.

Kosovo then twice missed chances to take the lead. Lindon Emerllahu fired just wide in the 17th minute, and Caoimhin Kelleher was called into action for the first time a minute later to deny Vedat Muriqi.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter suddenly took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, a red-card incident sparked by Moylan's cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott.

His effort - clearly goalbound - was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately shown a red card by Latvian referee Edgars Malcevs.

Parrott stepped up and gave Arijanet Muric no chance when he rifled into the top right corner to set the Republic on their way.

It remained just a one-goal advantage at the break despite a handful of chances falling the Republic's way, while the visitors created one when Kelleher denied Ilir Krasniqi with 10 minutes remaining to ensure there would be no first-half equaliser.

There was a flurry of Republic chances immediately after the second half kicked off before Parrott added his second penalty.

Muric had just denied Jayson Molumby's effort from range and Parrott was rushing forward to meet the loose ball when he was taken down by the Kosovo keeper.

This time he dove in the right direction, but failed to stop Parrott from doubling the hosts' lead.

The Republic were less successful from open play, unable to put the game away from a string of subsequent chances despite finding themselves in plenty of space, and should have added a third before the hour.

Moylan's persistence finally paid off with 15 minutes remaining, nodding home substitute Liam Kitching's cross in off the post.

The Republic nearly added a late fourth when Adam Idah stung the palms of Muric with two minutes left.

Parrott dreaming of home Euros

Republic of Ireland striker Troy Parrott speaking to RTÉ about the 2028 Euros:

"I've been thinking about it since I was a kid, I think everyone has.

"Look, it's not a guarantee that we are going to qualify for that tournament, so I think tonight was very important to get into pot two so that we have a better draw.

"We'll be going into the qualifiers now, trying to make sure that we qualify for the tournament.

"A tournament that's one of the host nations being Ireland, without Ireland it would be heartbreaking for all of us, so I think it's a mission now to make sure that we're there.

"It was disappointing that we didn't win the group because that's what we all wanted to do at the start.

"There's been so many nearly matches where we've nearly won, we've played really well and haven't won, and I think tonight we went out there with the mindset that no matter what we have to win.

"Obviously the red card helped us, but I have no doubt in my mind that group of players who were out on that pitch would have won that game."

'We want to play the top teams'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson speaking at his post-match press conference:

"Everybody, and especially us, likes to play the top teams. To compare yourself with the best teams, that's one thing.

"Second is those teams will expose your weaknesses, and that helps you in your growth to play these teams, so we can continue our growth.

"We're already looking forward to March. Tough teams in the pot. Whoever we draw is going to be a tough two games, and it's good for this team at this time to play these matches instead of friendlies.

"We're really excited for March, and looking forward to meeting the players again."

Sports.title: Kalajdzic scores late as Republic of Ireland taste defeat in Austria
Sports.content:
Sasa Kalajdzic dealt the Republic of Ireland a late blow in Linz with the only goal in Austria's 1-0 Nations League victory at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The result ensured that, no matter how the closing contests in Group B play out, Austria sealed promotion to League A.

Ireland enter Tuesday's critical home clash at the Aviva Stadium in third place, with one point fewer than their final opponents, Kosovo.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men were not without chances, but only Kalajdzic made one count when he broke the deadlock in the 79th minute.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: The chaotic five days that almost ruined the biggest fight in British boxing history: Netflix piggy-backed off Tyson Fury's schizophrenia contradiction to flog documentary - but brutal reality of boxing world has left them red-faced
Sports.content:
'I was hearing voices – horrible, scary voices. At night my head was full of terrifying screams,' Tyson Fury once harrowingly confessed.

Does Fury suffer from schizophrenia? His wife Paris certainly thinks so, or thought so before abruptly changing her mind.

Her bombshell revelation – used as a hook by Netflix to promote their documentary – threatened to derail the streaming giant's own fight. As own goals go, they don't come much more calamitous.

Netflix expect 60 million subscribers to tune in for Fury's showdown with Anthony Joshua, Dana White predicts a Principality Stadium gate of £26million and the fighters are to split £150m between them. A late cancellation of the biggest fight in British boxing history would have been catastrophic.

In boxing terms, the company worth £185billion trying to cut it with the pros in sport's broadcasting dropped their hands like a rank amateur and ate a right hook. A knockout blow would have done enormous reputational damage.

The British Boxing Board of Control (BBoC)'s rules are clear. Fury couldn't fight if he was suffering 'any psychological disorder such as depression, schizophrenia or hyper-mania.'

Netflix will broadcast the Tyson Fury fight against Anthony Joshua but put their own event under threat with their Fury documentary, which was swiftly edited before release

Fury and his wife Paris both previously said he'd been diagnosed with schizophrenia before she made a U-turn and said he doesn't have the condition

On Monday, Netflix distributed a teaser for their eponymous 90-minute Fury documentary to news organisations across the globe.

Those outlets then reported the top line, declared by Paris, who said: 'He’s a mild schizophrenic and even then the penny didn’t drop. I thought, “Don’t be silly, what’s she on about? Maniacs are schizophrenic.”'

Her information was also confirmed by Fury himself, who said while promoting the film: 'I went to a leading specialist and was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar. I learned that you can never truly get away from mental health. You can only learn to manage and maintain.'

Daily Mail Sport's boxing doyen, Jeff Powell, then exclusively reported on Thursday evening that the revelations flying in the face of the BBoC's rules had thrown the December 11 fight into chaos.

The rest of the British media followed behind, latching onto our exclusive as it became one of the stories of the week and rang alarm bells, not least with the BBoC's general secretary, Robert Smith, who insisted to us: 'Tyson will not be allowed to enter the ring unless our doctors are satisfied there is no risk to his health.'

The promoters and Netflix were also put in a tailspin and by the following morning, they'd scrambled to make a late cut to the documentary just hours before the global release – editing out Paris' claim about her husband suffering schizophrenia.

They said 'new information' had come to light. That new information was Paris' hastily-written statement, performing the mother of all U-turns: 'I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word "schizophrenic".

'Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

'Mental health is complex, and it isn’t always easy to find the right words, especially when you’re living it with someone you love.'

So Paris denied her husband has been officially diagnosed but Fury not only said he had been, but added that it came from a 'leading expert'.

Fury and Joshua are due to split a pot of £150million for their massive showdown

The contradiction was clear and embarrassing. The BBoC accelerated their medical checks in light of our story, completing a swift examination late on Thursday.

Smith then confirmed on Friday morning that doctors had found Fury fit to fight, saying: 'All up to date medicals satisfactory and the promoters informed.'

WHAT IS SCHIZOPHRENIA: Schizophrenia is a serious long-term mental health condition with no known cause or cure. Symptoms can include: - Hallucinations - Delusions - Muddled thoughts or speech - Losing interest in everyday activities - Not wanting to look after yourself or caring about personal hygene - Feeling disconnected from emotions It can be treated with medicine and therapy or a combination of the two. More serious cases involve suffering psychosis. The person may not always be able to distinguish their own thoughts and ideas from reality. Symptoms most commonly begin in late adolescence or young adulthood and the illness affects roughly one in 300 people. There are varying degrees of severity but old classifications such as 'paranoid' or 'catatonic' are no longer used by all healthcare professionals due to there being overlap between them.

Fury's recollections of the worst of his illness came after he was crowned world champion for the first time in 2015 after beating Wladimir Klitschko.

He said: 'For that whole period I was screaming out for help, but everyone around me wanted to put me in a rematch.

'It was like I was a demon possessed and I needed a hospital rather than a ring. I was hearing voices – horrible, scary voices.

'At night my head was full of terrifying screams, to the extent I thought someone was in the room. Alcohol and drugs played a part, and I was also comfort eating – mainly sugar.'

Netflix being oblivious to the threat their own documentary bombshell posed to the mega-fight is perhaps not a huge surprise despite their heavy investment into boxing.

Their cameras have followed the lives of the Fury family since 2023 but when the documentary director, Lucy Wilcox, was asked why the coverage did not include the loss of his previous world title to Oleksandr Usyk, who beat him twice, she admitted she had never heard of the Ukrainian war hero and boxing legend.

There appears to be a chasm between the level of expenditure and sporting expertise.

The streaming behemoth does not publicly disclose its spending but it is understood that around 5 per cent of its £15billion annual content budget was set aside for boxing content this year.

With that kind of outlay, comes huge sway. The fight between two British juggernauts was originally touted for Madison Square Garden. It would have made little sense to anyone other than the money men.

Fury, pictured when he was 27 stone, struggled with his mental health after 2015 and spoke of hallucinations before making a remarkable comeback

Thankfully common sense prevailed and the fight was set for Cardiff's magnificent 80,000-capacity Principality Stadium was chosen as the location - with Turki Alalshikh key to the decision - but Netflix still managed to get its way in tailoring the start time for an American audience.

Two British sporting superstars, thousands of British fans in attendance but a production catering to punters on the other side of the Atlantic, it's a move that has rightly irked fans on these shores.

The fighters will make their ring walk at 1am and it might not all be wrapped up until 3am when the well-lubricated masses flood onto the streets of Cardiff.

The city's Council's Licensing Sub-Committee only recently gave the green light for those start times, with special dispensation having to be granted.

To some degree Netflix are learning on the job and there has never been a fight of such magnitude with conflicting interests that's easy to put on.

History is littered with huge bouts that collapsed before the pugilists could land a blow on each other – not least Fury v Joshua which many thought might never happen.

Hearn's ongoing feud with White over promotional control of the fight and conflicting announcements between both factions threatened to derail it.

Alalshikh is playing the role of peacekeeper between them, with UFC president White adamant he will be involved in the production of the event with his Zuffa Boxing company and attend in Cardiff on December 11.

Hearn previously said: 'Ultimately, and I don’t mean to sound arrogant, [White] cannot be involved in the fight unless myself and Anthony allow them to be.

Dana White (left) and Eddie Hearn (right) pictured during more amicable times, have been at loggerheads over the promotion of the fight

'They seem to be very desperate to be involved in the fight, and Turki [Alalshikh] wants them to be involved in the fight, and so do Netflix. And I get, like, it’s great for the promotion. So I’m not against it – I just want you to tell me and explain why. Why should I? What’s in it for Anthony? What’s in it for us? And once we establish that, we can make a decision.'

The warring promoters present another headache for Netflix and it will be fascinating to see how the broadcast unfolds.

Their previous offering of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson suffered issues with buffering, delays and crashes.

The tolerance level from fans if those mistakes are repeated for a fight in a different league to the Paul circus will be far lower.

For all their bungling in the build-up, Netflix must now show they can deliver top echelon live sport when the heat is on.

Sports.title: Netflix deletes Tyson Fury schizophrenia revelation from documentary after Paris claimed boxer has NOT been medically diagnosed with condition - after bombshell plunged $150m Anthony Joshua fight into chaos
Sports.content:
Netflix has been forced to remove a revelation that Tyson Fury has schizophrenia from their documentary on the boxer after it threatened to put his $150million fight with Anthony Joshua in jeopardy.

The bombshell had come from Fury's wife Paris, who had said 'he’s a mild schizophrenic' in promotional material for the programme, which was released this morning.

The disclosure had put Fury's upcoming heavyweight bout at risk of being cancelled as official regulations state boxers cannot fight with 'any psychological disorder such as depression, schizophrenia or hyper-mania', as reported by Daily Mail Sport.

It sparked panic at Netflix, which is also broadcasting the lucrative showdown and expects 60 million subscribers to watch.

Fury, 38, now needs to be rigorously assessed to determine whether he is mentally fit to fight AJ on December 11 and cash in on the enormous $150million (£115million) pot to be split between them.

It would be disastrous, and hugely expensive, for Netflix and the fight's venue, the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, if Paris's original statement led to the fight being cancelled and she has now retracted her claim.

The 36-year-old has tried desperately to row back on her original claims, saying Tyson 'doesn’t have' schizophrenia and 'has never received a diagnosis'.

Tyson Fury (left) will be rigorously assessed by doctors before his fight with Anthony Joshua can go ahead as they check his mental capacity to compete

Netflix confirmed that Paris's suggestion has been removed from the documentary.

A statement read: 'Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.'

After that 'new information' was received, Paris said: 'I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary.

'I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word "schizophrenic".

'Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

'Mental health is complex, and it isn’t always easy to find the right words, especially when you’re living it with someone you love.

'I’m so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we’ve received as a family.'

Robert Smith, the general secretary of British Boxing's Board of Control, confirmed Fury has no chance of being allowed to fight Joshua unless doctors are convinced he is mentally stable.

'Only one thing is certain,' he said. 'That Tyson will not be allowed to enter the ring unless our doctors are satisfied there is no risk to his health.

His wife Paris now insists that he is not schizophrenic having originally claimed he had 'mild schizophrenia'

Fury's fight with AJ has been years in the making and has been plunged into chaos yet again

'We are reviewing all the information about his mental condition and will come to a decision about authorising the fight in the next few days.'

The board's consultants will be checking if there is any proper medical evidence to support the anecdotal broadcast. Or if the now-deleted allegations in the documentary are at best exaggerated or at worst sensationalised.

In the 90-minute documentary, Fury opens up on his mental health, admitting: 'Words can’t explain the darkness I was in.

'It was like the living version of the pits of hell’s fire. I 100 per cent thought I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked and that scared me so much.'

Even if Fury is not diagnosed as schizophrenic, doctors will also have to confirm he is not currently suffering from the depression that has plagued him at various points during his career that he regularly refers to in the documentary.

If the BBC's medical team find him to be in the grip of the illness again, they will not be able to allow the heavyweight superstar to step in the ring for one of his biggest paydays.

Fury and AJ are in line to bank $150million between them for the night's work, while the Principality Stadium, Saudi Arabian backers under His Excellency Turki Alalshikh and hotels, bars and restaurants in Cardiff would also be stung if the fight was unable to go ahead.

The British Boxing Board of Control could have to pull the fight if Fury is found to be suffering from schizophrenia or even depression

Netflix want to use the all-British showdown to cement their move into major boxing but persisting public doubts still linger about whether the fight for which the sporting world has waited for a decade will indeed take place in a fortnight.

The start time of the fight was moved to the early hours of the morning at Netflix's request in a bid to cater to an American audience and maximise the numbers tuning in.

That meant Cardiff Council had to grant special dispensation for a 1.30am UK fight time on December 11 and locals complained the extended curfew could cause issues in the surrounding area.

Despite early reports of an 80,000-plus sell-out in just an hour on the day tickets went on the market, there are still hundreds of seats for sale. Some being pushed with an offer of beer being thrown in.

This raises further concern about the impact of alcohol on the traditionally rowdy Friday night in Cardiff when the Stadium empties the crowd onto the street at around 3am. So much so that the police are considering breathalysing late arrivals at the fight.

For now, Netflix and all of the many parties with an interest in the fight going off without a hitch will be sweating on the outcome of Fury's medical review in the coming days.

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: The day Tyson Fury threatened to have me 'annihilated' and my 'jaw broken' after I published his disturbing views on paedophilia, homosexuality and Satan - and the signs of his mental health struggles that were already there
Sports.content:
OLIVER HOLT: The day Tyson Fury threatened to have me 'annihilated' and my 'jaw broken' after I published his disturbing views on paedophilia, homosexuality and Satan - and the signs of his mental health struggles that were already there

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

As the build-up to his eagerly awaited fight with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff next month gathers pace, a new Netflix documentary about Tyson Fury will hit our screens on Friday. There is, apparently, no mention of the backdated two-year doping ban he served between December 2015 and December 2017, which is disappointing but predictable.

There is another episode that I would wager ended up on the cutting room floor, too. In November 2015, a few days before Fury beat Wladimir Klitschko for the world heavyweight title, the fight that changed his life for better and for worse, he gave an interview to Kugan Cassius of the popular iFLTV channel.

Fury and his entourage – including his brother, Shane, and one of his team, 'Cliff' – were in the thick of fight week but when Cassius asked the Gypsy King about the controversy that had followed an interview he had done with me in The Mail on Sunday a couple of weeks earlier, and mentioned my name, Fury’s expression changed.

‘Oliver “The W**kstain” Holt?’ Fury said, with the beginnings of a grin. ‘He tried his best to get me in trouble and it didn’t work, did it? So I’m not really too bothered what he does or anybody else like him. Men meet before mountains, don’t they?

‘And when they do, see Big Shane there, have a look at Big Shane, 6ft 6in and 25 stone, he’s going to break his jaw completely with one straight right hand. I’m not going to do it because I’ll get in trouble but the big fella there will annihilate him.

‘So Oliver, take a good look at him because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck. And that’s the face (gesturing towards Cliff) you’re going to see when he’s jumping up and down on your head. What are you going to do him, Cliff?’

‘I’m going to f**k him up,’ said Cliff.

I interviewed Tyson Fury back in November 2015, and the boxer caused outrage by conflating homosexuality and paedophilia

A few weeks later Fury beat Wladimir Klitschko in Germany to win the world heavyweight title

I did not want to be blasé but I did not take the threats too seriously. The Mail asked if I wanted to get the police involved and I declined. I took the threats as a mixture of bravado, bullying and slapstick. Boxing’s a rough trade and this was a long way from its outer borders. Fury’s nods to retribution felt more performative than sinister.

I was also aware by then that Fury’s mental health was in a precarious state. It is claimed in this new documentary that a few months after the threats he made to me, he was diagnosed with anxiety, depression, OCD, ADHD, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

Some years earlier, he had told the journalist Don McRae: ‘One minute I'm over the moon and the next minute, I feel like getting in my car and running it into a wall at a hundred miles an hour.’

And when we had talked a few weeks before the Klitschko fight, in an interview arranged at a hotel at Bolton Wanderers’ stadium, the base for his training camp, Fury had spoken in a stream of consciousness. He was hugely engaging and fascinating, too, but some of the things he said were disturbing as well as provocative.

‘We live in an evil world,’ he said that day. He spoke breathlessly and with the kind of troubled intensity that has never left him. ‘The devil is very strong at the minute, very strong, and I believe the end is near. The Bible tells me the end is near. The world tells me the end is near. Just a short few years away, I reckon, from being finished.

‘Abusing the planet, the wars in the Middle East, the famines, the earthquakes, the natural disasters, all these things were talked about 2,000 years ago. Prophesised. So now it’s all coming true…

‘There are only three things that need to be accomplished before the devil comes home: one of them is homosexuality being legal in countries, one of them is abortion and the other one’s paedophilia. Who would have thought in the 50s and 60s that those first two would be legalised?

‘When I say paedophiles can be made legal, that sounds like crazy talk doesn’t it? But back in the 50s and early 60s, for them first two to be made legal would have been looked on as a crazy man again. If I would have told you 120 years ago, that a 1,000-ton aeroplane is going to float through the sky, a piece of steel – ludicrous.

‘When Christopher Columbus said the world was round, he’s an idiot. All these things that happen in the world, wise men already know they’re going to happen and they see what they really are.

Fury on his way to a victory over Klitschko - who, he told me, was a devil-worshipper - that changed his life for better and for worse

Fury was incensed by the fact I reported what he had said in our interview in Bolton

‘Foolish people follow the system, get caught up in media news, what the government wants you to believe and all the higher powers want you to believe and go down the same path as all the sheep in the cattle market.’

And so it went on. Fury said that Klitschko was a devil-worshipper. ‘They are involved in bigger circles and stuff like that and they do magic tricks and whatever,’ he said. ‘All these rock stars and singers and these famous people, it is common knowledge that they are all involved in an occult group of Satan-worshippers and all that sort of stuff.’

Some of it felt like an extreme attempt to promote the fight with Klitschko. Fury was not box-office back then. He was on the margins. He was regarded as a talented, quirky curiosity but promoters were not quite sure what to do with the then-27-year-old. He had sublime skills but he was not an explosive fighter.

All that was about to change. The interview – and particularly his comments conflating homosexuality and paedophilia – caused outrage. He claimed, initially, that I had misquoted him but then the Mail on Sunday published the transcript of the conversation. He stopped claiming he had been misquoted.

He doubled down. He said he imagined Olympic champion heptathlete Jessica Ennis-Hill ‘slaps up good’ and that he believed ‘a woman's best place is in the kitchen and on her back’. There were demands he be removed from the shortlist for BBC Sports Personality of the Year, demands which the BBC resisted.

If the signs of his struggles with his mental health were already there before he produced a masterful performance to beat Klitschko in Dusseldorf in November 2015, his own version of shocking the world, the documentary charts Fury’s psychological and physical decline in the two years after it.

If Fury’s fight against Joshua next month feels like a natural end for what has become a remarkable career, the documentary paints a picture of that momentous victory over Klitschko 11 years ago as almost the beginning of the end.

It claims that triumph cast Fury into a pit of self-loathing and despair that contributed to him being diagnosed with schizophrenia several months later. He had started to hear voices in his head, he told Louis Theroux, in a podcast timed to coincide with the film’s release.

Fury poses for Daily Mail Sport at our 2015 interview

Fury will fight Anthony Joshua on December 11 in one of the most eagerly awaited Battles of Britain of all time

He suffered from cruel delusions that his wife, Paris, his dad and his best friend were involved in a plot to kill him. The revelations are such that, even though the alleged diagnosis is more than a decade old, they have prompted some disquiet about the fighter’s welfare and whether Fury should be allowed in the ring to face Joshua.

The Netflix documentary addresses some of this but skips over his ban for use of the anabolic steroid nandrolone and his former connections with management and promotions company MTK Global, whose boss was suspected Irish crime lord Daniel Kinahan.

‘I do like him,’ documentary-maker Lucy Wilcox told the media ahead of the film’s release. ‘He’s gentle, he’s quite camp, quite feminine. Not everyone’s gonna like Tyson, but I wanted people to understand him.

‘I wanted to understand him, because I wasn’t sure if I liked him. He’s not sexist, he’s not homophobic. But when you question him on certain things, he doubles down, like my kids would.’

A bizarre twist last night saw Paris claim her husband has not actually been diagnosed with schizophrenia — despite her saying so in the documentary — but it is undeniable that Fury has struggled with his mental health.

His openness in discussing it will have helped many people to confront their own issues and to attempt to get help for them. Fury deserves, and has been given, much praise for that.

It is also undeniable that Fury has caused a lot of a pain to others. And we are talking about the type of pain that goes beyond the kind he inflicts with his fists inside the ring.

The Netflix documentary presents the arc of his career as a redemption story but that is only partly true. If his openness about mental health has helped some people, his cruel comments about homosexuality and his casual misogyny will have caused hurt and pain in the lives of countless others and legitimised similar attitudes in the minds of the more impressionable of his fans.

In the decade and more since I spoke to him at what was then the Macron Stadium in Bolton, I have tried several times to arrange another interview, all without success. Frank Warren, his highly respected promoter, interceded on my behalf some years ago but to no avail.

In the decade and more since I spoke to him in Bolton, I have tried several times to arrange another interview, all without success

I don’t blame Fury for that. He can speak to whoever he wants and in the past few years, it has become unfashionably inconvenient to mention, or even to acknowledge the drugs ban and his links to Kinahan. It gets in the way of the redemption story and redemption sells better than a reality that is not quite so clear-cut.

The truth is that much of what Fury says and does is unsettling. It is the way he is and it is the way he wants it to be. He is a compelling talker, a conspiracy theorist, a man who wears a hat saying ‘Donald Trump for Prime Minister’ but he is not an urbane man. He is charismatic but it is not an easy charisma.

The worry – and he has admitted this himself – is that he will miss the discipline of boxing and training for fights when his career comes to an end. He is 38 now and he has enough money to last several lifetimes but no amount of money can buy him the peace that he finds through the purpose that boxing brings him.

It is the same for many sportsmen when it is over. They miss the lights. They miss the attention. They miss the focus. Fury has always been smart enough to recognise that there is a form of dependence there for him. Maybe that explains the fact there is an uneasy watchfulness about him. He prides himself on being awkward.

‘Awkwardness to the utmost, highest level,’ he said in that interview in Bolton in 2015. ‘Whatever is conventional, I am the opposite. If you want to walk in a straight line, I am going to walk in zig-zags. If you want to throw a one-two, I’ll throw a two-one. I don’t want to be an ordinary person. Because if you are ordinary, you do ordinary things.’

Sports.title: Former world champion boxer known as 'Beefy' denies punching hotel concierge 'and attacking man as he lay on the floor'
Sports.content:
Former world champion boxer known as 'Beefy' denies punching hotel concierge 'and attacking man as he lay on the floor'

Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has denied attacking a man at a luxury apartment block.

Smith, 38, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, allegedly punched the concierge worker outside the Blade, in Manchester city centre.

The alleged attack, on September 13, is said to have happened as the man lay on the floor and he suffered facial injuries that needed hospital treatment.

The fighter - nicknamed 'Beefy' - appeared at Manchester Crown Court on Thursday and denied charges of causing grievous bodily harm with intent and inflicting grievous bodily harm.

He did not enter a plea to a public order charge of racially aggravated behaviour over alleged 'racist words' he used prior to the alleged attack.

Smith was granted bail with conditions not to contact the complainant, and not to enter Manchester, unless to attend court, or for appointments with his solicitor.

He's due to face trial on March 15, 2028.

Smith, now of Formby in Sefton, was due to make a comeback in a fight on 4 September in Finland, but pulled out due to a calf injury, according to reports.

Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has denied attacking a man at a luxury apartment block

Smith, 38, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, allegedly punched the concierge worker outside the Blade, in Manchester city centre

He is one of four Liverpool brothers who all boxed professionally and all won titles at British level and has fought some of the biggest names in the sport including a defeat to Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

Smith won the vacant WBO light-middleweight world title in October 2015 when he stopped American John Thompson in Manchester and successfully defended the belt twice before losing it to Mexican superstar Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez the following year.

A former Commonwealth and British champion, Smith compiled a record of 33 wins, four defeats and one draw across a professional career spanning almost two decades.

More recently he fought British rival Chris Eubank Jr twice, defeating him in the first fight in January 2023, before suffering a defeat in the rematch eight months later.

Sports.title: Paris Fury breaks down in tears over heartbreaking first miscarriage as Tyson reveals he buried the baby in his dad's garden
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and his wife Paris have opened up about the devastating loss of their baby, with the former heavyweight world champion revealing how he brought their child home from hospital and buried him in the garden at his father's house.

The British boxing star has spoken about the miscarriage in a heartbreaking new Netflix documentary, with Paris breaking down in tears as she relives the moment they discovered they had lost their child.

The couple suffered their first miscarriage in 2014, more than a year before Fury's career-defining victory over Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Now, the Gypsy King has revealed the unimaginable grief he was carrying into one of the biggest fights of his life.

In an emotional recollection, Tyson explains how he was able to take his baby son home from hospital, despite it not normally being permitted, before laying him to rest in the garden at his father John's house.

Speaking in the new Netflix documentary, TYSON FURY, Paris said: 'I was expecting my third child so I was at home. Then I got a call from the doctors to say the baby was gone and that I had to born it (give birth to it).

'I kept it quiet because Tyson already had his uncle in the hospital and I didn’t want to add any more pressure. Then it came to this point where there was no viable answer, no more reasons why I couldn’t talk about it.

Tyson Fury and his wife Paris have opened up about the devastating loss of their baby

The British boxing star has spoken about the miscarriage in a heartbreaking new Netflix documentary called TYSON FURY

'I had to go into the hospital and born this baby. I told Tyson. We went through it together. We made the decision to take it home.'

Tyson then recalled the heartbreaking decision to bring their son home and bury him in the garden at his father's house, where he could later visit his grave.

'I remember it all,' Tyson said. 'At that age, they don’t usually let you take them home. I said no, that’s my family, I’ll take it.

'I had this big fancy watch for years ago. It came in this big box, hard wood. Mahogany. The baby was literally this big. And I just took the baby to my dad’s and buried him in the garden. Me and my brothers.'

Paris added: 'I don’t really remember a lot in that week. I remember being at home and seeing the little garden where he was. And, that was that.'

The tragedy came as the Fury family were already enduring an incredibly difficult period, with Tyson's uncle Hughie seriously ill in hospital.

'Hughie was still in hospital,' Tyson said. 'Some days I was thinking he’ll come out of this for sure. He was moving his hands and moving his eyes. He was blinking and stuff.

'Thinking back to that, I can’t remember the day that it was but the family decided that was enough. He had been through enough. So they decided to switch the machine off.'

Tyson and Paris pictured with their family ahead of the launch of At Home with the Furys 2

Tyson explained how Hughie's illness added another layer of heartbreak to an already painful period, particularly with his uncle having been a source of support throughout his boxing career.

'With Hughie I could just nip round and see him. Ask him what I should do in this fight. All the hard work building up to the fight. He missed all the best parts. I’m the one that’s got to be strong.

'I’m the one that has to pretend everything is OK. So that’s the job I took on. Protect and provide and that’s the job men should do.'

Paris admitted that neither of them was able to properly process the loss at the time, with the couple struggling to speak about what had happened.

'We didn’t really talk about what had gone on. I couldn’t talk about it. I couldn’t talk about what happened with me and the baby.

'Even now I just don’t like talking about it. We were both heartbroken. The pain you feel. You can’t imagine it’s going to go away.'

Tyson, meanwhile, revealed how he buried his emotions as he focused on preparing for the biggest challenge of his professional career.

'There was so much s**t going on, so much pain. Just putting it in the back of my mind, back of my mind, back of my mind. Not talking about it.

Tyson said he blocked all of his emotions out as he prepared to fight Wladimir Klitschko

'It was in the deepest darkest locker I could put it in and just lock it away. All those horrible instances. I just put a lock on them because I was preparing for Klitschko.'

But the emotional toll of that period would eventually catch up with the British heavyweight, who went on to produce one of the greatest performances of his career against Klitschko in November 2015 before spiralling into depression.

Travelling to Germany as the underdog, Fury stunned the boxing world by beating the long-reigning Ukrainian on points, ending his 11-year unbeaten reign and claiming the WBA, IBF and WBO heavyweight titles.

Following his triumph in Germany, Fury struggled with depression, anxiety and substance abuse.

Fury's struggles ultimately saw him relinquish his heavyweight world titles, with the boxer later returning to the ring in 2018 after battling his demons and embarking on a remarkable comeback.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury's $150m showdown vs Anthony Joshua is plunged into chaos: Boxing chiefs to assess Gypsy King's mental health... but his wife Paris insists he 'does NOT have schizophrenia' after claims in Netflix documentary
Sports.content:
The biggest money fight in British boxing history will be called off if Tyson Fury is found to be mentally unfit to do battle with Anthony Joshua, despite wife Paris' insistence late on Thursday that he does not have schizophrenia.

The British Boxing Board of Control are studying reports of the Gypsy King suffering from the condition as well as being bi-polar before giving the go-ahead for his world heavyweight title clash with AJ in Cardiff's Principality Stadium late on the Friday night of December 11.

'Only one thing is certain,' says Board general secretary Robert Smith. 'That Tyson will not be allowed to enter the ring unless our doctors are satisfied there is no risk to his health. We are reviewing all the information about his mental condition and will come to a decision about authorising the fight in the next few days.'

The fight – along with purses of more than $150million between the two combatants – has been put in jeopardy by the Netflix documentary which claims that Fury has been diagnosed with schizophrenia as well as an historic bi-polar admission.

The US television streaming giant would also be among the heavy financial losers, having invested in Fury-Joshua in expectation of attracting more than 60million subscribers to cement their move into major boxing.

Just hours after we broke the story, the Furys scrambled to salvage the situation as his wife rowed back on talk of schizophrenia. 'I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,' she said. 'I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word "schizophrenic".

'Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis. Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I’m so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we’ve received as a family.'

Tyson Fury is due to fight long-time British rival Anthony Joshua on December 11 in Cardiff

However, that $150million fight is now at risk as the the British Boxing Board of Control are studying reports of the Gypsy King suffering from schizophrenia

His wife Paris insists that he is not schizophrenic with their Netflix show to be amended

Netflix added in their statement: 'Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.'

They would not be the only ones who took a financial hit if the fight was off. The Saudi Arabian backers under His Excellency Turki Alalshikh, the Stadium itself, as well as the city of Cardiff and its South Wales surrounds would suffer.

Smith, a leader in the worldwide campaign for making boxing safer for fighters, went through a similar situation before when Fury blamed clinical depression for an adverse drugs finding.

There is no suggestion whatsoever of wrongdoing by Fury in the current situation, except perhaps shooting his own bank balance in the foot. Although the context of the documentary which focuses principally upon Fury's state of mind and the family traumas bears discussion.

This piece of work came too close for comfort to putting the words mentioning 'mild schizophrenia' into the mouth of Tyson's wife Paris. And when its director, Lucy Wilcox, was asked why the coverage of his darker hours did not extend to the loss of his previous world title to Oleksandr Usyk, who beat him twice, she admitted she had never heard of the Ukrainian war hero.

Fury, natural born performer that he is, went along with some of the more extreme takes on his mental health.

The Board's consultants will be checking if there is any proper medical evidence to support the anecdotal broadcast. Or if the allegations in the documentary are at best exaggerated or at worst sensationalised.

Persisting public doubts still linger about whether the fight for which the boxing world has waited for a decade will indeed take place in a fortnight. Despite early reports of a one-hour 80,000-plus sell-out on the day tickets went on the market, there are still hundreds of seats for sale. Some being pushed with an offer of beer being thrown in.

Which raises further concern about the impact of alcohol on the traditionally rowdy Friday night in Cardiff when the Stadium empties the crowd onto the street at around 3am. So much so that the police are considering breathalysing late arrivals at the fight.

The odds favour Fury vs Joshua going ahead. If it does, the Welsh capital will be relieved if it ends without major incident.

Sports.title: 'I thought Paris was trying to get me killed': Tyson Fury reveals the 'dark, demonic' paranoia that consumed him after schizophrenia diagnosis
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has revealed voices in his head told him to take his life, and that he thought his wife Paris was trying to kill him.

In a candid interview on The Louis Theroux Podcast, boxing star Fury, 38, said the 'voices' convinced him that those closest to him were 'setting me up to get killed'.

'I thought me dad was in on it,' Fury told Theroux. 'I thought me best friend Dave was in on it. I lost it completely, gone.'

Fury also revealed that, despite being a giant of a man, he was in such an agitated state that he had to keep the light on when sleeping.

Asked what the voices were saying, Fury said: 'The voices were telling me to kill meself. Very, very dark, demonic place I never ever wanna return to, ever.

'That was what I was living with constantly. And I thought that I would end up in a padded room and nowhere else or, or dead.

'Dead was an easy option really, but I thought I was gonna end up in a straightjacket. I was horrified of it.'

Tyson Fury has opened up on his mental health in a candid interview with Louis Theroux (Source: Netflix)

Fury and his wife Paris have been married since they were teenagers and share seven children

'The problem is what state I was in mentally,' he said of his obsessive-compulsive disorder and the condition's impact on his life. 'It got to a point where I couldn't sleep without the light on. I'd go around and check every window and door like 100 times.

'And then got to a point where I thought I was like gonna get attacked and people were gonna break into me house all the time.'

All that was left for Fury to do to pull himself out of it was to attempt to achieve 'short-term goals,' he told the podcaster.

'Whether it be weight loss, eating a certain diet, whatever,' Fury added. 'Kept myself busy and active. I kept around people.

'I couldn't be on me own, even when I was making a comeback. Even when I had my first fight back against Sefer Seferi in '18, I still couldn't sleep with the lights off. Seven foot tall world heavyweight champion has to sleep with the light on 'cause he's scared!'

The Gypsy King suffered a breakdown after achieving his life's obsession of defeating Wladimir Klitschko in 2015, during which time he suffered a bout of psychosis and began to hear voices.

It has now been revealed that Fury suffers from schizophrenia, a lifelong mental health condition that can cause an individual to have hallucinations, delusions and lose touch with reality.

The boxer has also been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety, OCD and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Paris was accused of trying to order a hit on him with his closest friends and family all involved

The Gypsy King shared that he had suffered a breakdown after his victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015

Before returning to the ring to face Sefer Seferi in 2018, Fury struggled with his mental health, addiction and his weight

Speaking on Tyson Fury, a feature-length documentary about the boxer's life and career which streams on Netflix from Friday, Tyson's wife Paris explained that upon reflection, she could always see signs that he was struggling with his mental health.

Paris, 36, said the signals were visible in their teenage years, as she recalled: 'When we were going out I saw differences in his brain pattern to other people.

'He didn't just have that level, one-tier personality. It was highs, it was lows, it was always like a different kinda person, you know?'

She explained that their differences caused issues in their marriage, saying it got off to a 'rocky' start because Tyson was obsessed with training and clean-living while she wanted to go out dancing.

'It was two worlds completely colliding,' Paris recalled. 'I couldn't understand why he would want to train, eat, sleep, repeat...

'So we were two teenagers, very young, headstrong people getting married and being put in a 24ft box caravan together.'

Fury told Theroux that the victory over Klitschko in 2015 left him feeling 'depressed' rather than elated.

'Where I should have been the happiest moment of my life, I've become world heavyweight champion, the childhood dream had happened, I was almost depressed straight away,' he said.

'Deflated, didn't care, and it was like, "Mm, I beat my man now, and that's it. There's nothing else." And it was everyone saying, "Oh, let's move the goalposts and keep going and keep doing," but it's very difficult.

'I spoke to a few people who experienced the same thing, and they called it paradise syndrome. It's where you put all your eggs in one basket, and everything you do in your life is for that one moment in time. And people make a lot of mistakes where they think I was interested in the belts or that. I only ever wanted to beat Wladimir.'

In the thick of a reflective period of his life, Fury admitted to Theroux that he had broken down multiple times after watching his documentary back.

'I thought it was brilliant,' he admitted. 'I knew what was coming, and it still made me cry.

'All of it. I cried about 15 times.'

During the latest documentary of Fury's life, Paris opens up on the challenges of his mental health crises and difficult times (Source: Netflix)

Fury is now preparing for his highly anticipated fight against his compatriot Anthony Joshua

But Fury will soon step back into the ring for his long-awaited bout against fellow British heavyweight Anthony Joshua, after almost a decade-long battle to secure the match-up.

The showdown is now booked for December 11 in Cardiff, with the most expensive general sale tickets costing £13,128 - more than top face-value prices for the 2026 Super Bowl and the World Cup ticket prices.

Fury, 38, returned to the ring in April after another retirement announcement, beating Arslanbek Makhmudov on points. The former WBC heavyweight champion has won 36 of his 39 professional contests, with two defeats and one draw.

Joshua, 36, won Olympic gold at London 2012 before becoming a two-time unified heavyweight world champion. He has recorded 30 victories, including 27 knockouts, alongside four defeats.

Sports.title: Melbourne boxer's career in turmoil after Australian Idol star exposes his vile private messages - as Anthony Mundine vows to 'teach him a lesson'
Sports.content:
Melbourne boxer Tommy Pedis has been dumped from Victoria's boxing team days before the national championships after sending vile messages to Australian Idol contestant Majeda Beatty.

Beatty went public on Monday with screenshots and a video she said the Craigieburn boxer had sent her directly.

In the video, Pedis used a racist slur, called Indigenous Australians 'petrol sniffers' and told them to 'leave our country'.

Beatty, who competed on Australian Idol in 2025, said the experience had been 'incredibly upsetting, confronting and honestly exhausting'.

'I've been riddled with anxiety today. It's one thing to experience racism, but it's another to have someone deliberately direct it towards you, continue to antagonise you and make you feel as though you're powerless to do anything about it,' she said.

'I never intended to spend my day having to defend my existence, my identity or my people. I'm proud to be Aboriginal, proud of my heritage and proud of the communities I come from. I will not be intimidated into silence or made to feel ashamed of who I am.

'Racism isn't banter, it isn't a joke and it certainly isn't something we should have to tolerate. Boxing is a sport that brings people together from all walks of life, and there should be absolutely no room for racism within it.'

Pedis claimed his remarks had been 'meant to be a joke' and acknowledged that his language was racist, saying he took full responsibility.

Melbourne boxer Tommy Pedis as been booted off the state team just days before the national championships after racist remarks he directed at a former Australian Idol contestant emerged online

He later issued an apology for the vile messages after Majeda outed him online

Majeda publicly exposed him on social media for making the vile comments

'I understand that people are disappointed and angry at me. I don't blame them,' he said.

'I can see my action, what I've done was wrong, it has hurt certain people, and in future I would not do that again.

'My comments were completely unacceptable, and I take full responsibility for what I said.

'There is no excuse for my behaviour, and I deeply regret the hurt and offence I have caused.'

On Tuesday, the VABL and ANABA suspended Pedis from all their events with immediate effect and until further notice, and dropped him from Team Victoria for the national championships.

Former world boxing champion Anthony Mundine challenged Pedis to get in the ring with him.

'This is the s*** I fought against my whole life,' Mundine said.

'Get in touch with me brah, and I'm going to teach you a lesson.

'I don't want to be a bully, but you need to be put in line.'

Sports.title: F1 Qatar GP: Antonelli remains on top in FP2 stalled by two red flags
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has swept Friday's running at Formula 1's Qatar Grand Prix in Doha after topping a second practice session that was interrupted by two red flags.

Second practice in the cooler evening conditions presented more relevant conditions ahead of Saturday's qualifying session around the same time, with the track temperatures around 10 degrees lower than the afternoon's sweltering FP1 session.

As was the case earlier, though, Mercedes still took charge of the timesheets from the start, with Russell's early effort of 1m23.715s bested b Antonelli's 1m23.077s as nearly the entire field donned medium tyres for the opening stages.

The drop in track temperatures didn't appear to make Lusail's high-downforce motorcycle circuit much easier to tame though, with Charles Leclerc suffering huge spin in the Ferrari coming out of Turn 7. Leclerc wasn't alone in his handling difficulties, with Lewis Hamilton reporting his rear was very loose, very unstable, at least one thing the two Ferrari aces can agree on.

The number of off-track excursions even prompted a red flag around the halfway mark, allowing marshals to clear the gravel that Leclerc and others had thrown onto the racing surface.

The brief stoppage formed a natural crossover point for more teams to switch to soft tyre running. Alpine's Pierre Gasly was unable to report back on those as he spun into the gravel trap at Turn 14 and ended up beached into the runoff area.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Karim Jaafar / AFP via Getty Images

With 15 more minutes on the clock when the session resumed one more time, race control decided to extend the session by 13 minutes. That allowed teams to make up for lost time, the majority pivoting to more long running on mediums rather than chasing a time on soft tyres.

In doing so, Hamilton and Max Verstappen found each other on the main straight, with Verstappen passing Hamilton as they were preparing a lap, the kind of move that drew Russell's ire so much in Las Vegas. Hamilton swiftly repassed the Dutchman and drifted towards him approaching the braking zone, much to the displeasure of the Red Bull driver. The incident was noted by race control for "driving erratically", but it didn't warrant further investigation.

The emphasis on longer runs meant Antonelli's early benchmark, which was almost matched by Russell before the first red flag, was never really threatened after that. What didn't help was a late virtual safety car for Hamilton as he appeared to suffer a power unit shutdown on his Ferrari.

As was the case in FP1, Antonelli and Russell put Mercedes on top with a four-tenth gap to McLaren's Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who were still running McLaren's older floor specification on Friday before being expected to move to the newer version on Saturday.

Verstappen and Hadjar were fifth and sixth for Red Bull, with Leclerc and Hamilton seventh and eighth one second in arrears. Continuing to run two by two, Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10 for Racing Bulls.
