Ghana News.title: Wa East records 53 development projects, achieves 99.99% revenue target
Ghana News.content:
The Wa East District Chief Executive (DCE), Adamu Sayibu, has reported significant progress in the district’s development agenda, with 53 projects initiated since June 2025, 35 of which have been completed, while the rest are at various stages of implementation.

Presenting his stewardship report to the people of Funsi, Mr Sayibu said the projects covered key sectors, including education, health, water and sanitation, central administration and road infrastructure.

He explained that 14 projects were in the education sector, 12 in health, 18 in water and sanitation, and six in central administration, while three roads had been opened up to improve access to farming communities.

Of the projects undertaken, 10 education projects, nine health projects, eight water projects and all six administration projects had been completed, with work continuing on the outstanding ones.

The DCE also highlighted the construction of Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compounds, the furnishing of schools, the provision of water facilities and the rehabilitation of key roads as some of the interventions undertaken by the Assembly to improve living conditions across the district.

In addition, two projects funded by the Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) are under construction, while work is progressing on a District Health Insurance office.

On road infrastructure, Mr Sayibu disclosed that six bridges had been constructed along the Loggu-Jeyiri-Tiisa stretch, while work was ongoing on a 37-kilometre road from Bulenga to Yaala under the government's Big Push programme.

He further announced that a rural electrification project, which had remained stalled since 2016, had been re-awarded, with work now underway to bring electricity to the beneficiary communities.

Revenue mobilisation

On the Assembly's revenue performance, the DCE reported that GH¢649,936 had been mobilised as of November 20, 2026, against a target of GH¢650,000.

The amount represents 99.99 per cent of the target, leaving a marginal shortfall of only GH¢64, a performance he described as unprecedented in the district's history.

He said the Assembly had received a total of GH¢14,739,104.65 and expended GH¢10,576,082.66, representing 71.76 per cent of its total receipts.

Government programmes

Touching on the implementation of the government's flagship programmes, Mr Sayibu said the land acquisition challenge confronting the proposed 24-hour Economy Market had been resolved, paving the way for progress on the initiative.

He also disclosed that 28 master craftsmen and their apprentices had benefited from the National Apprenticeship Programme, while allowances due Assembly members had been paid promptly on a quarterly basis.

Under the Feed Ghana programme, fertiliser had been distributed to beneficiaries, alongside support provided through the Nkoko Nkitikiti initiative.

The DCE further said Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) had benefited from assistance through the five per cent allocation of the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF).

He said the allocation had consistently been disbursed to support beneficiaries in various areas, including business development, education, healthcare and farming, to improve their livelihoods and economic independence.

Funsi SHS disturbances

Mr Sayibu also addressed the recent disturbances at Funsi Senior High School, which were triggered by electricity supply problems in the boys' dormitory, inadequate water supply and delays in relocating female students to their newly constructed dormitory.

He said normalcy had since returned to the school following the restoration of electricity to the boys' dormitory.

Work is also underway to connect the new girls' dormitory to the electricity supply to enable the students to move out of the administration block, where they are currently accommodated.

However, he acknowledged that the persistent water shortage at the school remained a major concern and appealed to the Upper West Regional Minister and relevant sector institutions to assist in finding a lasting solution to the problem.

Appeal for more infrastructure

The DCE expressed appreciation to President John Dramani Mahama for including Wa East in the government's Big Push programme, describing the intervention as an important step towards addressing the district's road infrastructure needs.

He appealed to the government to extend the initiative to other critical roads in the district under its second phase to improve transportation, facilitate trade and enhance access to essential services.

He also called for the speedy completion of the Agenda 111 hospital, the upgrading of the Bulenga Health Centre to polyclinic status and the construction of roads within Funsi township.

Other priorities he outlined included improved road links to market centres and the extension of electricity to newly established communities to support economic activities and improve living conditions.

Despite the progress outlined in his report, Mr Sayibu acknowledged that Wa East continued to grapple with significant development challenges, particularly poor road networks, inadequate access to potable water and limited access to educational and healthcare facilities.

He said addressing the challenges would require sustained collaboration between the government, traditional authorities, local communities and other stakeholders.

Emphasising the importance of a peaceful environment in advancing the district's development agenda, the DCE urged chiefs, opinion leaders and the youth to promote dialogue, mutual respect and tolerance.

“Development can only thrive in an atmosphere of peace and unity,” he said.

Ghana News.title: CSOs reject five-year presidential term, demand changes to MMDCE election proposal
Ghana News.content:
Civil society organisations (CSOs) have rejected the proposed extension of Ghana’s presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years, while demanding changes to government proposals on the election of Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs).

The groups argue that the existing four-year mandate, which allows a President to seek re-election for a second term, is sufficient for elected officials to implement their governance programmes.

They also insist that citizens must be allowed to elect their local government leaders without presidential interference.

The positions emerged from a two-day engagement between the Constitutional Reform Implementation Committee (CREC) and more than 100 civil society organisations as part of efforts to build consensus on proposed amendments to Ghana’s 1992 Constitution.

The Executive Secretary of the Committee, Oliver Barker-Vormawor, said the engagement had made significant progress, with civil society organisations agreeing with approximately 89 per cent of the government’s proposed reforms.

“Over the past two days we've been engaging with over a hundred civil society organizations to build consensus around some of the packet of reforms. We're at a stage where civil society is coming out with resolutions on some of the things that they agree with,” he said.

“So many of the other issues, I think that about 89% of what the government is proposing, civil society organizations are agreed with that, and so we have made significant headway.”

Mr Barker-Vormawor said the discussions had also helped reduce the number of outstanding issues from an initial 41 to 10.

He explained that the Committee had been engaging stakeholders to identify areas of agreement and disagreement, with unresolved matters to be referred to Cabinet for possible reconsideration.

“Now the issues on which we are not able to reach some consensus, in particular the question of the four or five-year term, for instance the demand for MPs not to be ministers, those questions we have a mandate to refer back to Cabinet, because the decision-maker is Cabinet, for Cabinet then to revisit its positions on those issues,” he said.

He stressed that the Committee's responsibility was to accurately communicate the concerns raised by stakeholders rather than independently alter the government's position.

“Our understanding is that the document is a Cabinet position, which then means that for changes to happen, Cabinet has to reconsider,” he added.

The proposed extension of the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years remains one of the major contentious issues in the reform discussions.

Koku Anyidoho, an adviser to the General Secretary of the Christian Council of Ghana, said the participating groups were united in opposing the proposal.

He said 18 position papers had been presented during the two-day engagement, with stakeholders reaching broad agreement on several issues.

“Two specific issues that come up is the fact that, to a man, that is every grouping here gathered, does not accept the government position on increasing the term limits of the President from four years to five years. Same as the MPs,” he said.

Mr Anyidoho argued that the existing arrangement, which allows a President to seek a second four-year term, provides sufficient time to implement a governance agenda.

“They believe that within the four-year space, it should be possible to carry out a governance agenda that will sit well. The person gets four years, gets another four years, that's eight years. It looks like the consensus is that that is enough,” he stated.

The Head of Programmes at Star Ghana Foundation and co-convener of the Citizens Platform on Constitutional Reforms, Eunice Rachel Agbenyadzi, also said maintaining the four-year presidential term was among the positions supported by stakeholders.

She explained that the Constitution Review Commission had proposed a five-year presidential term, which the government endorsed but other political parties rejected.

“One of the things is maintain the presidential term at four years,” she said.

MMDCE elections

The proposed election of MMDCEs also featured prominently in the discussions, with stakeholders supporting direct elections but raising concerns about the government's proposed arrangements.

Mr Anyidoho explained that although the government's position paper agrees with the Constitution Review Commission's recommendation for the election of MMDCEs, it proposes a process that would allow the President to nominate candidates.

He said the proposal initially provided for five presidential nominees, a number that was subsequently reduced to three, from whom one person would be elected.

However, civil society organisations want the President completely removed from the process.

“The government position paper was like, okay, there will be election, but whoever is President will nominate five persons. It's watered down to three, and then one is voted for,” he explained.

“Of course, a cross-board consensus has been built that no, the presidency or the President of central government should have no hand in that election process, and that for our decentralization and local governance process to really have greater roots, let's allow the base to elect their own MMDCEs,” he added.

Ms Agbenyadzi said the groups believe direct elections would make local government leaders more accountable to the people they serve.

She, however, noted that discussions were still ongoing over whether the elections should be conducted on a partisan or non-partisan basis.

“There is consensus that there should be election. Now what we need to figure out is whether it should be on a partisan basis, which some of the parties hold views on,” she said.

She also said civil society organisations had rejected the government's proposal to introduce a nomination process for the elections, insisting that there should be no restrictions or filters on who can contest.

MPs as ministers

Another major issue is whether Members of Parliament should continue to be appointed as ministers.

Ms Agbenyadzi said citizens were concerned that allowing MPs to serve in ministerial positions could weaken Parliament's ability to effectively perform its oversight responsibilities.

She said the government's position was to retain discretion over the number of MPs the President could appoint as ministers, but civil society organisations were advocating a stricter separation of powers.

“This is a very sensitive issue. Citizens are saying no, because we believe that a strong Parliament delivers good governance for Ghana,” she said.

“The point is that the government says, give us discretion. Don't restrict that in terms of how many MPs can be appointed as ministers, but the consensus here is that there should be strict separation of powers,” she added.

Mr Barker-Vormawor confirmed that the appointment of MPs as ministers was among the issues on which stakeholders had not reached consensus and which the Committee intended to refer to Cabinet.

Proportional representation

The introduction of proportional representation in Ghana's electoral system is another issue under consideration.

Ms Agbenyadzi said the proposal was intended to address the inadequate representation of groups such as women, young people and persons with disabilities in governance.

She explained that the Constitution Review Commission recommended that the country consider introducing the system following a study to determine how it could be implemented.

However, the government has proposed beginning with a pilot involving 24 parliamentary seats.

“The evidence shows clearly that there are certain groups like women, young people, persons with disabilities that are not well represented in governance,” she said.

She added that stakeholders believed the proposal should be approached carefully, with further assessment of how the system would work.

Mr Barker-Vormawor also pointed to other proposals under consideration, including ending the payment of ex gratia, introducing a binding national development plan, requiring the President to pay tax and directly electing district chief executives.

He said the ultimate decision on proposals requiring a referendum would rest with the Ghanaian electorate.

“A hundred civil society organisations and a constitutional committee can agree, but the people of Ghana will go and say no. Our job is that they understand what they are going to vote for and then they express their view,” he said.

CSOs call for broader consultations

The renewed engagement has also been welcomed by civil society organisations, which say the process must remain open to different stakeholder perspectives.

Ms Agbenyadzi said the Citizens Platform on Constitutional Reforms, convened by Star Ghana Foundation, the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD) and Democracy Hub, had spent the past two years building public understanding and momentum around the reform process.

She said one of the concerns raised by the platform following the government's position paper and the inauguration of CREC was the need to clarify the Committee's mandate, particularly its responsibility to build consensus beyond the government's proposals.

According to her, the Committee had since become more receptive to position papers and recommendations from other groups.

“We really, really think that this is progressive because we believe that it offers us the opportunity to build this constitutional reform process as a national project where different stakeholders' inputs are recognized and are honored, even when we cannot agree on everything,” she said.

She said stakeholders had agreed that the Committee should continue engaging civil society organisations through further dialogue, meetings and the submission of memoranda.

She also called for dedicated engagement with the New Patriotic Party (NPP), describing it as a critical stakeholder whose views must be considered to ensure that all political interests were represented in the process.

Mr Anyidoho said the renewed consultations were important, particularly after concerns that the consultative process had ended.

He welcomed the Committee's decision to reopen discussions and create opportunities for more groups to participate.

“Without building consensus and engaging in a process that has a lot of integrity, then it creates a lot of challenges,” he said.

Public education crucial to referendum

Beyond reaching agreement on the proposed amendments, stakeholders say public education will be crucial, particularly for changes to entrenched provisions of the Constitution.

Mr Anyidoho warned that inadequate civic education could undermine the entire reform process, as the Constitution requires significant voter participation and support for entrenched amendments to be approved.

He explained that at least 40 per cent of registered voters must participate in the referendum, with 75 per cent of those voting required to support the proposed amendments.

“Until you get good civic education, good public engagement, you're not going to get the buying, and the numbers are there on the voters register. Once we finish voting, we don't have the numbers. Then it derails the whole process,” he said.

He called for coordinated public education to help citizens understand the proposed changes and appreciate their importance before the referendum.

Mr Barker-Vormawor also emphasised that the people of Ghana would ultimately determine whether the proposals requiring a referendum should be adopted.

He noted that while non-entrenched amendments would go through Parliament, the House would have to undertake its own deliberations and secure the required two-thirds majority.

“We are not looking for Parliament to settle all disagreements before the bill is laid. Parliament is a deliberative body, they are going to deliberate on them, convince people to vote or not vote,” he said.

He added that previous constitutional amendment bills had failed to secure the required parliamentary support, underscoring the need for consensus-building within the House.

The engagement ended with stakeholders expressing support for continued consultations and public education as the Committee prepares to present outstanding issues to Cabinet.

With 10 issues still requiring further consideration, the next stage of the process will depend on the government's response to the concerns raised and whether the emerging consensus can be sustained through the parliamentary and referendum stages.

Ghana News.title: RON Foundation invests in digital education at Atwima Koforidua with modern ICT lab commissioning
Ghana News.content:
A philanthropic organization, RON Foundation, has cut the sod for the construction of a modern Information and Communication Technology (ICT) laboratory at Atwima Koforidua in the Ashanti Region to boost digital and Artificial Intelligence (AI) education among pupils in the area.

The project, with an estimated cost of GH¢750,000, is anticipated to be completed within a period of nine to twelve months, and is expected to be equipped with 32 computers as well as a printer, scanner and photocopier.

The laboratory, which will accommodate computers for 30 pupils and two others for supervisors, will have networking infrastructure and appropriate furniture, among other essential learning accessories.

Speaking at the sod-cutting ceremony, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation, Ing. Richard Okyere Nketia, said the initiative forms part of his commitment to bridging the digital divide and promoting quality education in the Atwima Nwabiagya North District.

He stressed that early exposure to digital learning is key, noting that children who are introduced to technology at a young age are better positioned to compete in a global economy that is increasingly driven by innovation, data and digital tools.

According to him, the centre would equip pupils of his alma mater with AI knowledge, technology and IT skills, which he described as critical to development in the modern world.

"My decision to fund the ICT centre was born out of my personal connection to the town and concern about the poor state of infrastructure at my former school, Atwima Koforidua D/A Basic School," he said.

The Ghanaian civil and structural engineer is positive that the facility, when completed, would not only transform teaching and learning at the school but also open opportunities for the wider Atwima Koforidua community to acquire digital skills.

"Our vision is to create a facility where technology becomes an everyday learning tool rather than a privilege available only to children in well-resourced schools. We are not just building an ICT centre; we are building access, opportunity, and a brighter future for our children," he stated.

Beyond the Koforidua project, the RON Foundation CEO encouraged collective participation in national development.

Ing. Nketia said nation-building should not be left to government alone, stressing that individuals who have benefited from the country have a duty to give back to society.

He urged people who have risen through education and opportunity in Ghana to remember the communities that shaped them and to return to support the next generation.

"If everyone does a little in their own hometown, the whole country will move forward," he said. "I will therefore appeal to Ghanaians in the diaspora, old students, philanthropists, churches, corporate bodies and other well-meaning individuals to invest in their hometowns' development."

The School Improvement Support Officer (SISO) for the Akropong Circuit of the Atwima Nwabiagya North Education Directorate, Mr. Steven Anim Adu, described the ultra-modern ICT laboratory project as a major boost to teaching and learning.

He explained that many pupils in various basic schools in the district do not have direct access to computers and therefore learn ICT largely in theory, which limits their practical understanding of the subject.

"Direct access to computers will give our schoolchildren the practical aspect of computing. When they have constant contact with computers, it will help them learn better and improve education in the school," he said.

Mr. Anim Adu commended Ing. Richard Okyere Nketia and his foundation for the project.

This intervention comes at a time when Ghana is pushing to deepen digital literacy from the basic school level, with ICT now a core subject at the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) level and a growing national conversation about AI, coding and STEM education.

For many rural and peri-urban basic schools, however, access remains a major challenge. Pupils often learn ICT largely in theory, without computers to practise on, a situation that affects their confidence, performance and interest in technology-related careers.

The new centre at Atwima Koforidua is therefore expected to bridge that gap, giving pupils the opportunity to learn through hands-on practice, rather than theoretical learning.

Ghana News.title: Galamsey, erratic weather cause unprecedented decline in Ghana’s cocoa production – Kuapa Kokoo MD
Ghana News.content:
Concerns over the future of Ghana's cocoa industry are growing, as farmers warn that the destruction of forest reserves, illegal mining and changing climate patterns could further undermine cocoa production.

The activities of illegal miners, popularly known as galamsey and chainsaw operators are not only destroying forest cover but also polluting water bodies and threatening the survival of cocoa farms in several farming communities across the country.

The concerns dominated discussions at the 32nd Annual Delegates Conference of Kuapa Kokoo Farmers, held under the theme "Protecting Our Forest, Securing Our Future."

Addressing the conference, the Managing Director of Kuapa Kokoo, Emmanuel Kwabena Arthur, raised serious concerns about the low cocoa production recorded this year, describing the current situation as unprecedented.

"First of all, we have a problem with production itself. For the first time, as far as I am concerned, at the peak of the season, we don't have a lot of cocoa available, and that is unprecedented," he said.

He noted that with the season approaching the end of November, cocoa production should be very high, but the situation on the ground tells a different story.

"Around this time, as we get to the end of November, cocoa production should be very high, but when you go to the bush and you see the trees, the kind of pods you see on the trees is not encouraging," he added.

Mr. Arthur said many cocoa farms have been abandoned and taken over by galamsey operators, reducing the total hectares of land available for cocoa production.

According to him, illegal mining activities have also polluted river bodies, leaving farmers without clean water to irrigate their farms and to mix pesticides and insecticides to treat their cocoa.

"Farmers don't get clean water to water their farms and to also get clean water for their pesticides and insecticides to actually treat the cocoa. All these things are affecting cocoa production," he said.

Touching on other factors contributing to the low cocoa production, he pointed to changing climate patterns.

According to him, it had disrupted rainfall distribution and affected flowering and pod formation on cocoa trees.

He explained that the erratic weather conditions is making it difficult for farmers to predict planting and farm maintenance schedules, further worsening the already declining output from cocoa farms across the country.

Mr. Arthur warned that production for the season could fall further below expectations, contrary to earlier projections by the Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD).

"COCOBOD has even projected that there will be less produce this year than we got last year, but I believe that if we are not careful, the production level will be very low, lower than what we actually expect," he said.

The Kuapa Kokoo Managing Director is urging government to strengthen the fight against illegal mining and chainsaw operations, particularly in forest reserves and cocoa-growing communities, to protect the country's cocoa industry and secure the future of farmers.

Meanwhile, the National President of the Kuapa Kokoo Farmers Cocoa Cooperative and Marketing Union, James Agyekum Kwarteng, has expressed deep concern over the declining interest of the youth in agriculture, particularly in the cocoa sector.

According to him, the situation is becoming alarming as most of the cocoa farmers currently engaged in production are aged.

He revealed that such a development poses a serious threat to the future sustainability of cocoa production in the country if nothing is done to address it.

He also called on the government to introduce deliberate policies and interventions to support young people in the agricultural sector.

Mr. Agyekum Kwarteng is of the view that such measures would help motivate other youngsters to venture into farming and ensure the continuity of cocoa production for generations to come.

The conference brought together delegates, farmers, management and stakeholders from across the Union's operational areas to review its performance, discuss challenges facing cocoa farmers and chart a way forward for sustainable cocoa production.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths
World.content:
Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.

Share Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths on social media

A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.

Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.

Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.

Earlier convictions

On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.

He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.

The Shakahola deaths

Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.

He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.

Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies. People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases: children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.

Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.



Calls for oversight

The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.

President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.

Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

World.title: US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade
World.content:
The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.

Share US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade on social media

The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.

Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.

US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.

The claims could not be independently verified.

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said on Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations “that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters”.

American blockade action

The US military has maintained a sizeable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.



American ships have been blockading Iranian ports since April, although the blockade was temporarily lifted during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabled those that refuse to comply.

CENTCOM, which has its headquarters in Florida, has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.

World.title: Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
World.content:
Flour and oil still reach markets in Hodeidah and Sanaa. But rising costs, scarce work and loss of food aid put them out of reach.

Share Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale? on social media

Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and takes on occasional domestic work to feed her family. Rising prices have changed how she shops. “Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera.

Food is still on the shelves. It was available in the markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment. Across Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent, or $91, more that month than in August, its highest level in a year.

Families on both sides of the front lines are struggling, and prices are rising faster in the government-held south, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). What sets the Houthi-controlled north apart is how little families there can earn and how little help is left.

Most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work a month, FEWS NET reported in October. The UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025, FEWS NET said. By mid-September 2026, WFP had begun a distribution round in government-held areas that aimed to reach about 1.7 million people.

In the last nationwide hunger analysis by UN agencies and their partners, published in mid-2025, the only people projected to face catastrophic hunger, about 41,000, were in four districts of Amran, Hodeidah and Hajjah governorates – all under Houthi control.

On Friday, the WFP and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) named Yemen among its hunger hotspots of highest concern for the six months ending May 2027.



As fighting spreads and aid dries up, we look at why food on sale in northern Yemen is slipping out of reach of the families who need it.

Why are some families in Hodeidah buying food one day at a time?

Because a day’s work – when there is any – no longer pays for a day’s food.

Ahmed Arjash drives a rented motorcycle taxi near Hodeidah’s Othman market to support his family of six. Many of his former customers now walk to save the fare. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle,” he told Al Jazeera.

Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said some days pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said.

Fishing pays less, too. Salem, a fisherman in his 30s, said fuel, boats and equipment cost him more while fewer customers could afford his catch. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to,” he said. On some trips, he barely earns back what it costs to go to sea.

Families are adjusting by eating less. In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, many skip meals or go without meat, fish, milk and fruit, Al Jazeera found.

In Houthi-held areas, FEWS NET reported that higher taxes on street vendors and shops had already reduced demand for labour in September. In its outlook through May 2027, it expected more small businesses to close and those that stayed open to hire fewer workers.

How does food reach shops in northern Yemen, and what makes the journey more expensive?

Almost all of it comes by sea, and each step from ship to shop now costs more. Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to WFP. Hodeidah is the main port supplying the Houthi-held north, including Sanaa.

Food has kept arriving – data shows imports into Houthi-held areas rose 10 percent between June and August compared with the previous three months and doubled year-on-year – but fuel has not.

Fuel imports fell about 85 percent year-on-year in August, with no recorded arrivals of diesel or petrol through northern ports, according to the FAO. In September, the Houthi authorities raised the price of petrol by about 10 percent, the first increase in four years, Al Jazeera reported. Bread prices in Houthi-held areas rose 25 percent that month, FEWS NET said.

The ports themselves have come under attack. On November 2, the Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said Saudi aircraft had hit a pier and a commercial ship at Ras Isa port, north of Hodeidah, the news agency AFP reported. On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in Hodeidah, and the Houthis threatened to retaliate against Saudi Red Sea ports. Hodeidah port remains open, Al Jazeera reported. How the latest attacks will affect deliveries remains unclear.



Moving goods inland has also become slower and costlier. A truck travelling between the south and the north “now takes up to a week to reach its final destination”, Saleh Abdullah, a shopkeeper in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera in September. Before the renewed fighting, the trip took three days or less. Customers pay the extra transport and fuel costs, he said. “Whether it is the flour, the baby milk, the fruits, the vegetables, or anything else.”

When families cannot afford food, what stops aid from reaching them?

In the north, the main source of food aid has been switched off. WFP suspended its activities in Houthi-controlled areas in September 2025 after the group detained UN staff. Last month, WFP said 73 UN personnel, 38 of them its own staff, remained in detention.

Other aid organisations still operate in the north, but funding cuts and restrictions limit their reach.

On Thursday, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said a handful of overstretched and underfunded Yemeni and international organisations were the only remaining lifeline for millions there.

Funding cuts, sanctions and the UN’s pause in operations had all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, it added. The NRC said donors had provided just 16 percent of the money sought for food security across Yemen this year.

What does the UN’s new hunger warning tell us about northern Yemen?

The latest FAO–WFP report warns that fighting and economic hardship threaten to deepen hunger through May 2027. It names economic hardship among the threats, but it cannot say how many people in the north are going hungry. FAO and WFP said conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather drove the risk in the five hotspots of highest concern, the Reuters news agency reported.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the UN-backed system for measuring hunger, has not published a recent analysis of Houthi-held areas. Its latest figures – 5.4 million people facing crisis levels of hunger or worse between October and December, including 1.8 million at the more severe emergency level – cover government-held areas only.

In June 2025, the IPC projected that 18.1 million people in Yemen would face crisis levels of hunger or worse between September 2025 and February 2026. That was 52 percent of the population covered by the nationwide analysis.

FEWS NET expects emergency levels of hunger to persist in Hodeidah and Hajjah through May 2027.

At that level, families face large gaps in what they eat, or must sell what they need to make a living to buy food. The network’s gravest warning concerns Taiz, a government-held city besieged by Houthi forces, where it sees a credible risk of famine between February and May if the siege is prolonged and tightened.

In Hodeidah, the market still has flour. For families like Umm Sami’s, the question is how little of it they can afford. “Even bread has become a burden,” she said.

World.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
World.content:
Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.

The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.

“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.

The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.

An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado shook up Venezuelan politics with her surprise return from exile last month. Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 to take on Maduro in the following year’s election, but she was legally barred from running. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election, despite her exclusion from transition talks.



Despite being shut out, on Thursday Machado launched a system of neighbourhood assemblies aiming to gather proposals for a future government programme and democratic transition. The assemblies are expected to bring together over a million people over several months, according to Machado’s team.

“We listened to neighbours who are breaking down barriers that many thought were impossible, debating the issues that will lay the foundations for the Venezuela to come,” Machado said on social media on Thursday after the meetings. “We are designing the transition to democracy, the Venezuelan way.”

Around 2,000 meetings with residents were organised in Venezuela and abroad on the first day of the initiative, her team told the AFP news agency.

Nineteen questions are asked during the assembly, with responses fed into a digital platform. Issues of national interest range from dates for the presidential election to changes in the justice, education, health, wage and pension systems, as well as the role of the public and private sectors.

World.title: OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets as AI race heats up
World.content:
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition.

OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.

OpenAI is developing artificial intelligence-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf,” the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware products.

“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.

Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.

In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former employees, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations.

The litigation sets up a battle over who will control future AI devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of its own.



In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticised Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs.

OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.

OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

World.title: Putin unveils new Russian nuclear-powered submarine with hypersonic weapons
World.content:
The Kremlin plans to expand its naval fleet with five new nuclear submarines by 2030.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.

The Russians say they will add five more nuclear submarines to the country’s fleet by 2030.

Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm at the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk on Friday, marking the submarine’s formal transfer to the navy, according to video released by the Kremlin.

“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” he said.

Nuclear-powered subs are a key part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.

Putin said the navy will receive five more submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class, the same as the Perm. They can operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.

Putin also stated that Russia intends to continue modernising its navy and expressed confidence that all plans to build a powerful naval force will be implemented in full and on time.

World.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
World.content:
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, SÃ¡nchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

SÃ¡nchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

FeijÃ³o sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, AragÃ³n, and Castilla y LeÃ³n.

FeijÃ³o has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by SÃ¡nchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

World.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

World.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
World.content:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

World.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
World.content:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

World.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
World.content:
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.

The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (Â£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

World.title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
World.content:
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

World.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
World.content:
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

Regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

World.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
World.content:
