In a lecture titled “AAPSCOMMS and the Imperatives of Complementary Initiatives, Strategic Adaption and Peer Learning”, Olaopa provided what he considered a guideline for

the institutional reform of AAPSCOMMS as a community of practice set to heighten the constitutional mandate of preserving the vocational strength of the civil service system across Africa.

According to him, such reform would entail striving to maintain the institutional parameters of professionalism and independence that stand CSCs out for their mandate.

“The complementary initiatives to back all these responsibilities up lay elsewhere in those strategic shifts that consolidate its operational mandates”, he said.

He stressed the urgent need for AAPSCOMMS, as a formidable continental administrative hub, to start an incremental expansion of its operational visibility in ways that transcend its traditional Anglophone sphere.

This, to him, would entail overcoming a language, ideological and administrative divide that separates the English-speaking from the French-, Arab-, and Portuguese-speaking regions and contexts as these regions constitute entire administrative contexts that cannot be left out of sight.

“And this is not just in terms of membership mobilization but even more fundamentally to transform the experience of peer review and peer learning. Befriending them and initiating longstanding relationships with their CSCs also make AAPSCOMMS’ projects more attractive to funders interested in pan-African administrative relations”, he said.

Olaopa urged AAPSCOMMS to extend its significance away from periodic meetings and conferences to moderating continuous practice and sustained seminal engagements. He said that this move would involve setting up mechanisms of practice, like building a digital library as a repository of shared continental knowledge in terms of capability frameworks, performance dynamics, ethics, recruitment and appointment standards, and so on.

For Olaopa, there is also the need for AAPSCOMMS to take the lead in initiating crucial brainstorming on emerging technologies, digital transformation and comparative data sharing and others that affect the enabling of citizen-friendly and citizen-facing civil service operations and ultimately improve engagement, transparency and participation, as well as pushing shared insights on e-recruitment and personnel record.

Olaopa also stressed the need for AAPSCOMMS to play the very cogent role of leading the debate on ethical AI guidelines that the CSCs on the continent can all agree with.

“This should be complemented by the necessity of, on the one hand, helping CSCs on the continent to build resilient and capable institutions and structures, and on the other hand, establishing mechanisms that track measurable outcomes across the continent”, he said.

World.title: HURIWA Names DSS DG Ajayi Human Rights Man of ‘The Year 2026,’ Applauds His Institutional Reforms
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Human Rights Writers Association of Nigeria (HURIWA) has announced the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi, as its Human Rights Man of the Year 2026.

The civil society organisation (CSO) also applauded Ajayi for introducing institutional reforms, improving professionalism and promoting greater respect for human rights since assuming leadership of the nation’s intelligence service.

According to a statement by HURIWA’s National Coordinator, Comrade Emmanuel Nnadozie Onwubiko, the nomination recognises Ajayi’s leadership, institutional reforms and demonstrated commitment to promoting greater respect for human rights, accountability and professionalism within Nigeria’s intelligence community.

Onwubiko explained that the recognition was also intended to encourage public officials and security institutions to embrace reforms that place human dignity, accountability, justice and the protection of citizens’ fundamental rights at the centre of governance.

He further disclosed that the certificate of award would be formally presented to the DSS Director-General on 10 December 2026, during the association’s Human Rights Festival, organised to commemorate the 2026 International Human Rights Day in Abuja.

Onwubiko urged the Director-General to sustain the momentum of the reforms, deepen institutional accountability and ensure that respect for fundamental human rights remained an integral part of the service’s operational philosophy.

The association maintained that the success of an intelligence institution should be measured not only by its effectiveness in protecting national security but also by its commitment to safeguarding the rights, freedoms and dignity of the citizens it serves.

HURIWA congratulated Ajayi on the nomination and encouraged other public institutions to embrace reforms that strengthen democratic governance, accountability and respect for human rights.

The association also commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for appointing one of the most competent and thoroughly professional officers to head the DSS at this critical time.

Onwubiko stressed that Ajayi had demonstrated that effective intelligence gathering and national security operations could coexist with respect for fundamental human rights, the rule of law and human dignity.

He applauded his efforts to review inherited security watchlists, address cases of prolonged detention, resolve wrongful restrictions imposed on individuals and introduce greater accountability into the operations of the service.

HURIWA also acknowledged the DSS leadership’s interventions in cases involving mistaken identity, wrongful detention and operational errors, including the release of individuals whose continued detention could no longer be justified and the payment of compensation to persons affected by wrongful security actions.

The association said these measures represented important steps towards transforming the DSS into a more accountable, professional and human rights-conscious intelligence institution.

HURIWA observed that intelligence agencies had enormous responsibilities in protecting national security but insisted that such responsibilities must never override the constitutional rights and dignity of citizens.

The CSO urged Ajayi to consolidate the reforms, strengthen internal accountability mechanisms and institutionalise respect for human rights across the service.

World.title: Constituent Sues INEC, Guardian Newspaper over Senator Adeola’s Credentials
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Alex Enumah in Abuja

An indigene of Yewa Land in Ogun, Mr Ayansiji Omoniyi, has prayed the Federal High Court, Abuja, for an order seeking to compel the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and Guardian Newspapers Limited to release Certified True Copy (CTC) of documents, credentials and forms submitted to them by Senator Solomon Adeola.

Omoniyi, who is suing for himself and on behalf of concerned members of Yewa Land, is specifically seeking an order, granting him permission to apply for an order of mandamus compelling INEC and Guardian to release to him, the CTC “of the documents, credentials, and forms of Senator Solomon Adeola which is currently within each respondent’s custody.”

The applicant in the suit filed through his team of lawyers, led by Oluseyi Oyagbile, is also seeking another order of the court, deeming the already filed motion on notice as being properly and legally filed.

Adeola, popularly called, Yayi, is the current senator representing Ogun West Senatorial District at the National Assembly, and governorship candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in next year’s general elections.

The applicant named INEC and Guardian Newspapers Limited as 1st and 2nd respondents in the suit, marked: FHC/ABJ/C’S/2883/2026, and filed on November 24.

Omoniyi, in his 13-ground argument, averred that by a letter, he applied for the CTCs of the 2015 and 2023 documents, credentials, and forms and other documents of Senator Adeola which are currently within the respondents’ custody.

He stated that he is currently among the constituents being represented by the lawmaker in the Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

The applicant said he had cause to suspect that Adeola gave incorrect information to the respondents in his bid to become a senator of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

Omoniyi said he is proposing to file a suit to enforce his right to qualitative representation in the Senate.

He said he requires access to the information in the custody of each respondent to establish critical factual assertions in the said impending lawsuit which he is proposing to institute.

He described INEC, the 1st respondent, as the statutory custodian of all information about all candidates to electoral offices in Nigeria, while the 2nd respondent, Guardian Newspapers Limited, was a former employer to the Senator.

Omoniyi further averred that he made a formal request to the respondents for the certified true copies of the said information, but the respondents failed, refused, or neglected to release them.

“In spite of the receipt of the application for certified true copies of the said information, the respondents failed or refused to release the said information to the applicant,” he said.

He said in the consequence of the failure of each respondent to perform its public duty of releasing copies of any information applied for, he filed the application for leave to apply by way of judicial review for an order of mandamus.

The applicant argued that the information applied for is necessary for a fair, just, and expeditious determination of the issues in an impending lawsuit to be instituted by him.

He also contended that the refusal to release the information violated his right to a fair hearing and access to vital evidentiary documents.

He maintained that the court has the power to compel the respondents to release the certified true copies of the required information to him, and that he needs the leave of the court to apply for an order of mandamus.

No date has been fixed for hearing of the ex-parte application as of the time of filing this report.

Also, in a letter dated November 25, 2026, and addressed to the Guardian Newspapers Limited, Omoniyi had requested for the records of Adeola when he was an employee of the firm.

The letter is titled: “Application for the Staff Records of Distinguished Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola” reads: “I, Ayansiji A. Omoniyi, a Nigerian, hereby request your office to kindly supply me with the staff records of one of your former staff members, including the circumstances of his exit from the company.

“The said former staff member is now the Senator representing Ogun West Senatorial District in the Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

“This request is made pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, 2011.”

“

World.title: FG Unveils Sweeping Education Reforms
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

* Highlights N379bn student loan disbursement, 2.8m TVET applications



Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

The Federal Government has unveiled a series of far-reaching reforms and investments aimed at transforming Nigeria’s education sector, with particular emphasis on skills development, teacher professionalism, digital learning, student financing and infrastructure expansion. The Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, disclosed this on Thursday at the ministerial session of the 70th National Council on Education (NCE) meeting in Maiduguri, Borno State. Alausa said the interventions, being implemented under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda, were designed to expand access to quality education, strengthen teaching standards, bridge skills gaps and improve learning outcomes across the country. Highlighting the Federal Government’s achievements, the minister disclosed that the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) had processed approximately 2.65 million applications, with about N379 billion disbursed to support students pursuing higher education. He also revealed that the Federal Government’s Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) programme had attracted more than 2.8 million applications, reflecting growing interest in vocational and technical skills acquisition. On teacher development, Alausa said more than 80,000 teachers were undergoing certification and licensing through the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN), with the government targeting 75 per cent teacher certification by the end of 2027 and the certification of all senior secondary school teachers by 2028. The minister further highlighted major investments in tertiary education, including N55 billion for medical education infrastructure, N150 billion for tertiary institution revitalisation and N32 billion for needs-assessment projects in public colleges of education. He added that N39 billion had been released to 166 public tertiary institutions under the Needs Assessment programme. On basic education, Alausa cited the $532 million HOPE for Basic Education programme, alongside the expansion of the Adolescent Girls’ Learning and Empowerment Project from 18 to 21 states, as part of efforts to improve access to education for vulnerable, displaced and disadvantaged children. He also disclosed that the government was expanding digital learning through the installation of 34 solar mini-grids in tertiary institutions, plans to provide independent solar power to all federal tertiary institutions by 2028 and the allocation of more than N11 billion for digital skills development. According to him, over 40,000 geo-located schools have also been integrated into digital education management systems to strengthen planning, monitoring and school safety, while approved educational platforms are benefiting from zero-rated internet access. Alausa commended the Borno State Government for its remarkable progress in education, particularly the increase in school enrolment from approximately 770,000 learners in 2018 to about 1.8 million. He attributed the development to purposeful leadership, investments in school infrastructure, improved security and the resilience of the people. The minister also praised the quality of public school facilities inspected during his visit to the state, noting that some compared favourably with private schools. He urged members of the National Council on Education to ensure that deliberations translated into concrete improvements in the sector, stressing that infrastructure development must be accompanied by teacher welfare, professional development, accountability and improved learning standards. In his remarks, Borno State Governor, Babagana Umara Zulum, commended the Federal Government’s education reforms, particularly the initiatives aimed at expanding access to higher education, improving teachers’ welfare and addressing the disconnect between graduates’ qualifications and labour-market demands. Zulum stressed the importance of strengthening collaboration between educational institutions and industries, noting that technical and vocational education would equip young Nigerians with relevant skills, improve employability and reduce unemployment. He also praised NELFUND for providing financial opportunities to students who might otherwise struggle to access higher education. The governor disclosed that his administration was establishing 27 high-skilled colleges across the state, with 15 already completed and the remaining facilities expected to be completed before the end of the year. He explained that the institutions would promote skills acquisition and create pathways linking non-formal education with the formal education system through literacy, numeracy, digital learning and other specialised programmes. Zulum reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to expanding educational infrastructure, recruiting teachers, improving their welfare and providing incentives to encourage excellence in the teaching profession.

World.title: Julius Malema wins court battle against Helen Zille
World.content:
EFF leader Julius Malema has secured an interim court interdict against the DA’s Helen Zille, who previously refused to retract her allegations against him. Images: X

EFF leader Julius Malema has secured an interim interdict against the DA’s Helen Zille over allegations she made about his involvement in Johannesburg’s affairs during Herman Mashaba’s previous tenure as mayor.

The Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg ruled in favour of Malema and the EFF on Friday, 27 November.

The ruling came on the same day that Zille lost the Johannesburg mayoral race to Mashaba.



COURT BARS ZILLE FROM REPEATING MALEMA ALLEGATIONS

The dispute stems from an eNCA interview on Sunday, 8 November, during which Zille accused Malema of influencing municipal decisions while Mashaba served as Johannesburg mayor.

Judge Marcus Senyatsi barred Zille from repeating four specific allegations against the EFF leader.

These relate to Malema’s alleged control of City Power, interference in municipal fleet tenders, influence over Shadrack Sibiya’s appointment as head of Johannesburg’s anti-corruption unit and use of the EFF’s political support to secure these decisions.

The court found that Zille had not presented sufficient evidence to substantiate the specific allegations at this stage of the proceedings.

ZILLE REFUSED TO APOLOGISE

Malema’s lawyers recently sent Zille a letter of demand on 9 November, calling on her to retract her statements and publicly apologise.

Zille responded with a single word on social media: “No.”



She maintained that her allegations were true and indicated that she was prepared to defend them in court.

Malema denied the allegations and, together with the EFF, launched an urgent court application.

MALEMA GIVEN 15 COURT DAYS

The court gave Malema and the EFF 15 court days to institute defamation proceedings.

Should they fail to meet the deadline, the interim interdict will lapse.

The court also ordered Zille to pay the legal costs of the application, including those of two counsel where applicable.

However, Friday’s ruling does not prevent Zille from criticising Malema, the EFF or Johannesburg’s coalition arrangements.

The trial court will ultimately determine whether Zille’s allegations were defamatory and whether she can substantiate them.

World.title: Mashaba wins Joburg mayoral vote, Zille vows to fight on
World.content:
ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba has reclaimed the Johannesburg mayoral chain after defeating the DA’s Helen Zille. Image: X

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba has reclaimed the Johannesburg mayoral chain, prompting a swift response from defeated DA candidate Helen Zille.

Zille took to Facebook on Friday, 27 November, to take aim at ActionSA and its coalition partners, vowing that the DA would continue fighting for Johannesburg residents.

“For the DA, it was just the end of the beginning. For ActionSA and their coalition of chaos, this is the beginning of the end,” Zille wrote.



“We will fight for you!”

MASHABA DEFEATS ZILLE IN JOBURG MAYORAL VOTE

Mashaba secured 170 votes against Zille’s 97 during Friday’s Johannesburg council sitting, returning to the position he vacated seven years ago.

His election followed days of coalition negotiations after no party secured an outright majority in the 4 November local government elections.

Mashaba secured the backing of the ANC, EFF and uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party.

Despite emerging as the biggest party in Johannesburg with 91 council seats, the DA failed to garner enough support to govern the metro.

I have been just elected as the Executive Mayor of Joburg! 🇿🇦



Now, it’s time to roll up our sleeves and hit the ground running. The hard work of delivering for the residents of Johannesburg begins immediately!#OperationFixJoburg https://t.co/IasaSuH8SF pic.twitter.com/crflbFA4cN  November 27, 2026

ZILLE REFUSED TO STEP ASIDE

Hours before councillors elected Mashaba, Zille defended her refusal to withdraw from the mayoral race.

ActionSA had previously proposed that both Mashaba and Zille abandon their mayoral ambitions, allowing the DA to nominate another candidate.

However, Zille described the proposal as undemocratic, arguing that Mashaba had no right to dictate who the DA nominated.

“Then Herman Mashaba may as well be the leader of the DA,” she said.

ACTIONSA SECURES TWO GAUTENG METROS

Earlier this week, ActionSA’s Nasiphi Moya defeated the DA’s Cilliers Brink to retain her position as Tshwane mayor.

ActionSA now holds two of Gauteng’s three mayoral positions.

Mashaba’s return comes exactly seven years after his resignation as Johannesburg mayor took effect on 27 November 2019.

He previously served as mayor under the DA banner before founding ActionSA in 2020.

World.title: Bitter SWEET: Geely E5 Apex Plus driven
World.content:
Warning, this Geely E5 Apex Plus drive fully is a purely subjective piece. It will likely not resemble anything a customer of this excellent EV will actually experience. However, it is what we experienced during our test. And so, it is what we must convey.

Firstly, woah, what a brilliant vehicle. Congrats, Geely. We’ve driven more or less every new-energy entrant from China in the last two years. And the E5 Apex Plus is definitely out of the top drawer. We’d probably put it in the same rarefied category as the Haval H6 PHEV and BYD Dolphin Surf, which we rate very highly.

GEELY E5 APEX PLUS DRIVE

However, coming to this conclusion was no easy feat due to a number of logistical challenges, shall we say. The vehicle arrived with no charging card. Now, to the fleet manager’s credit, she did warn me beforehand. For those who don’t know – most EVs do have a dedicated card. It’s just easier for the manufacturer to pair a card with their vehicle than have every journalist setup multiple accounts for any possible charging scenario.



Also, when you buy one of these wonderful Geely E5’s, you’ll most likely get the home charger fitted. So, like we said, this scenario won’t even occur for an actual owner. Nevertheless, here we are, charged (pun intended) with reviewing this car, but without many of the physical tools to do so …

TETHERED-CABLE CHARGERS

What a truly wonder space to occupy. Centre screen is massive and responsive. Wireless phone charger works well. And the seats are wonderfully comfortable. Image: Ray Leathern

We took delivery of the EV in the city with roughly a quarter charge, a range of 140 km. It’s about a 40 km drive down South where we’re based. And the public charging infrastructure is sorely lacking beyond the city. Wanting to top up the battery right away, we headed for the Constantia Emporium, where the Rubicon Charging app reliably told us a charger was available. Some shopping while the Geely E5 tops up? Lovely …

Except, of course, this particular charger doesn’t have a tethered cable. We rummage beneath the cavernous boot to find only a charger with a three-prong wall socket. Not good. Between here and home there are no more chargers. One possible option is to double back to Canal Walk where we know there’s a DC fast charger with a tethered cable.



TIME-MILEAGE MANAGEMENT

However, just to get there will use up perhaps half of the already limited range, and it is late afternoon. Then there’s the thought of what if it’s offline or occupied when we get there? Now we don’t have enough range to get home and we’re stuck in rush-hour traffic, driving even less efficiently. We cut our losses and head home instead. At least we’ve got the wall-socket connection …

Of course, it’s not advisable to charge a full EV like the Geely E5 through a wall socket. But this is beginning to feel like an emergency scenario. A 68 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery does not like that sort of treatment. It’s the equivalent of a trickle charge. We know this because we used to charge an e-Golf – one of the few brought in by Volkswagen a few years back – through a wall socket at our old office. A full 9 am-to-5 pm charge wouldn’t come close refilling the battery.

TRIP THE SYSTEM

With nowhere to go, we had plenty of time to poke about. Under the bonnet is the 160 kW electric motor that drives the front wheels exclusively. Image: Ray Leathern

True to form – with range down to 100 km – we get the Geely E5 connected to a wall socket at home. The computer says a full charge will take 14 hours. Oh well, could be an interesting exercise to see how this goes. About one hour in, the house power trips. The cable is burning hot when we go to disconnect it. In that time, that battery has gained about 5 km range.



Wait for everything to cool and try the wall socket again. Another hour goes by and, boom, house power goes down again. We decide to abandon this plan of attack and save a potential visit from the fire department. And would you like to know the craziest part? Just two hours quadrupled our daily energy consumption. Four times what we spend on any given day to run an entire house won’t so even get us back over OuKaapsWeg.

AND SO IT GOES

Later in the week, we try a slow charger down at the Sun Valley mall. It has a tethered cable but in our experience it rarely works. As it proved yet again. The issue is there’s no QR code/command screen, you must swipe a physical card. Of course, we have the Rubicon app with the charge wallet topped up, but the charger simply won’t initiate.

Despite this, in between our attempts to recharge, we were boundlessly impressed by the Geely E5 Apex Plus. The steering is light and quick but still feels sporty and connected. Its performance is perfectly adequate, all in sumptuous comfort and silence. Interior tech and connectivity are some of the best in class. You have the option of auto-cooled seats, which work brilliantly well, along with numerous seat massage functions.



THE VERDICT

A 68 kWh battery requires proper juice for an efficient recharge, don’t mess about with the wall socket. Image: Ray Leathern

Finally, days later, with the range down to 60 km, we bit the bullet and set course for Canal Walk. No matter if it took all day, we would plug in there. Well, that was the plan until we encountered roadworks on OuKaapseWeg. Normally free flowing mid-morning, we must’ve sat stationary for nearly 30 minutes in a stop and go, range silently draining away. We abandoned this plan, too, and chalked the whole thing down to bad EV juju.

In conclusion, even in our limited time behind the wheel, the Geely E5 impressed immensely. If you’ve driven any of the competition, you’ll be able to tell right away this is one of the good ones. However, we’d love another crack it at. Either starting with a full charge, a charge card or, at the very least, a suitable range of cables included.

World.title: Level 2 water restrictions: Joburg residents face tariff hikes next week
World.content:
Tariff hikes will come into effect alongside Level 2 water restrictions in Johannesburg. Image: Pexels

The City of Johannesburg will be implementing Level 2 water restriction tariffs next week.

Last week, the City introduced the new water restrictions until further notice in order to protect the municipality’s water supply system and prevent reservoir depletion.

Now, these restrictions come with higher municipal water tariffs, which will take effect from next Tuesday, 1 December 2026.



WATER RESTRICTIONS: WHAT TARIFFS ENTAIL

As the City of Johannesburg explains, the Level 2 residential restriction tariffs apply to all household and multi-dwelling residential accounts.

“Because deemed-consumption customers pay a fixed charge and prepaid consumption is not regulated through monthly stepped billing, these areas are not affected by the stepped tariff adjustment and will instead be managed through a 20% flow reduction on zone supply meters,” they said.

The City notes that commercial, industrial and other non-residential categories are not included in this residential tariff adjustment. Nevertheless, all water users must adhere to Level 2 water-use restrictions.

Although the City’s tariff schedule labels this tariff tier as “Level 2 – 20%”, this does not mean that Joburg residents’ water bills will increase by a flat 20%.

Rather, households’ monthly water usage is divided into consumption bands. You will be charged the rate applicable to each band as you use it, rather than the highest rate on your total consumption.

WATER TARIFF ADJUSTMENTS

Under normal residential tariffs, the first six kilolitres (6 000 litres) of monthly water consumption are charged at R0.00 per kilolitre.



From 1 December 2026 the 0-6 kilolitre band will be charged at R7.80 per kilolitre. For example, a Johannesburg household using exactly six kilolitres in a month will pay R46.80 for water consumption instead of R0.00 (excluding VAT and other standard municipal charges).

Here’s how Level 2 restriction tariffs will affect typical monthly household water consumption charges (excluding VAT, refuse, sanitation and other fixed charges):

Monthly Household Usage Normal Tariff Charge Level 2 Tariff Charge Extra Monthly Cost Overall Change 6 kL (6,000 litres) R0.00 R46.80 +R46.80 New charge 10 kL (10,000 litres) R134.28 R196.72 +R62.44 +46.50% 15 kL (15,000 litres) R309.48 R404.27 +R94.79 +30.63% 20 kL (20,000 litres) R555.13 R703.37 +R148.24 +26.70%

In the case of qualifying registered indigent / Expanded Social Package (ESP) households, they will continue to receive their approved Free Basic Water relief in accordance with the City’s indigent policy.

HOW TO SAVE WATER

Residents are advised to practise water-saving habits. Image: Pexels

Per the City, Johannesburg’s water network is under severe pressure. This is a result of sustained high water demand, warmer temperatures and prolonged dry weather patterns.

As of writing, the City of Gold is consuming an average of 1 709 million litres of water per day against its bulk supply allocation of 1 524 million litres per day. This represents an excess of roughly 185 million litres daily.

To protect the water supply, as well as save on your water bill, you are advised to:

Fix leaking taps, toilets and pipes.

Take shorter showers and turn off taps while brushing teeth or shaving.

Refrain from watering gardens or washing paved areas with a hosepipe.

Only run washing machines and dishwashers with full loads.

Check your water meter regularly to spot hidden underground leaks early.

Report burst pipes and street leaks to Johannesburg Water immediately.

In other news, residents of Cape Town are revisiting familiar water-saving habits as Level 1 water restrictions take next Tuesday, 1 December 2026.

World.title: Black Friday 2026: Capitec clients spend millions on KFC
World.content:
Capitec clients spend millions on KFC on Black Friday. Image via KFC

According to data shared on a live dashboard, Capitec clients spent millions on takeaways – namely KFC – on Black Friday

The bank also records that shoppers stocked up on groceries and treated themselves to retail therapy using “Buy Now, Pay Later” payments.

WHAT DID CAPITEC CLIENTS SPLURGE ON?

According to financial journalist Maya Maven, a live dashboard at Capitec’s head offices revealed data about what its 26 million clients were spending their money on on Black Friday.



Maven reported that Capitec clients had spent R7,6 million on KFC by midday.

She also made the following observations

Around 600 transactions occurred each second, with a total cost of R345 000

Over R1 billion in cash withdrawals by midday

While in-store was the preferred choice, clients spent significantly on gambling sites and online vouchers.

By midday, shoppers had spent more than R30 million on “Buy Now, Pay Later” payment methods.

I am standing at Capitec head office watching the Black Friday dashboard which is showing the live transactions of its 26 million clients.

Absolutely fascinating! By 12pm clients had spent R7.6 million on KFC but Shoprite/Checkers absolutely dominates in instore spend.

What is…  November 27, 2026

According to Capitec group executive for marketing and communications Francois Vivers, R3,7 billion was spent by late afternoon, of which R2,8 billion was in-store purchases.

Shoprite emerged as the biggest beneficiary in-store on Black Friday, with many shoppers prioritising essentials.

Viviers told The Citizen: “People are typically prioritising essential spending first over luxury electronics, clothing, and other goods”.



Capitec also recorded an increase in international purchases and from South African e-commerce site, Takealot, which is the country’s largest online retailer.

R300K SINGLE BLACK FRIDAY PURCHASE

Meanwhile, Ecentric Payment Systems’ live Black Friday transaction dashboard recorded the largest single transaction, amounting to a R300 000 purchase made before midday.

The transaction was made around 10:00 in-store and was an electronic purchase.



Ecentric recorded the largest transaction this week: an R500 000 purchase of clothing and footwear in-store on Tuesday, 24 November.

World.title: UEFA punishes Aden McCarthy again
World.content:
UEFA has officially extended former Kaizer Chiefs defender Aden McCarthy’s automatic one-match suspension to two matches following his straight red card while playing for Sabah FK earlier this month.

The 22-year-old was sent off in the 77th minute of Sabah’s 4-1 defeat to Norwegian side Viking FK after making a studs-up challenge.

Following a review of the incident, UEFA ruled that McCarthy’s challenge endangered the safety of his opponent, resulting in an additional one-match suspension.



Having already served the first game of his suspension against FC Barcelona, McCarthy will now also miss Sabah FK’s trip to Spain to face Villarreal on 8 December 2026.

The centre-back will only be eligible to return to European action when Sabah take on Napoli on 20 January 2027.

This could prove to be a frustrating setback for McCarthy, particularly with Sabah FK facing the possibility of elimination from the competition in the coming weeks.



As a result, the former Amakhosi defender could have very few opportunities to feature in European competition again this season.

McCarthy has had a good season in Europe

Ever since leaving Amakhosi for Sabah, the young defender has enjoyed his time in Azerbaijan. He made his UEFA Champions League debut at Old Trafford against Manchester United before scoring his first goal in the competition a few weeks later.

Will Aden bounce back?

World.title: IN PICS: Preparations underway for Mlambo-Ngcuka's funeral
World.content:
EXESI - Preparations for the funeral of the late former deputy president Dr Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka were in full force in eXesi on Friday.

Members of the South African Defence Force planned and practiced ceremonial elements for the late former president's Category 2 State Funeral.

The State Funeral forms part of the official framework for honouring those who have served the country at the highest levels of public office, as well as South Africans who have recorded outstanding achievements or served with distinction.

Last week, President Cyril Ramaphosa directed that the national flag be flown at half-mast from Sunday morning, 22 November, until the evening of Saturday, 28 November 2026, as a mark of respect.

Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka's public service career included serving as the Minister of Minerals and Energy, Deputy Minister of Trade, and Executive Director of UN Women.

Mlambo-Ngcuka is survived by her husband, Bulelani Ngcuka, and her five children.

World.title: Number Of The Day | R4 | 27 November 2026
World.content:
When Fuel Prices Fall, Why Does The Cost Of Living Take Longer To Recover?

South Africa's anticipated December fuel price reduction exposes the difference between slowing inflation and restoring household purchasing power.

For a household that has spent much of the year adjusting to higher transport costs, a cheaper tank of petrol is welcome news. But it cannot undo the journeys that became unaffordable, the money diverted from savings or the purchases postponed when fuel prices were climbing. The financial consequences of rising prices can outlive the economic conditions that caused them.

This is one of the less visible challenges of recovering from a cost-of-living crisis. Economic indicators can improve considerably before households experience anything resembling a return to financial stability. South Africa's anticipated December fuel price reduction offers an opportunity to examine that disconnect.

The hidden cost of expensive fuel

Fuel is an unusual household expense because its influence extends well beyond the people buying it. A motorist encounters its price directly at the filling station, while a commuter, supermarket customer or small business owner may experience it indirectly through the cost of transport, distribution and services.

When fuel becomes more expensive, households and businesses must decide where to absorb the additional expense. A family might reduce discretionary spending, while a small retailer might accept lower margins or increase prices. These decisions can accumulate over several months, leaving financial consequences that are not immediately reversed when fuel becomes cheaper.

The distinction is important because a reduction in the rate at which living costs increase does not necessarily mean that those costs have returned to their previous levels. Even an unusually large fuel price reduction may represent only a partial recovery of the purchasing power lost during a prolonged period of economic pressure.

Why economic relief is rarely shared equally

The extent of the anticipated December relief illustrates another complication: households and businesses experience the same economic developments differently.

In the 27 November edition of eNCA's Number of the Day, Francis Herd estimates that 95 petrol could decrease by R3.57 per litre after accounting for a reduction in government fuel levy relief. The anticipated reductions for diesel are considerably smaller. These remain preliminary estimates rather than confirmed prices.

The difference between petrol and diesel matters because it complicates expectations of a broader reduction in living costs. A petrol-driving household could experience meaningful savings on its next journey, while a business dependent on diesel may see a much smaller improvement in operating expenses.

Even when businesses benefit from cheaper fuel, they may first need to recover margins eroded during the period of higher prices. Others may face contractual obligations or unrelated operating costs that limit their ability to reduce prices. Lower fuel costs create room for economic relief, but they do not guarantee that the benefit will immediately travel through the entire economy.

From surviving higher prices to rebuilding financial resilience

The festive season presents an interesting test of how households respond when some financial pressure begins to ease. The temptation is to regard cheaper fuel as additional spending money, particularly when holidays and family commitments have already placed demands on December budgets.

Yet the opportunity created by falling prices extends beyond more affordable travel. For households that have spent months absorbing higher living costs, even modest savings can create room to restore depleted emergency funds, reduce financial commitments or rebuild the flexibility that rising prices took away.

There is also a broader lesson for how economic recovery is communicated. Celebrating improvements in international markets is understandable, but the experience of households cannot be measured through commodity prices alone. Affordability, disposable income and the ability to withstand another unexpected expense provide a more complete picture of whether financial conditions are genuinely improving.

A cheaper tank of petrol may make the December holidays more affordable. The more meaningful recovery, however, will be when South Africans can absorb the next economic shock without having to sacrifice another part of their lives.

World.title: Making Sense | AI Doomsday Fears: Are Businesses Asking The Wrong Questions? | 27 November 2026
World.content:
The Biggest AI Risks May Be Closer To Home Than We Think

The debate surrounding artificial intelligence seems increasingly divided between two competing visions of the future. In one, AI unlocks unprecedented human progress. In the other, humanity creates something it can no longer control. Both are compelling possibilities to contemplate, but between them lies a more immediate question that deserves considerably more attention: what happens when ordinary people and businesses place extraordinary trust in a technology they do not fully understand?

The consequences of that question are becoming increasingly relevant as AI moves beyond computer screens and into the systems through which people work, travel, communicate and make decisions. The challenge is not simply understanding what artificial intelligence can do. It is deciding what we should allow it to do on our behalf.

When convenience becomes dependency

Part of AI's appeal lies in its ability to conceal complexity. A person can ask a sophisticated question in everyday language and receive an answer within seconds. That accessibility is enormously valuable, but it can also create the impression that a technology capable of producing convincing answers is capable of exercising reliable judgement.

Speaking to Francis Herd on eNCA's Making Sense podcast, South African AI researcher Professor Etienne Barnard argues that artificial intelligence should be approached as a transformative technology whose capabilities and limitations must be understood before it is integrated into existing systems.

The distinction matters because the consequences of an AI error depend heavily on where it occurs. An inaccurate restaurant recommendation is an inconvenience. An unreliable assessment used to determine someone's access to credit, employment or healthcare could have considerably more serious implications.

In South Africa, this tension already intersects with existing legal protections. Section 71 of the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) places restrictions, subject to specified exceptions, on certain significant decisions based solely on automated processing of personal information. The principle is particularly relevant as businesses consider delegating more consequential decisions to machines.

Safety is something we design

Much of the public conversation about AI safety centres on whether intelligent machines might eventually develop intentions of their own. Yet a system does not need consciousness or malicious intent to cause harm. It can produce damaging outcomes simply because it has been given inappropriate access, poorly defined instructions or insufficient safeguards.

Consider the difference between an AI system recommending a driving route and one authorised to influence the operation of a vehicle. The underlying technology may be sophisticated in both instances, but the acceptable margin for error changes dramatically.

This is where conventional engineering principles remain relevant. Defining what a system should achieve, establishing its boundaries and testing how it behaves under different conditions are essential parts of responsible implementation. The extraordinary nature of AI does not eliminate the need for these ordinary disciplines. If anything, its complexity makes them more important.

The responsibility cannot belong to the machine

For businesses, there is a temptation to treat AI adoption as primarily a technological challenge. Find the right software, appoint a specialist and introduce automation wherever possible. But this approach risks overlooking the people who remain responsible for the consequences.

An AI specialist may understand how a system operates without understanding the full implications of a financial, marketing or customer-service decision. Responsible AI adoption therefore requires more than technical expertise. It requires people with different forms of expertise to remain accountable for the decisions within their respective areas.

That means introducing AI through controlled experiments, measuring results and maintaining oversight as the technology evolves. Businesses should be prepared to reconsider systems that no longer serve their intended purpose, rather than treating adoption itself as evidence of progress.

The future of artificial intelligence remains uncertain, and concerns about its long-term development should not be dismissed. But uncertainty about tomorrow cannot become an excuse for neglecting the responsibilities we already have today.

Perhaps the most revealing question about our relationship with AI is not whether machines will eventually become more powerful than humans. It is whether humans will exercise the judgement required to use that power responsibly.

Watch the full conversation with Professor Etienne Barnard on Making Sense.

Barnard's arguments about technological limitations, engineering safeguards and organisational responsibility are drawn from the supplied episode transcript.

The reference to POPIA is additional, independently sourced South African legal context.

The credit, employment, healthcare and navigation examples are illustrative editorial applications, not reported incidents from the interview.
