World.title: ‘Shocking’ decline seen in hep B vaccination against incurable virus, including babies with infected mothers
World.content:
Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found.

As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.

Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds.

The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year.

During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year.

“It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.”

The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.)

The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks.

Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.

“We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.”

The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%.

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations.

Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth.

“Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,”

Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

World.title: Power being slowly restored as heavy Thanksgiving storm eases
World.content:
Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some places stayed on guard for high-tide flooding following a round of holiday storms.

The storms snarled travel and downed trees and power lines. The heavy weather led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, preparations were underway to hold Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.

Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.

Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.

There were 2,893 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday afternoon, with another 151 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

The number of power outages, which peaked Thursday at more than 900,000 customers, fell by approximately 50% by Friday afternoon to under 400,000, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us. Of those, about 90,000 were in Pennsylvania.

Bad weather in the East is taking its time to go

Conditions were expected to improve Friday across the entire eastern U.S., "but this huge system will take some time to weaken," the National Weather Service said on its website. Coastal flood warnings were posted from New Jersey to Virginia.

"A lot of standing water, tree branches, siding ripped off of houses and buildings," homeowner Chris Rizzo told CBS New York.

Waves crash against Virginia Beach Fishing Pier on Thanksgiving Day in Virginia Beach, Virginia, on Nov. 26, 2026. L. Todd Spencer/AP Photo

In Hampton, Virginia, the storm toppled a beloved landmark at Grandview Beach: a weathered, leafless tree known as the "Grieving Tree" or the "Shell Tree." Visitors regularly decorated its branches with seashells, and it became a popular subject for photographers.

After surviving many storms, the tree "may have finally met its match," local meteorologist Ricky Matthews wrote on Facebook, sharing a photograph.

Roofs in Ocean City and Rockville collapsed. In Norfolk, Virginia, crews rescued 39 people and two dogs, City Councilman Tommy Smigiel posted.

In Baltimore, the storm brought a record 3.04 inches of rain to BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport on Thursday, while high tide in Annapolis reached 4.48 feet that night, a level officials said was among the 10 highest on record.

Part of a fishing pier collapsed in Virginia Beach, Virginia, closing a 3-mile section of beach, including the boardwalk, "due to dangerous conditions," the city said.

Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey, scrambled to pump out saltwater Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community's history. More than 1,100 people participated in a charity run, and Santa Claus was scheduled to arrive on a fire truck by evening to light the Christmas tree.

Conditions were a "million times better than they were 24 hours ago," borough business administrator Scott Wahl said.

Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding has become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

A damaged traffic light pole lies across a flooded street in Ocean City, New Jersey, on Nov. 27, 2026, after heavy rain on Thursday. Allie Ippolito/AP Photo

"Our family has been here for 36 years," McKenna said. "But honestly, we're thinking, is this the right place for us to be? We're now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this."

Another round of rain and strong winds are expected to hit the East Coast by Sunday evening, potentially disrupting the Monday morning commute. Up to 2 inches of rain and wind gusts of 65 mph are possible in some areas, according to CBS News meteorologist Nikki Nolan.

Parts of South and Midwest see snow, while California contends with coastal flooding

Part of Tennessee was under a winter storm warning for up to an inch of snow Friday, after rain turned into light snow on Thanksgiving. Conditions were calmer for the Midwest, compared with Thanksgiving, when as much as 15 inches of snow fell in eastern Missouri.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in early Thursday.

Snow is expected to begin falling Saturday from Montana to Colorado, with accumulations of up to 10 to 18 inches in some areas, according to Nolan. The storm will then move into the Midwest and Gulf Coast on Sunday, bringing rain to cities including Chicago, St. Louis, Nashville and New Orleans.

A pedestrian is hit with water as a wave crashes into a seawall during inclement weather in Pacifica, California, on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific Coast and continued to affect train service Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.

Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

Heavy snow was expected in parts of Montana and Wyoming. A renewed surge of moisture associated with an atmospheric river across the Pacific Northwest moved toward the northern Rockies, the weather service said.

World.title: OpenAI countersues Apple over allegations of stealing trade secrets
World.content:
OpenAI on Friday responded to Apple's June lawsuit accusing the company of stealing trade secrets by countersuing.

The ChatGPT maker alleged that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing proprietary information. Apple created "a situation in which it can accuse virtually any departing employee, and their new employer, of 'stealing' purported Apple trade secrets," the suit, filed in the Northern District of California, claims.

In a statement provided to CBS News Friday, an Apple spokesperson said that the case "is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information."

Apple's complaint in June accused OpenAI and two of its employees, Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan and Chang Liu, a technical staffer at the company, of stealing Apple's proprietary information to help OpenAI develop its own hardware. Both formerly worked at Apple.

OpenAI claims in its countersuit Friday that Apple's employment practices are designed to set a trap for a departing employee and their future employer — "a trap that can be sprung whenever Apple sees an opportunity to slow down a potential competitor."

Tech analysts expect OpenAI to make a foray into hardware design, putting it in more direct competition with Apple. In July 2025, OpenAI acquired the AI device startup of former Apple star designer Jony Ive, io Products Inc.

World.title: 25-year sentence sought for former chef who aided 14 suicides
World.content:
Canadian prosecutors on Friday requested a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold poison to help people die by suicide, stressing his victims were largely young and experiencing mental distress.

Former chef Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally through a series of online forums.

Prosecutors had also charged him with murder but, citing a lack of evidence, agreed to withdraw the more serious accusations in exchange for Law pleading guilty to lesser offenses.

That decision drew widespread condemnation, notably from friends and family of victims who believed Law was directly responsible for killing their loved ones, but prosecutors maintained they would still seek a stiff penalty.

"An appropriate global sentence to impose in this matter is 25 years less (time already served)," Crown prosecutor Katie Doherty told the court.

Courts often use comparable cases in determining sentencing, but Doherty noted there is "no case even remotely similar to Mr Law's conduct."

The Canadian public was shocked when the breadth of Law's operation was revealed following his arrest.

Kenneth Law pictured in a handout photo from Canadian Police. Peel Regional Police

He sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the United Kingdom, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defense and prosecution. There, 79 deaths are linked to him, according to Canadian prosecutors.

He admitted to entering suicide chat forums under an alias, identifying people considering ending their lives and then directing them to one of his online shops where he sold lethal concentrations of the meat preservative sodium nitrite.

In 2023, Canadian police released photos of the sodium nitrite, adding that a joint operation led by 11 police agencies from across Ontario were investigating the case.

"Investigators are asking members of the community to be alert of any packaging or label identifying sodium nitrite," Constable Sarah Patten said at the time.

Law, who was born in 1965, sold poison to people who were "just starting off their lives" and "battling mental illness," Doherty said.

That is "a very significant aggravating factor in this case," Doherty said.

The judge is expected to make a final sentencing decision over the coming weeks.

Prosecutors in the U.K. decided not to charge Law despite investigating him for dozens of deaths.

The Crown Prosecution Service and the National Crime Agency said they had decided Law "should be sentenced for the full extent of his offending within a single sentencing process in Canada."

In a letter to bereaved families, the organizations said it had been a "difficult decision."

"No outcome in any court can remove the pain victims and their families have suffered," they said.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Powerful Thanksgiving storm causes flooding, power outages
World.content:
A Thanksgiving storm brought foul weather to the East Coast and Midwest on Thursday, causing major power outages, disrupting holiday travel and prompting the historic postponement of New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

More than 440,000 customers were without power Friday afternoon across the Midwest and Northeast, according to the utility tracking website PowerOutage.us. Of those, more than 109,000 customers were without electricity in Pennsylvania, along with more than 68,000 in New Jersey and 54,000 in Maryland. The outages reached more than 800,000 customers at the height of the storm Thursday night.

There were 2,286 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday afternoon, with another 137 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. That nearly equals the 2,500 flights to or from U.S. destinations delayed on Thursday, though more than 460 were canceled, according to FlightAware.

The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York, following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.

Two men kayak down Hampton Boulevard as rain continues to fall, flooding streets and stranding drivers, on Thanksgiving morning, in Norfolk, Va. Stephen M. Katz/The Virginian-Pilot via AP

Stormy weather creates havoc in New York City

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning that two people had to be rescued from their cars because of flooding. He cautioned people not to attempt to walk, bike or drive through flooded areas.

"We want to remind everyone to stay safe and there is no destination worth your safety," Mamdani said.

The New York City Emergency Management agency reported that the city received 1.5 to 2 inches of rain on Thanksgiving, with some parts seeing up to 3 inches. High tides brought flooding to the city's coastal areas, including portions of Staten Island and Long Island.

A person wears a poncho in high winds and rain during a Thanksgiving Day storm in New York City on Nov. 26, 2026. Adam Gray / Reuters

Central Park saw wind gusts higher than 30 mph, the agency said, while LaGuardia Airport recorded winds of 56 mph. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported.

Macy's postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade's massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.

A car is seen stalled out in flood waters in Far Rockaway in New York City, on Nov. 26, 2026. Theodore Parisienne/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images

A high school marching band from Pearland, Texas, near Houston, said it raised a staggering $350,000 to allow its 500 members to stay in New York City for two extra nights.

"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band for Pearland High School, told CBS News on Thursday.

Visitors who had traveled to New York to attend the parade were forced to make last-minute changes to their travel plans. Amanda Anderson, a Florida-based makeup artist who was hired to do makeup for parade performers, told CBS News New York she was able to rebook her flights so she could stay an extra day.

A child stands in front of a chain-link fence looking towards idle parade floats in New York, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo

"I was in Macy's, actually, when I found out, and I look up and there was like three girls crying already," Anderson said when she learned the parade had been postponed. "People were sitting down, very somber. It was an experience."

Major roadways flooded, holiday travel disrupted

The storm flooded coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in Thursday morning. Roads were closed and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.

Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said.

"Not quite Hurricane Sandy," Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south of New Jersey's Atlantic coast.

Floodwaters washed debris over the road next to the shore, and a few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

Heavy rain and strong winds from a powerful coastal storm cause flooding across streets in Ocean City, New Jersey, on Nov. 26, 2026. Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images

Lance Miller, 54, said floods in his neighborhood of Ocean City, a small coastal town in New Jersey, are about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest grocery store would probably "destroy your car."

"I wouldn't do that, I'm a car guy," said Miller. "You're gonna have a good foot of water that you'd have to drive through."

Miller, who had his Thanksgiving Day meal preparations set, said he would be staying indoors and have dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends in the area were "not so lucky" and had flooding inside their homes.

"So they're dealing with cleanup, you know," he said.

Flooding in Margate City, New Jersey, on Nov. 26, 2026. Margate City Fire Department

The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted a video on Facebook of water pouring through the city's streets on a gray day even before heavy rains started.

A firefighter there said the tide was coming in ferociously and it was still an hour before its peak. Water closed in on steps to houses, and businesses had sandbags piled in front of their doors.

A stretch of U.S. Route 30, a major artery that goes into Atlantic City, was shuttered in both directions due to heavy flooding, the Absecon Police Department reported.

"Please stay off the roads until conditions improve," Absecon police said. "Do not attempt to drive through flooded roadways or around barricades."

Chester County Hospital in West Chester, Pennsylvania, sustained a partial power outage on Thursday afternoon, but power was restored before patients had to be transported to other facilities.

Residents of the Pennsylvania community of Springfield Township north of Philadelphia were asked to temporarily evacuate out of caution after a tree fell on a propane tank, local officials said. That evacuation advisory was later lifted.

A Lime scooter is swallowed up by floodwaters on Thanksgiving morning, in Norfolk, Virginia, on Nov. 26, 2026. Stephen M. Katz/The Virginian-Pilot via AP

The storm prompted the temporary closure of some coastal highways and bridges. The nearly 18-mile Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel over the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway.

North Carolina was particularly hard-hit by heavy rain. Emerald Isle, in the state's Outer Banks, received 9.16 inches of rain. Atlantic Beach, North Carolina, saw 9.06 inches.

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, which are in the Washington metropolitan area, were asked to conserve water by the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. The water conservation request, which applied to all 1.9 million WSSC customers, was due to the risk that power outages posed to the agency's two water filtration plants.

Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches of snowfall. French Village, Missouri, received 15 inches of show while Ste. Genevieve recorded 14 inches.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city.

The rain isn't quite over yet for the Northeast. More storms are expected Sunday night into Monday morning for New York City, Philadelphia and Boston.

World.title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
World.content:
Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson.

"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said in her daily news briefing.

Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.

"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups."

"It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added.

Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?"

Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.

"Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.

U.S. steps up pressure on Mexico

The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination."

On Nov. 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "El Chapo Isidro," a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction. The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The military operation o capture him tsparked panic in the region, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks. In clashes with security forces, 16 cartel suspects were killed, officials said, and four soldiers also died.

Isidro Meza, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence. Mexico Government

Mexico requested Washington's support for the operation, and the United States sent a drone to help gather information about the drug lord's whereabouts.

The U.S. has requested Meza Flores' extradition, but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he will be tried in Mexico.

Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.

Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.

The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Although cooperation between the two countries went smoothly in that operation, tensions arose between Mexico and Washington in late April after federal prosecutors in New York made public a drug trafficking indictment against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya, a member of Mexico's governing party. He and nine other officials were accused of collaborating with a faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which the Trump administration has designated a foreign terrorist organization.

Amid the controversy, Rocha Moya took an indefinite leave of absence, and his bank accounts in Mexico were frozen. But Mexican authorities refused to carry out the U.S. request to arrest him. Former Sinaloa Security Secretary Gerardo Mérida Sánchez surrendered to U.S. authorities in May.



DEA accused of "walking" fentanyl

DEA whistleblowers in June revealed to the AP how agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction."

That denial, however, was further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history.

The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage showing dealers moving large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states.

This photo shows fentanyl seized by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at an Extra Space self-storage facility in Albuquerque, New Mexico, April 28, 2025. U.S. Department of Justice via AP

The Mexican president in her comments Thursday called the DEA's decision to permit fentanyl to hit the streets the "Fast and Furious of Fentanyl," a reference to the 2011 gun-walking scandal in which straw buyers smuggled some 2,000 assault weapons into Mexico with the intent of tracing the firearms to cartel leaders.

"What is the United States doing in the United States?" Sheinbaum asked. "We have a prosecutor's office here, and the Security Ministry works here. So they should pay close attention to the other side of the border."

The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cole said a channel for submitting tips about the state of Jalisco would be made public Thursday. The state is a stronghold of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known by its Spanish initials CJNG, which Washington also designated a terrorist organization.

Meanwhile, a veteran DEA agent also told CBS News last month the agency has contributed to the problem by allowing fentanyl pills to reach the streets.

"For three years, I've told my DEA managers that we're allowing dangerous amounts of fentanyl to hit the street, and we're doing nothing to stop it, and they didn't listen to me," DEA Special Agent David Howell told CBS News in his first television interview.

World.title: Pregnant inmate escapes in prison SUV after stop at Whataburger
World.content:
A pregnant prisoner is on the run in New Mexico after escaping in a corrections department SUV following a prenatal doctor appointment on Wednesday.

Rebecca Taylor, 26, who was not restrained at the time because of her pregnancy, managed to slide into the front seat of the Dodge Journey transport vehicle and drive away as she was returning to Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants from the appointment in Albuquerque, according to the corrections department.

Taylor escaped while the correctional officers accompanying her had stopped at a Whataburger, according to The Associated Press.

The Dodge Journey was later located via GPS, but Taylor was no longer in the vehicle, corrections officials said. Her prison jumpsuit was found near the vehicle, the AP reported.

Rebecca Taylor, who is pregnant, escaped from the custody of the New Mexico Corrections Department after a prenatal appointment. New Mexico Corrections Department

Taylor is serving time after pleading guilty to four offenses related to the theft of a vehicle, vehicle burglary and receiving a stolen car, according to court records.

She is from Cleveland, Texas, which is located outside of Houston, where she also has ties, according to authorities. Officials said they were following up on leads she may have taken public transportation and were checking Greyhound buses and Amtrak trains.

The U.S. Marshals Service is offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to her arrest.

Taylor is about 5-foot-7 and 180 pounds and has blue eyes and red hair. Authorities are asking anyone who sees her to call 911.

All prison facilities in New Mexico were put on lockdown in the wake of the escape as a precaution. That lockdown was lifted at 6 a.m. on Friday.

World.title: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
World.content:
Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.



🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.

Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.

The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.

Behind the story

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/Getty Images

This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent

I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."

Sponsor Message

After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.

New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.

Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.

Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.

I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).

Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.

Once again, my shopping cart is empty.

My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Getty Images/Bob Riha Jr.

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: The holiday season is packed full of can't-miss films. These are 17 movies that you should see before the year ends.

📺 TV: Parks and Recreation star Amy Poehler and creator Michael Schur reunite for Dig, an ensemble comedy about a team of archaeologists caught up in a series of mysterious events after uncovering an ancient artifact in Greece.

📚 Books: Why settle for one book recommendation when you can get more than 300? Now's the time to browse this year's Books We Love.

Sponsor Message

🎵 Music: NPR Music's Stephen Thompson and Lars Gotrich join host All Songs Considered Robin Hilton to attempt to build a canon of music for giving thanks, spending time with loved ones and, of course, celebrating food. Check out their playlist here.

🍴 Food: A few years ago, Israeli American chef Alon Shaya spearheaded the Rescue Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, exploring food's role in World War II. He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Steve Donahue for The National Dog Show.



Rocker the coonhound has won best in show at this year's National Dog Show. His glossy coat and big, floppy ears bested six other dogs that each won top honors in their groups. When Dungeons & Dragons came on the scene 50 years ago, some parents complained it kept their kids holed up inside. These days, the once-nerdy pastime is a screen-free parent's dream. Bakers across the country have taken inspiration from Little Free Libraries to offer free sweet treats to their neighbors.

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
World.content:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault

toggle caption i Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.

Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Sponsor Message

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.

The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.

The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.

A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.

"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.

Sponsor Message

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").

The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.

Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate

The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."

The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.

In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.

His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

World.title: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
World.content:
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.

More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA .

Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.

toggle caption i Noah Berger/AP

Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.

Sponsor Message

And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.

"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.

"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.

On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.

Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/AP

New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.

Iconic Macy's parade postponed

Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.

Sponsor Message

Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.

There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.

Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.

"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.

"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.

Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.

Black Friday kicks off

Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.

The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.

Sponsor Message

The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.

The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.

Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.

World.title: Can luxury save Macy's?
World.content:
Can luxury save Macy's?

toggle caption i Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images



Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.

"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

Sponsor Message

As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.

The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.

How Macy's got squeezed in the middle

Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.

The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.

And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."

When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.

The way out is up

At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.

Sponsor Message

But it didn't work.

toggle caption i Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.

Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.

As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.

"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.

"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."

The new luxury vision

Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.

The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.

In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."

It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.

"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.

"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."

Putting the higher prices to the test

In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.

The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.

Sponsor Message

Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."

toggle caption i Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.

"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."

How far can luxury sales take Macy's?

Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.

"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.

Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.

"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.

"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."

One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.

But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.

"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

World.title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
World.content:
Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it

toggle caption i Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images

For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.

The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.

The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Sponsor Message

In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.

"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.

Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.

Sponsor Message

But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.

Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.

In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.

The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.

If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."

Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.

Sponsor Message

One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.

Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.

"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.

But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.

toggle caption i John Moore/Getty Images

In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.

It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.

Sponsor Message

Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.

"He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.

According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.

The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.

"Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.

During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.

Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."

Sponsor Message

In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.

"There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.

She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

World.title: Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
World.content:
Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons

toggle caption i Lauren Migaki/NPR

Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than 50 years.

In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10-minute piece on it in 1979.

More recently, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows including Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.

Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream — a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.

Sponsor Message

"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of 9- to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."

Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host events like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.

toggle caption i Sequoia Carrillo/NPR

"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.

In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.

"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."

"And collaboration!" added her 9-year-old brother Leo Watson.

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Lauren Migaki/NPR

For fellow 9-year-old Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.

"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.

And for Benjamin Cho, also 9, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."

Edited by Lauren Migaki

Audio story edited by Lauren Migaki, Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

Audio story produced by Lauren Migaki

Visual design and development by LA Johnson

World.title: 12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
World.content:
12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start

toggle caption i Raquel Alvarez Tabernero/iStockphoto/Getty Images

Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.

For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.

Sponsor Message

In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.

A score for your brain

So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.

It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.

"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."

The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:



Sponsor Message

Physical health: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight



blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight Lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol



diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol Social and emotional health: stress management, relationships and a sense of purpose

According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."

Why blood pressure matters for your brain

High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.

"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.

That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. If you've been prescribed medication for high blood pressure, he says, taking the medicine is one of the most important things you can do.

Small gains add up

What if you take the quiz and don't love your number? The whole point of knowing your score is to use it as an assessment, a place to begin and a way to strategize about what changes you can make to your daily lifestyle habits. There's no need to overhaul your life.

In an analysis of real-world data from thousands of adults, each one-point improvement in the Brain Care Score was linked to up to a 4% lower risk of dementia, stroke or late-life depression. And even people who change their habits late in life can benefit.

Sponsor Message

The key is to pick one change that feels doable, such as:

Adding 30 minutes of sleep to your daily routine if you're not well rested

Putting an extra serving of greens on your plate

Adding in a 20-minute walk each day and resistance bands for strength training

Calling a friend to get together or joining a group activity

Getting your blood pressure checked



Researchers say one healthy change often leads to others. Better sleep, for example, can make it easier to exercise and eat well, so the benefits can multiply across the score.

Purpose and connection count too

One part of the score that surprises people is the value placed on relationships and purpose. A 2025 study found that people with a higher sense of purpose were about 28% less likely to develop cognitive impairment.

That means joining the class or the volunteer gig you've been putting off can be considered a form of brain care.

You can retake the quiz over time to track your progress, and you can share it with family and friends. Healthy habits can be contagious.

World.title: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.

At the same time, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has threatened Bell with a fine of up to $10 million for violating the government's wireless rules by selling customers cellphones locked to its network.

The CRTC's decision targets charges for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan. The regulator ruled on Friday that a cellphone handling charge from Bell, a cellphone setup charge from Rogers and a SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from Telus are prohibited.

The CRTC also ruled that fees charged by Rogers and Telus to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, nor are the shipping fees charged by Rogers.

SIM cards are microchips needed to connect a customer's device to a mobile network.

In June, the regulator banned fees to activate, change or cancel internet and cellphone services. Following that ban, major carriers introduced SIM card and other hardware-related charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees.

"We identified a number of fees charged by certain of the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. We notified them that the fees may be out of compliance," Sheehan Carter, the CRTC's acting vice-president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing on Friday.

"Since these companies chose to continue those fees, and they argued that they were not prohibited, we immediately took action to decide the issue."

WATCH | Bell, Rogers and Telus ordered to stop charging prohibited fees: Bell, Rogers and Telus ordered to stop charging prohibited fees | Duration closed caption 3:17 Canada's telecom regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus are charging consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act. The decision targets fees for providing and setting up phones when signing up for a service plan.

In a statement to CBC News on Friday, Rogers said it disagrees with the CRTC's position on device set-up charges.

"These charges help recover real costs, and we're pleased the CRTC's decision on the shipping charge and SIM replacement fee clearly reflect this," a Rogers spokesperson told CBC News in an email.

Spokespeople for Bell and Telus say their respective companies are reviewing the regulator's decisions.

According to a CRTC report released in February, Bell, Telus and Rogers collectively controlled nearly 90 per cent of Canada's mobile wireless sales and roughly 86 per cent of wireless subscribers, as of 2024.

WATCH | How a $31B merger deal could reshape Canada's wireless market: Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill | Duration closed caption 4:07 Quebecor has launched a massive $31-billion bid to take over Telus, a move that would crown it Canada’s largest telecom company — and potentially shrink the wireless market back down to three major players in B.C. The CBC’s Lien Yeung breaks down why Telus is pushing back and what this blockbuster merger could mean for your monthly phone bill.

Matt Hatfield, executive director of the non-profit advocacy group OpenMedia, says Friday's ruling blocks some anti-consumer practices adopted by Canada's three largest telecom providers. However, he worries they will simply tweak their fees again to get around the rules.

"This is just one round of whack-a-mole in a game customers always lose. Canada's telecom companies keep finding new ways to lock in and surcharge their customers," he told CBC News in an emailed statement.

"As it stands, these practices were a net win for the companies. They profited while they lasted, and they'll now start on new ways of abusing customers that the CRTC will take time to identify and address."

Bell faces up to $10M fine

The CRTC also said Friday it found that Bell sold customers cellphones that were locked to its network — limiting their ability to take advantage of better offers from rivals.

"The CRTC rules require that cellphones must be unlocked, so that Canadians have the freedom to choose their provider," Carter said.

He said the CRTC is considering fining Bell up to $10 million, in the "upper range" of what's allowed under the Telecommunications Act. Earlier this month, BCE, Bell's parent company, booked $6.18 billion in operating revenue for the three months ending Sept. 30.

The CRTC banned phone locking in 2017, along with the unlocking fees carriers had been charging, in a bid to make it easier for consumers to switch providers.

WATCH | Bell targeted in AI-powered cyber attack: Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier | Duration closed caption 1:49 Bell Canada has confirmed that an ‘agentic’ threat actor breached its systems on Nov. 17, which may have exposed personal information belonging to customers of Bell, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile.

In August, the CRTC temporarily suspended this requirement, allowing carriers to lock devices for up to two business days, after which they unlock automatically. It required that consumers be able to request immediate unlocking at no charge. This followed applications from Bell and Telus, which argued that selling unlocked phones increased theft and fraud.

In July, Telus filed an application for a temporary exemption from the regulator's phone-unlocking rules. The company proposed to start locking devices for 60 days.

On Friday, the CRTC formally denied this request.

Carter said the regulator had seen no evidence that Telus had actually sold locked devices, only that it intended to do so. As a result, he said no fines were appropriate at this time.

In June, the CRTC warned Telus in a letter that its $15 charge for SIM cards may be considered an activation fee, which is prohibited under the Telecommunications Act.

"Every SIM card and eSIM comes with real costs associated with providing it to customers, and we believe those costs should be reflected in the price of the product, rather than requiring carriers to provide it free of charge," a Telus spokesperson stated in an email.

Keldon Bester, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Monopoly Project, sees charges for SIM cards as an activation fee in disguise.

"You really cannot access telecom services without access to a SIM card," he said. "To break that out as a separate charge, I think, runs in the face of the CRTC's aim, which is to say that the process of moving carriers should be as seamless as possible."
