More than seven years after it was passed, Bill 21, which prohibits public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, has survived a legal challenge that climbed all the way up to the Supreme Court of Canada, with one exception.

World.title: The future of the notwithstanding clause is now up to political leaders
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two weeks after he pieced together the "kitchen accord," Jean Chrétien stood in the House of Commons as justice minister to present a new constitutional resolution, including a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

In his remarks on that momentous occasion, Chrétien made a specific effort to defend the presence in the Charter of an "override" clause.

"The effect of this provision is, first, that it will be politically very difficult for a government to introduce without very good reason a measure which applies notwithstanding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Constitution," he said on the afternoon of Nov. 20, 1981.

Chrétien quoted a prominent lawyer — Alan Borovoy, the general counsel for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association — who said the notwithstanding clause would be a "red flag for opposition parties and the press."

"This will make it politically difficult for a government to override the Charter," Chrétien quoted Borovoy as saying. "Political difficulty is a reasonable safeguard for the Charter."

Forty-five years and one week later, amid growing concern that the clause is now being invoked too easily and too casually by governments and legislatures to pass laws that would otherwise be found to violate the rights of Canadians, the Supreme Court of Canada delivered a landmark ruling on the political compromise of 1981.

The court upheld the Quebec legislature's use of the clause in the case of Bill 21 and it did not find that there should be new limits on how the clause can be used. A majority of justices did find that the invocation of the clause does not prevent a court from publicly declaring that the rights of Canadians are being violated — a measure that may, in future, make it somewhat harder for governments to do so.

But the larger task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If the notwithstanding clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to political actors.

'The courts have a crucial role to play'

The question of whether courts might provide "declaratory relief" — a judicial declaration on whether rights have been unreasonably infringed, but without invalidating the law in question — even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked had split the governments that filed arguments with the Supreme Court .

The federal government as well as the governments of Manitoba and British Columbia thought it permissible and potentially useful. Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec were opposed (Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon reiterated his province's opposition to declaratory relief on Friday).

The seven justices of the Supreme Court were also split, but with the majority in favour.

"The five-year expiry period set out in [the notwithstanding clause], which corresponds to the maximum duration of the House of Commons or a legislative assembly under s. 4 of the Charter, is clearly intended to place in the hands of the electorate the choice of whether to renew the override provision," Justice Nicholas Kasirer wrote in Friday's ruling.

"Furthermore, the court's opinion is useful for the public, particularly where a vulnerable minority is affected by an overriding statute."

WATCH | Critics warn of fallout from Bill 21 ruling: 'A full attack on Charter rights': Critics warn of fallout from Bill 21 ruling | Duration 1:59 Civil liberties advocates are condemning the Supreme Court of Canada's 4-3 ruling to uphold Quebec's Bill 21 on Nov. 27. Canada's top court found the use of the notwithstanding clause to shield the province's secularism law from constitutional challenges was applied correctly, though it also struck down one part, which banned members of the National Assembly from wearing face coverings. Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said the ruling opens 'the floodgates for a full attack on the Charter right of Canadians,' warning more provincial laws could follow Quebec’s path to target Canadians' constitutional rights.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O'Bonsawin concurred that, "courts have a crucial role to play in dialogue between the legislatures and electorate by informing both of the scope of a Charter right and whether and to what extent it is infringed by a statute that invokes the notwithstanding clause."

That courts can offer comment even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked also goes some way toward answering concerns about recent "pre-emptive" uses of the clause — when governments invoke the clause even before a court has had a chance to pass judgment on the law.

"The court confirmed that Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked," Sean Fraser, the federal justice minister, said in a statement on Friday. "This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy."

That may be of limited solace to those whose rights are in question. But it points back to the political arena.

The price of liberty?

Even if one disagrees with all previous uses of the clause there might still be a case for what Chrétien called a "safety valve" (one of those who pushed for the clause was Allan Blakeney, the NDP premier of Saskatchewan). And even critics of the clause might need to wrestle with arguments that there could be significant downsides to doing away with it — that, in the absence of a notwithstanding clause, courts might only become more politicized, with political leaders more incentivized to appoint judges who will decide a certain way (as it is in the United States).

A future court may some day decide that a particular use of the notwithstanding clause has gone too far (in Friday's ruling, three justices seemed to allow that there could be some theoretical outer limits). For now, the options for outright overriding the override may be limited to either the difficult (constitutional negotiations to amend the Charter) or the dangerous (reviving the federal Parliament's power to disallow provincial laws).

If the court had ruled on Friday that there were significant legal limits on the use of clause, the result could have been a constitutional crisis.

WATCH | Carney says his government won't use notwithstanding clause: Carney says his government won't use notwithstanding clause following Supreme Court ruling | Duration closed caption 2:50 Following Friday's Supreme Court of Canada decision to uphold most of Quebec's controversial secularism law, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government's job is to defend the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. 'The benefit of constitutionally protected rights is most important for minorities, those most vulnerable in our society,' Carney said.

At the federal level — where the notwithstanding clause has never been invoked — Sen. Peter Harder has proposed a bill that would at least establish new rules and requirements around any use of the clause by Parliament. Under Harder's bill, for instance, the support of two-thirds of MPs would be required to invoke the clause.

It would, in other words, make it somewhat more difficult to invoke the clause.

Eugene Forsey , the late senator and constitutional scholar, once colourfully described the notwithstanding clause as a "dagger pointed at the heart of our fundamental freedoms." One might agree with that sentiment and yet still agree with Roy McMurtry, the attorney general of Ontario in 1981, who said that "political accountability is the best safeguard against any improper use of the 'override clause.'"

If it has become too easy to invoke the notwithstanding clause in recent years, it is still likely not for the court to rewrite the Charter — to change the result of a compromise brokered by political actors. Rather, it suggests that political accountability has been lacking.

"For those who remain concerned about the override clause, let me remind them that it has been said that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance," Chrétien told the House in November 1981.

It is actually unclear who, if anyone, ever actually said that. But the sentiment might still be worthy.

"Pressure groups must remain vigilant," Chrétien said, commending the "vigilance" of women who were then pushing for Section 28 of the Charter, on gender rights, to be excluded from the notwithstanding clause. (On Friday, the Court found Section 28 did not invalidate Bill 21.)

Vigilance may not be the most satisfying answer. But it might be the best or only one available.

World.title: Kenneth Law apologizes in court to families of victims
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details of suicide.

An Ontario man who sold products online to people who used them to take their own lives apologized in court today to the families of his victims.

Kenneth Law, 61, said his actions were "categorically wrong" and vowed never to repeat them. He made the comments from the prisoner’s box after lawyers for the Crown and defence laid out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for him.

On Friday, prosecutors argued money was the motivation for Law, who sold potentially deadly substances and equipment online to people knowing they would likely use the products to take their own lives. They sought a 25-year sentence for Law in what they called an unprecedented case.

Law's lawyers, meanwhile, argued the 61-year-old was not a "mercenary predator" but rather a misguided man committed to his belief in the right to die and whose actions did not warrant a "de facto life sentence."

Law's reasons for selling his wares over nearly two and a half years were a focal point as the Crown and the defence laid out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.

The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.

Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law's crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway. Some delivered the message in person, others did so by video and others in written statements read by prosecutors.

WATCH | Documentary speaks to the families impacted by Law's operations: Kenneth Law case: Families reveal the devastating toll in 'The Poison Seller' | Duration closed caption 5:47 Mississauga’s Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to aiding suicide after selling lethal chemicals online to people around the world. A CBC investigation linked Law to at least 147 deaths, but the real number might never be known. The Poison Seller, a documentary from The Passionate Eye, examines the investigation that left families asking why police didn't halt his operations sooner, and the CBC’s Kelda Yuen sat down with the filmmaking team behind it. If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In Canada, you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline. Kids Help Phone is available at 1-800-668-6868, or by texting 686868.

Both sides noted the unique nature of the case and the resulting absence of meaningful jurisprudence as they made their arguments in a Newmarket, Ont., court.

"No case such as this has come before this court, and hopefully it never will again," said Crown attorney Katie Doherty. "Part of ensuring that that happens is to denounce and deter the offender's conduct with a sentence that is fit and proportionate in all the circumstances."

The scale of Law's operations should be counted as an aggravating factor, as should the fact that his actions "actually caused death," she argued.

Ninety-three people died because they used the products purchased from Law, including 12 teenagers, she said.

"These were vulnerable people ... What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

Law's intentions not altruistic: prosecutor

Law's actions run contrary to his claim of an altruistic purpose, the prosecutor argued. The only factor that determined whom he sold to was whether they paid upfront, she said.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr. Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's guilty plea, which spared grieving families a lengthy trial, and his lack of a prior criminal record count as mitigating factors, she said.

The maximum sentence for aiding suicide is 14 years and Crown attorney Katie Doherty argued today that Law should face 12 1/2 years for each count, with two to be served back to back and the rest at the same time.

After subtracting credit for the time Law has spent in custody since his arrest in May 2023, he would be left with 19 years and 7 1/2 months to serve.

'Mr. Law did not kill anyone': defence

Defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that while Law sold the victims the tools they used to end their lives, he was not "the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all of these victims to seek out his products in the first place," nor did he play a role in their decision to use the products in the way they did.

"In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone," he said.

Law's actions and sentence should also be considered in the context of the ongoing, unresolved debate in Canadian society over assisted dying, Gourlay argued.

"To be very clear, the context in no way justifies Mr. Law's choice to act outside of lawful bounds," he said.

WATCH | Families share the impact of Law's products: Kenneth Law case: Families reveal the devastating toll in 'The Poison Seller' | Duration closed caption 5:47 Mississauga’s Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to aiding suicide after selling lethal chemicals online to people around the world. A CBC investigation linked Law to at least 147 deaths, but the real number might never be known. The Poison Seller, a documentary from The Passionate Eye, examines the investigation that left families asking why police didn't halt his operations sooner, and the CBC’s Kelda Yuen sat down with the filmmaking team behind it. If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In Canada, you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline. Kids Help Phone is available at 1-800-668-6868, or by texting 686868.

"But in my submission, you do need to look at that social context in order to evaluate what a proportionate sentence for Mr. Law might look like, and you have to do that especially because of the relative dearth of meaningful sentencing jurisprudence in this area."

An appropriate sentence under the circumstances would be 12 years — nine for the cases involving sodium nitrite and three for those involving other equipment, to be served one after the other — minus credit for the time he's already served, the defence lawyer argued.

Law should also receive enhanced credit for his time in detention due to the particularly harsh conditions he faced, which included lockdowns, triple bunking and "a life-threatening case" of flesh-eating disease he contracted at the Maplehurst Correctional Complex, he argued.

Law shipped products to over 40 countries

Law's plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims.

Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced.

An agreed statement of fact presented after his plea said Law ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other products that can be used for self-harm.

He shipped products to people in more than 40 countries, knowing his customers were likely to use them for suicide, the document said.

Law also went on a forum where people talked about using certain substances to take their own life, at times leaving comments and referring people to his websites, it said.

World.title: 'Big fat lady' hawk who ate too many chickens to fly soars free once again
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The red-shouldered hawk who gobbled up neighbourhood chickens until she could no longer move is slimmed down and out on the town.

The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center liberated its prodigious patient to much fanfare on Friday after downgrading her diagnosis from "too fat to fly" to just "a little over-chubby."

"We have finally released our big fat lady," Katherine McGrath, of the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"She was definitely ready to get out of the hospital."

LISTEN | Interview with Katherine McGrath, Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center: As It Happens 4:59 'Big fat lady' hawk who ate too many chickens to fly soars free once again Katherine McGrath, director of operations at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal she'll miss the prodigious patient, but hopes to "never see her again."

The hefty hawk was found belly-up last month in a driveway in Roanoke, Va. Staff at the wildlife centre ruled out injuries or illness before declaring that she had simply feasted on too many fowls to fly.

She weighed 910 grams — almost twice the average weight for her species. Meanwhile, residents reported that their free-roaming chickens had been mysteriously vanishing from their yards.

'She was crazy'

McGrath says staff put the big bird on a diet of 20 grams of mouse or rat per day, paired with "prescribed exercise where we would literally just follow her around a pen to force her to fly back and forth."

Over the course of about a month of birdy bootcamp, the hawk lost 230 grams and was cleared for takeoff.

When the big day finally came, McGrath says she was rearing to go, squawking and wriggling until the very last moment.

"She was crazy," McGrath said. "She was literally bouncing in her crate."

Katherine McGrath, director of operations at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, released the hawk on Friday outside a high school in Roanoke. (Submitted by Katherine McGrath)

McGrath says the chicken-owning neighbours have been warned of the hawk's release, and the bird has been tagged in case she ever gets herself in trouble again.

But while she admits she'll miss her feisty patient, McGrath says she hopes to "never see her again."

"It's always better for the animal to be free," she said.

'Internationally famous'

Dozens of people came out on Friday to watch the hawk take flight outside the local high school.

"They had seen her online. They were just in love with her story," McGrath said. "Roanoke, Virginia, isn't a big town. So having something go internationally famous here, you know it's something to show up for."

McGrath says the hawk didn't appreciate her brief stint in captivity, and that's a good thing. (Submitted by Katherine McGrath)

She says it's unlikely this experience has taught the bird a lesson about the dangers of overindulging on local, organic poultry. After all, she says, it's perfectly natural for a wild animal to gorge when it finds an abundance of food ahead of the long, lean winter.

But being caged, manhandled and put on a forced diet has probably taught her to deplore humans even more than she already did, which was quite a bit. While the wildlife staff loved her, McGrath says the feeling was decidedly not mutual.

"So, hopefully, she'll be a little more wary of people, which will help her stay away from those chickens," she said.

World.title: Lululemon founder makes 'egregious' remarks about women at Calgary leadership forum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It was meant to be an intimate chat about entrepreneurship with the founder of Lululemon.

Instead, Chip Wilson is under fire for his "egregious" comments about women's bodies and reproductive choices, which reportedly included his assertions that men are importing brides from Thailand to have their children.

"It sounds like you’re painting a future reminiscent of The Handmaid’s Tale," Nuvyn Peters, the CEO of non-profit Axis Connects, told Wilson during the fireside chat on Monday at the Axis Connects Leadership Forum in Calgary, referring to Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel.

More than 700 business leaders attended the women's forum, where some of the s peakers included former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, Olympic ice dancing gold medallist Tessa Virtue, musician Jann Arden and Wilson — the billionnaire founder of Lululemon Athletica who stepped down as company CEO in 2013.

Wilson's talk does not appear to be posted anywhere online. But CBC News has confirmed with two attendees at the forum that his comments, first reported by the Globe and Mail, are correct.

A screengrab of an Instagram post by Axis Connects from Oct. 1 advertises Lululemon founder Chip Wilson as a speaker at its Nov. 23 leadership forum in Calgary. (@axisconnects/Instagram)

They include that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development and that the top female brands are run by men because men know what looks good on women's bodies.

Wilson, 71, who was born in Los Angeles and has dual American-Canadian citizenship, also said that men are resorting to importing brides from other countries like Thailand, according to the attendees who spoke with CBC News.

Calgary career coach Madeleine Natale was at Monday's event and described Wilson's comments as "egregious."

"Coming on the heels of the empowering talk by Jann Arden, it felt like the wind was knocked right out of my sails," Natale said. "In this day and age, attention is one of the most precious gifts we can give. It didn't take me long to realize that my attention was not a gift I wanted to give during that talk."

'Concern and disappointment'

Wilson's event at the women-focused leadership forum was advertised online as an "intimate fireside chat" and an "honest conversation about how a serial entrepreneur thinks, builds, struggles and keeps moving forward."

CBC News reached out to Wilson but has not yet heard back. But a spokesperson for him told the Globe and Mail earlier this week, "This is an effort to discount Chip Wilson’s record of mentoring women who have become executives and entrepreneurs in their own right to drive revenue with a clickbait headline."

It's not Wilson's first controversy. He stepped down as Lululemon CEO in 2013 during the fallout from his comments that seemed to blame people's bodies for an issue the company was having with its pants being too sheer. That year, the company had recalled nearly one-fifth of its pants because of the problem.

"Quite frankly, some women's bodies just actually don't work for it," Wilson said in a Bloomberg TV interview. "It's really about the rubbing through the thighs, how much pressure is there."

A Lululemon store is shown in Toronto in November 2025. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Wilson, who remains one of Lululemon's top shareholders, also came under fire in 2024 for comments blasting the company's inclusion and diversity efforts, in which he o bjected to the company's use of models with a range of body types.

Axis Connects, a non-profit that works to advance women in business leadership roles, said Wilson's comments on Monday don't align with its values.

"We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the leadership forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects," the organization said in a statement to CBC News.

"We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community."

Natale, the career coach, said she's "very disappointed" by what she heard Wilson say on Monday, but she also wants the conversation to move on from one person's voice.

"I am choosing not to give these words any more of my energy than that," she said.

She lamented that Wilson's comments have received so much attention, " when so many other women's voices from the conference should be amplified." Arden, for instance, spoke about adapting to change and "held everyone's rapt attention," Natale said.

"This is a moment in time where we can all think a little more deeply about the challenges women continue to face in leadership."

World.title: Pedestrian killed in crash involving off-duty Vancouver police officer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A pedestrian was killed in Vancouver's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood Friday morning in a crash involving an off-duty police officer.

The officer was sent to hospital in critical but stable condition.

Vancouver police Supt. Dale Weidman said the officer was driving their personal vehicle northbound on Main Street at approximately 9:30 a.m. PT when the crash happened.

The officer crossed the intersection at Broadway and struck a light pole on the northwest corner of the intersection, hitting a pedestrian, Weidman said.

Vancouver police officers gather at the scene of a fatal crash at Main Street and East Broadway on Friday. (Shawn Foss/CBC)

The pedestrian, a woman believed to be in her 40s, died at the scene. Police say she was a local resident.

Weidman said the driver, a 49-year-old off-duty Vancouver police officer who has been with the department for two years, was alone in the vehicle.

Police say the investigation is in its early stages and have not determined what caused the vehicle to leave its path and strike the pole.

The Independent Investigations Office of B.C. (IIO), which investigates incidents involving police officers that result in death or serious injury, will take over the investigation.

B.C. Emergency Health Services said it received a call about the collision at 9:26 a.m.

Two ambulances staffed by primary care paramedics, three ambulances staffed by advanced care paramedics and a paramedic supervisor responded.

World.title: 'Breast bowl' from Marie-Antoinette's pleasure dairy sets new record at auction
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A rare porcelain "breast bowl" that France's Louis XVI commissioned for Marie-Antoinette back in the 18th century sold for about $4.5 million in Paris Thursday.

The unconventionally shaped drinking vessel (known as a jatte-téton) is a delicate porcelain bowl that imitates the shape of a woman's breast, complete with rosy pink nipple, and sits atop a tripod decorated with scrolling foliage and a trio of goat heads.

It sold for 2.925 million euros via the French auction house Coutau-Bégarie, marking a record high price achieved at auction for a piece by Sèvres — the famed porcelain manufacturer favoured by European royals in the latter half of the 18th century and early 19th century.

Long believed lost, the bowl turned up by chance in a crate at the Galerie Meyer in Paris, the auction venue l'Hôtel Drouot said in a social media post touting the record-setting sale.

Organizers had estimated it would sell for between one and two million euros (about $1.5 million to $3.1 million).

French auction venue l'Hôtel Drouot touted the record-setting price online. Three other such bowls from the original set are on display in public collections. (Hôtel Drouot/Instagram)

The identity of the buyer was not disclosed.

Proceeds of Thursday's sale will benefit breast cancer research, with the seller, auctioneer and venue each earmarking a portion of the sale's revenue for the French non-profit l'Association Ruban Rose.

Created for 'pleasure dairy'

Marie-Antoinette wasn't a fan of their Rambouillet estate, southwest of Paris, when Louis purchased it. So, to win her over, the king built her a luxurious "pleasure dairy" on the estate where she could entertain nobles and enjoy treats like fresh milk, cheeses and ice cream.

As part of the lavish gift, he commissioned Sèvres artisans to create a sumptuous set of porcelain servingware — including a quartet of jatte-téton, which were inspired by mastos, Greek breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets.

Though an urban legend purports the shape was moulded from Marie-Antoinette's own breast, Sèvres experts have dismissed the notion.

The three other Rambouillet breast bowls can be seen in the collections of France's National Ceramics Museum in Sèvres and Duca di Martina Museum in Naples.

World.title: The bizarre twists and turns of Colombia’s supermarket hostage siege
World.content:
Blackout drunk kidnappers, false statements by De La Espriella, and bogus accusations against hostages leave a trail of chaos and doubt.

Shortly after 76 hostages were liberated from the Exito Supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, corporate media broadcast a video of two of the men they claimed were involved in the attack.

​The two men, Carlos Tapia and Daniel Díaz, appeared in handcuffs, being escorted by police from the scene of a tense 18-hour standoff between criminals and police.

The media, with information from President Abelardo de la Espriella, suggested that Tapia and Diaz were two of four surviving members of the gang that attacked the supermarket.

​De la Espriella praised the operation he said “came off perfectly,” and released a video of himself mocking two different men, who police say were the actual kidnappers, together with one more person who was killed in the operation.

The president also released a video of himself making demands into a walkie-talkie, falsely claiming that he was in charge of negotiations with the hostage-takers.

According to the indictment from the Prosecutor’s Office, all negotiations and communications with the three hostage takers were handled by Colombia’s anti-kidnapping police unit, the GAULA.

​Tapia and Díaz were released by police just a few hours later, and cleared of any wrongdoing after police confirmed the men were hostages rather than hostage-takers. De la Espriella confirmed shortly afterwards that the men were innocent of any crimes.

​The two men have since both spoken with Colombian media, in interviews in which both men claimed they were mocked by De la Espriella and treated badly by police before being cleared.

​A third man, Edgar Díaz, was also falsely accused by police. He released a video to social media as well, claiming that not only was he mocked and verbally abused by the President, but also robbed of a gold chain by police. Diaz says he was leaving a gym where he works as a personal trainer, in the same mall as the Exito, when he was grabbed by men who appeared to be armed.

The stories of the falsely accused hostages aren’t the only odd parts of the official story surrounding the stand-off between 3 nominally armed men and hundreds of marines, police, snipers, helicopters, and riot police in the city of Cali.

​One of the hostage-takers was killed by police when they entered the supermarket around 1 a.m., after the hostage-takers missed a deadline of 12:30 to release all hostages.

​According to police, the three men attempted to rob an armored car transporting money around 8 a.m., but the car had already left by the time the men arrived. For unclear reasons, the three decided to take nearly 100 people hostage in the Exito supermarket instead, which is part of the same “mega-mall” where the men allegedly intended to carry out the hijacking.

​Two of the men carried long guns that, again according to police, were “traumatic weapons” (similar to Airsoft rifles, the weapons fire foam bullets meant to be non-lethal), and one was armed with another that resembled a shotgun.

Early in the morning, before the men blocked windows in the supermarket, Colombian media captured one of the men from a distance clad in black tactical clothing, body armor, and what appeared to be a heavy steel helmet with a facemask.

​Many of those who were held hostage, speaking with media, said the men were drinking heavily throughout the day, with one witness going as far as to say they were “blind drunk” by the end of the day.

​Workers at the Éxito, who were also taken hostage, said the men set up large speakers, blasted music, and demanded to be given bottles of whisky.

​The two men who survived the police assault that liberated the hostages were asleep when police entered the Éxito, likely why they survived, according to multiple witnesses.

​Confusing matters even further, the wife of the man who was reportedly killed by police, Javier Humberto Muñetón Zapata, had spent the previous 14 hours speaking with local media in Cartagena, looking for her husband, who she believed to be among the hostages.

​She says they lived nearby and went to the mall every day, and that her husband had a membership at the same gym where Diaz works. She claims she began searching for her husband, who had promised to drive her to work and bring pastries from the supermarket, after he suddenly stopped replying to texts.

​She showed Blue Radio a text message at 8:12 a.m. from her husband that said, “Okay, I’m going to pop into Éxito, and I’ll pick you up right away.”

​She claims that her husband ran a small business, regularly drove her to work, and has no criminal record — a fact that has since been confirmed by Cartgena’s mayor. She has made multiple statements to the media asking for clarification and more information, claiming he could not have been involved in any crimes.

Early statements by police, shortly after the hostage situation began to unfold, put the number of hostages at 50. After two releases of hostages by the nominal gunmen, police stated they believed 20 hostages remained as evening approached.

​Shortly after the operation to enter the Éxito, police released details about their raid, claiming that they had “drilled holes in the walls and inserted cameras,” allowing them to identify the kidnappers and estimate the number of hostages.

​They also stated they had men on the roof, in the warehouse of the supermarket, and stationed at the interior entrance to the Éxito, which connects to the mega-mall.

​But more than 70 hostages remained when the raid was successfully carried out.

The attackers claimed in a letter to authorities that if the store was entered by police they would detonate explosives placed near the entrances, killing the hostages.

Police later revealed there were no explosives, and the men were bluffing.

​The two men who were captured alive (and reportedly asleep), Juan Camilo Torres Manco, 33, and Jhon Albeiro Mejía Blandón, 44, are both from Antioquia and have previous convictions for “violent” crimes, according to police.

​Both men appeared intoxicated in videos shortly after they were captured. De la Espriella released a video in which he berates the two men, telling them, “You thought you could just kidnap people and get away with it? Welcome to the miracle country.”

​The bizarre details of the event, as well as misreporting by the media, inaccurate and even contradictory statements by police throughout the day, and general confusion, led some critics of De le Espriella to claim the entire event was staged.

De la Espriella’s efforts to insert himself into the situation, and false claims made by the president, worsened that dynamic.

​There is no evidence currently to support those claims, but with a story that is just straight-up strange, we can see how some people came to that conclusion.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: The deteriorating press freedom in Colombia and the Americas
World.content:
I sat down with Joshua Collins of Pirate Wire Services to discuss the deteriorating press freedom situation in Colombia and the rest of Latin America.
