“There can be no enlightened citizenry if citizens live with the fear of prosecution whenever they gain the courage to call out government wrongs,” he said in his eight-page opinion.

World.title: Baligod, group ordered arrested for cyberlibel
World.content:
Atty. Levito Baligod. Photo: Atty. Levito Baligod/FB)

A court in Lanao del Sur has ordered the arrest of lawyer Levito Baligod and the 18 witnesses under his watch for cyberlibel charges filed by a lawmaker.

According to the arrest warrant issued by Presiding Judge Samina Sampaco Macabando-Usman of Branch 8 of the Marawi City Regional Trial Court, bail was set at P30,000 for each of the accused.

READ: Arrest order issued vs Baligod, 18 bodyguards for cyber libel raps

Article continues after this 

It was not stated in the arrest warrant who the complainant was. But it will be recalled that Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong confirmed in June that he had filed cyberlibel charges against Baligod and his witnesses, all alleged bodyguards of fugitive and former lawmaker Zaldy Co.

‘Actual malice’

The 18 had claimed earlier that they delivered suitcases of cash to the lawmaker on Co’s behalf.

Adiong said in a statement back then he would seek a total of P25 million in damages due to that claim.

“The accusations hurled against me by the respondents are absolute fabrications, total falsehoods and malicious inventions,” Adiong said in his affidavit at that time. “I have never met any of these eighteen individuals. I have never received any suitcase of cash from anyone, and I have absolutely no involvement in the anomalous transactions they describe.”

Adiong said in his complaint the respondents “acted with actual malice because they published an unverified, logistically impossible narrative with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false.”

Article continues after this 

The complaint stemmed from a Feb. 24 press conference where Baligod and the 18 claimed that lawmakers had received kickbacks from Co when he was chairperson of the House committee on appropriations, in charge of infrastructure projects.

Despite Adiong’s denial, Baligod and his witnesses repeated that claim only on Thursday during a hearing by the Senate blue-ribbon committee prompted by the group of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano.

Article continues after this 

Adiong is not the only lawmaker to pursue charges against the Baligod group. Manila Rep. Bienvenido Abante Jr. had also filed cyberlibel charges against them over the same allegation, as did House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin.

World.title: ‘Fire on the shore’: Church sets mass action on SC fisheries ruling
World.content:
His Eminence, Pablo Virgilio S. Cardinal David, D.D., Bishop of Kalookan (Photo from Diocese of Kalookan)

Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David on Friday urged the Supreme Court to reconsider two rulings that weaken protections for small-scale fisherfolk and called on Church communities and concerned citizens to join a rally at the high tribunal next week.

In a pastoral statement titled “The Fire on the Shore,” David said on Friday the Dec. 3 rally that would gather fishers, clergy and young people would be a “peaceful but determined assembly, because to appeal to the Court is not to defy it.”

READ: CBCP joins call to protect fisherfolk, municipal waters after SC ruling

Article continues after this 

The appeal comes as small-scale fisherfolk face mounting challenges to their livelihood as rising fuel prices make it increasingly difficult for them to venture out to sea.

“Even the limited fishing grounds that sustain their families are under threat,” he said.

Implications

Two Supreme Court rulings could affect their access to municipal waters as well as the government’s ability to monitor commercial fishing vessels that compete with small fishers.

One ruling opened municipal waters to large-scale commercial fishing, while the other invalidated an existing regulation requiring electronic monitoring of commercial fishing vessels.

The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) has backed David’s appeal. Its president, Archbishop Gilbert Garcera of Lipa, endorsed his statement along with 30 other archbishops and bishops.

Article continues after this 

“We reaffirm our commitment to defending the rights and livelihood of our small-scale fisherfolk, whose preferential access to our communal marine and fishing resources is guaranteed by our Constitution,” Garcera said.

Call to assemble

He called on dioceses, parishes, religious communities, Catholic schools and lay organizations to support the initiative and take part in the Dec. 3 assembly.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cardinal David urges SC to review rulings on small-scale fishers

“May we never remain indifferent to their plight but instead become instruments of justice, compassion, and hope,” Garcera said.

Under the Philippine Fisheries Code, municipal waters extending up to 15 kilometers from the shoreline are primarily reserved for small-scale fisherfolk.

David cited Article XIII, Section 7 of the Constitution, which directs the state to protect the preferential rights of subsistence fishers to communal marine and fishing resources.

He questioned why commercial fishing operators with the means to venture farther out to sea should compete with small-scale fisherfolk whose boats can travel only a few kilometers.

Justice, not charity

“Are we opening the gates while disabling the very instruments that allow us to see who enters?” David said.

He said fisherfolk were not asking for charity but for justice. He called on the Supreme Court to uphold the constitutional protections for fishers.

“They are asking the guardians of our Constitution to uphold the rights that the Constitution itself guarantees them, in keeping with the principle that those who have less in life should have more in law,” David said.

He also called on Congress to strengthen protections for municipal waters and ensure the effective monitoring of commercial fishing vessels.

Your subscription could not be saved. Please try again. Your subscription has been successful. Subscribe to our daily newsletter SIGN ME UP

“This Advent season, let us give our fisherfolk a reason to hope, a reason to cast their nets again and something warm to come home to after a long night at sea,” David said. “Let us not allow Christmas to remain dark for our fellow fisherfolk. Together, let us light the fire of hope and justice for them.”

World.title: ‘Falling car’ probe: Building flaws or driving error?
World.content:
ACCIDENT SCENE Policemen secure the spot where a car landed after it fell from a fourth floor parking area of a hotel in Makati City on Thursday. The car’s driver died. —MAKATI CITY CENTRAL POLICE STATION PHOTOS

Police are looking into the health condition of the man driving a car that fell from the parking area of a hotel building in Makati City on Thursday, as investigators continue to determine if there was negligence or criminal liability involved in the incident.

In an interview on Friday, Lt. Margaret Panaga, public information officer of the Southern Police District, said the 55-year-old driver, who was employed by an “agency” that the police did not name, was a reliever designated to fetch a passenger on Thursday.

READ: Driver dies as car falls from 4th floor of Makati building

Article continues after this 

The driver died after his car fell from the fourth floor parking area of Citadines Benavidez Makati, an establishment offering serviced apartments and hotel rooms, on Benavidez and Jimenez streets in Makati.

Panaga said the driver was not used to driving the car involved in the accident as it was not the vehicle that he usually drove.

“We are awaiting the autopsy results to determine if the victim had any underlying health conditions. We are also looking into the parking facilities, specifically whether there were any lapses in their safety measures,” she said.

Coordination

According to the initial investigation of police, the victim was descending the driveway when he lost control of the car after hitting a wall. The wayward vehicle then struck a bollard before it fell into the street.

The management of Citadines Benavidez Makati said it was coordinating with authorities in the ongoing investigation.

Article continues after this 

“We are cooperating fully with the relevant authorities and remain in contact with individuals involved as investigations take place, while fulfilling our responsibilities in accordance with applicable laws and regulations,” it said in a statement on Thursday.

Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. ordered law enforcement authorities to coordinate with building administrators to identify potential hazards in public spaces that may put people at risk to prevent similar incidents.

Article continues after this 

“Our police commanders should strengthen coordination with local government units, building administrators and concerned agencies to … address safety concerns and ensure that threats to public safety are brought to the attention of the proper authorities,” Nartatez said in a statement on Friday.

World.title: Luistro on next defense witness: Same banana?
World.content:
Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro. —NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro on Friday reminded Vice President Sara Duterte and her defense lawyers that Cale88, a company registered as a banana chips maker and now under scrutiny in Duterte’s impeachment trial, is just one piece of the bigger puzzle regarding her alleged unexplained wealth.

Luistro said she also expected the next testimonies to be a mere “duplication” of what was said earlier this week about the company.

READ: Luistro to VP camp: Cale88 is just ‘one portion’ of allegations

Article continues after this 

Speaking as head of the House prosecution panel, Luistro made the remark after it was revealed that the defense would be calling two more witnesses to testify on Cale88, after hearing from two others earlier this week.

One of the upcoming witnesses is Dr. Lourdes Lebosada, a dentist of the Vice President and reportedly a former co-owner of Cale88 along with Duterte’s husband, lawyer Mans Carpio.

Luistro said she expected Lebosada to just repeat what had been established about the company’s background—but say nothing that can directly answer the prosecution’s allegations.

“With Dr. Lebosada, I think that will be a duplication of what has been testified to already by the previous witnesses,” she said. “Will she testify on the extent of ownership, registration with BOI (Board of Investments) and FDA (Food and Drug Administration)?”

Exciting

“Let us be reminded that the specific allegation of the prosecution dwells on the P817 million. This is (Duterte’s) unexplained wealth, undeclared property, and this Cale88 transaction is just a portion of the same,” Luistro added.

Article continues after this 

“So, I hope they also cover the huge part of this unexplained wealth and undeclared property (issues), which is the bulk, the substance, the core of the specific allegations of the prosecution,” she said.

Luistro stressed that, as earlier explained by financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera as an expert witness for the prosecution, the P817 million the Vice President allegedly failed to declare in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth involved more than just the money associated with Cale88.

Article continues after this 

Also on Friday, fellow House prosecutor and Bicol Saro Rep. Terry Ridon said the panel may ask Lebrosa about Cale88’s income.

Aside from the dentist, the defense is expected to present Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Agaton Teodoro Uvero.

“We will wait (for) the presentation of evidence. We expect that with the (testimony from an official of) BOC, they would want to show that there is really a legitimate exportation of their banana chips. And second, with Dr. Lebosada, I think this will be an exciting part of this trial,” Ridon said.

“They are among the few who can really shed light on the undeclared P500 million out of the P700 million that entered Cale88’s bank accounts. Because if we remember, we saw that they only declared around P200 million in Cale88’s financial statement,” he added.

World.title: Sara Duterte ‘prepared for worst’ as trial nears decision
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte attends the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P785.204-million 2027 budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) at the Session Hall of the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay City on Thursday, November 26, 2026.INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

Vice President Sara Duterte said on Friday that her office and staff would conduct business as usual if she were acquitted in her Senate impeachment trial, but she was also prepared “for the worst” in case she is convicted.

Duterte is being tried for unexplained wealth, which allegedly amounts to at least P817 million and possibly up to P1.5 billion, according to the prosecution panel of the House of Representatives.

READ: VP Duterte prepared for verdict of Senate impeachment court

Article continues after this 

Duterte met with reporters on Friday for “thanksgiving,” a day after she visited the Senate, which approved the proposed P785.2-million budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for 2027. It was her second time showing up at the Senate since her impeachment trial began in July.

“We’re always preparing for the worst,” Duterte said when asked about her thoughts on the possible outcome of the trial.

“We will accept whatever is the judgment of the Senate impeachment court with the impeachment trial,” she said.

“We will have to deal with the consequences of this out-of-mind decision of President Marcos,” Duterte added, pointing out that she was elected by popular vote.

READ: VP Sara Duterte’s dentist expected as next defense witness

Article continues after this 

“I will be replaced by someone who is appointed by the President,” she said. “So, think about it if it will be accepted by the people, if it will help them in how they will relate to the government that is, in the first place, very fragile, because people are truly disappointed in government.”

Duterte, who has announced that she would be running for President in the 2028 national elections, will be removed as Vice President if she is found guilty and could be banned from ever holding public office.

Article continues after this 

Article VII of the 1987 Constitution mandates the president to nominate a senator or a member of the House to serve as vice president in case of a vacancy. The nominee will assume office once a majority of the Senate and the House vote to confirm his choice.

Duterte expressed concern that once she is removed from office, OVP employees who are coterminous with her would lose their jobs. She added that around 300 families in the OVP satellite offices across the country may also be affected.

In addition, the OVP staff may also have to move out of the building in Mandaluyong that they have occupied since the 2022 election campaign, which she and Mr. Marcos won. The erstwhile allies had a falling out in 2024.

Duterte also told reporters that she was planning to sell several properties to pay the P5 million she owed her friends to cover her expenses in her impeachment trial and in the crimes against humanity case her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, is facing before the International Criminal Court. These include her visits to him in The Hague.

She did not say how much she had spent in total for the two cases. She said, however, that her expenses this year may be higher than last year’s as she has not yet paid her debt to her friends.

She noted that she had already announced two properties in Davao City that she planned to sell.

Duterte said one of her lawyers in the impeachment case, Michael Poa, had constantly told her not to pay him.

“Although he says not to pay him, but I was also a lawyer, and I know how difficult the job is, that’s why I need to pay their legal fees,” Duterte said.

Done by Dec. 18?

Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro, the lead House prosecutor, earlier said she hoped that the trial would end on Dec. 18, the last session day of Congress before it adjourns for the Christmas holiday.

The prosecution presented at least 40 witnesses in the charges against Duterte and the defense presented eight so far. The trial will resume on Dec. 1. —WITH A REPORT FROM INQUIRER RESEARCH

World.title: Congress urged to redirect flood control funding to Mindanao
World.content:
Mel Senen Sarmiento—OPAPRU PHOTO

COTABATO CITY—Presidential Peace Adviser Mel Senen Sarmiento had asked Congress to boost government’s funding for peacebuilding initiatives to help transition once war-torn communities into peaceful and productive zones, using funds cut from flood control projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

This developed as the Senate on Friday approved its P9.4-billion budget for 2027.

READ: Opapru to Congress: Divert flood control funding for ‘peace investments’

Article continues after this 

“The peace investment will fund ongoing transformation programs for former combatants, their families, and their communities across the agency’s various peace tables,” the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (Opapru) said in a statement.

“These include the implementation of peace agreements and normalization tracks with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), localized peace engagements with former communist rebels, and closure agreements with the Cordillera Bodong Administration-Cordillera People’s Liberation Army (CBA-CPLA) and the Rebolusyonaryong Partido ng Manggagawa ng Pilipinas-Revolutionary Proletarian Army-Alex Boncayao Brigade (RPM-P/RPA/ABB),” it added.

Sarmiento thanked the Senate for its steadfast support, noting that the budget is critical to sustaining peacebuilding interventions on the ground.

“We extend our deepest gratitude to the Senate for approving this P9.4-billion peace investment. Their support is a strong vote of confidence in our collective mission to bring lasting peace and inclusive development to conflict-affected areas,” Sarmiento said.

“Every peso here is an investment in stability. By empowering former combatants and their families through our transformation programs, we are ensuring that the gains of our peace process become irreversible,” he added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ex-DOE chief: Tap flood infra funds for Visayas power

Sarmiento said the agency is still seeking additional support, in line with the directive of President Marcos toward the eventual signing of the exit agreements—particularly those under the Bangsamoro peace process—before the President’s term ends.

Article continues after this 

In a statement on Thursday, Sarmiento explained that this additional funding would enable the Opapru to effectively carry out and expand its ongoing programs, fulfill existing commitments under all signed peace agreements, and sustain the continued transformation of former combatants.

The Opapru carries out peace deals the government inked with formers rebels of the CPLA, RPM-P/RPA/ABB, MNLF and MILF.

The funds also cover various socioeconomic initiatives, including Payapa at Masaganang Pamayanan infrastructure projects in conflict-affected and conflict-vulnerable areas nationwide.

‘Significant progress’

“We have made significant progress in pushing forward our nation’s comprehensive peace process. But we cannot afford to lose momentum. Peacebuilding requires sustained peace investments, and we need adequate resources to ensure that the gains we have achieved are preserved and strengthened,” he said in a statement.

Sarmiento’s move came as the southern Philippines started the celebrations for the annual Mindanao Week of Peace on Nov. 26.

Congress is currently deliberating the 2027 budget for various line agencies, including Opapru.

Sarmiento expressed optimism his proposal will be considered by Congress.

“This is not just a matter of implementing projects. Our main goal is to invest in lasting peace. Therefore, our peace agreements and commitments must translate into real opportunities that will uplift the lives of our people who have endured decades of armed conflict,” he stressed.

Opapru’s mandate covers several peace tables and programs, with each requiring significant government support and resources to ensure that they make an impact on the lives of the people and their communities, the peace adviser said.

Resilient communities

Aside from the implementation of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, Opapru is also working closely with the regular Bangsamoro government and other local and international partners to transform former MILF camps into productive and resilient communities.

In the same statement, Sarmiento said the implementation of the Transformation Program for MNLF members, as well as the Local Peace Engagement and its Transformation Program for former rebels, their families, and communities continues to gain ground.

All these require sufficient funding that Congress has the power to consider, especially as the government strengthens its engagement with local government units, civil society organizations, indigenous communities and former rebel-led people’s organizations, Sarmiento said.

“The signing of peace agreements is only the beginning of more work ahead. We must help communities rebuild, provide livelihood opportunities, improve access to basic services and create an environment where people can live with dignity and security,” he added.

Sarmiento said investing in peacebuilding complements the government’s broader development agenda while roads, bridges, and other infrastructure are essential to improving people’s lives.

World.title: More Multinationals Exit Myanmar as Economic Turmoil Deepens
World.content:
At least four more international brands announced their withdrawal from Myanmar this month, as deepening post-coup turmoil triggers a fresh exodus of foreign investment.

They joined a broader retreat of multinational businesses since the 2021 military takeover, driven by regime import and currency controls, soaring production costs, power outages, and international sanctions.

On Thursday, Singapore-based Pezzo Pizza announced it would close all branches in Myanmar starting today (Nov. 27), ending 10 years of operations. The company entered the market in 2016, operating five branches across Yangon and Mandalay.

The announcement came a day after The Manhattan Fish Market shuttered its last Yangon outlet, at Myanmar Plaza, ending the Malaysia-based seafood chain’s 12-year presence.

On Nov. 13, Japanese automaker Isuzu announced it had ended Myanmar repair and maintenance operations after liquidating its local service unit.

Meanwhile, British consumer goods giant Unilever will exit Myanmar after 16 years by selling its shares to Centig Holding, a subsidiary of local partner Europe and Asia Commercial (EAC), with the deal expected to close in 2027.

While the four companies gave no reason for their exit, the World Bank 2026 report notes that Myanmar’s private sector is operating in “a highly challenging and uncertain environment” driven by conflict, macroeconomic pressures, policy reversal and weakening state capacity. It adds that firms are facing “higher cost, greater compliance risks, [and] weaker incentives to invest, expand and innovate.”

According to a Myanmar Peace Monitor report released on Nov. 27, the post-coup flight of foreign investment encompasses nearly 40 multinational companies across 16 countries ranging from neighboring Thailand, Malaysia and India to the U.S., UK, Spain, Germany, Austria, Italy and Norway. It said the withdrawals were being driven by the spread of armed conflict and a collapsing business environment.

The departing businesses span major sectors such as oil and gas, mining, banking, telecommunications, real estate, and manufacturing, including 12 global clothing brands whose exit has dealt a severe blow to local garment workers.

“More companies are monitoring the situation and planning exit strategies,” a Myanmar policy analyst told The Irrawaddy, blaming currency controls and raw material shortages triggered by regime import controls.

“Foreign investors can’t endure these losses any longer,” he said, adding that he expects the situation to worsen amid rising unemployment, soaring inflation and shortages of basic goods.

World.title: Beijing Shields Myanmar Regime After Genocide Ruling, Naypyitaw Begs for Energy Investment, and More
World.content:
Myanmar seeks more Chinese energy investment at Belt and Road forum

Naypyitaw’s reliance on China for energy investment, fuel supplies and electricity infrastructure is deepening all the time, with Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin using his latest trip to China to seek yet more investment across the sector.

At the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministers’ Conference in Qingdao on Nov. 25-26, Ko Ko Lwin met officials from China’s National Energy Administration (NEA), urging them to help Myanmar meet its electricity and energy needs. Discussions covered new offshore gas exploration, hydropower projects, cross-border power lines, solar and wind projects, and energy storage batteries.

Much the same topics were on the agenda when Ko Ko Lwin traveled to Kunming and Beijing in April to secure lower rates for fuel imports from a number of Chinese firms. Myanmar relies on imports for 97 percent of its gasoline and diesel needs, a dependence that had already taken a serious toll on the cash-strapped regime before the Middle East crisis triggered shortages and price hikes.

Regime officials are also asking Chinese state enterprises to invest in refinery projects linked to the Myanmar–China oil pipeline network. In April the regime signed a deal with China’s North Petro-Chem to increase production at the Htaukshabin-Kanni oil field in Magwe Region’s Minbu.

It has also revived the Thanlyin No. 1 Oil Refinery near Yangon with Chinese assistance, potentially enabling it to bypass jet-fuel sanctions and sustain air operations. The facility’s expected output of up to 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually roughly matching Myanmar’s imports last year.

China defends Myanmar regime after ICJ genocide ruling

China has publicly defended Myanmar after the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s landmark ruling that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing “noted” the ruling but argued that the Rakhine issue should be handled cautiously given its “complex historical, ethnic and religious dimensions.” He urged the international community to avoid “complicating” the issue and reiterated China’s support for dialogue and the repatriation of displaced Rohingya.

China also raised concerns about what it called judicial “overreach” and questions of jurisdiction by international courts.

The ruling stems from a case brought by the Gambia over the Myanmar military’s 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighboring Bangladesh.

Guo also defended the Chinese judge on the ICJ, Xue Hanqin, who voted in Myanmar’s favor, saying she had “acted independently in her personal capacity.”

As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China has consistently pushed back against international pressure on Myanmar over the Rohingya crisis, arguing that it should be resolved through dialogue and cooperation between Myanmar and Bangladesh rather than external intervention.

However, the ruling, the first finding of state responsibility for genocide in the ICJ’s 81-year history, places China in an awkward position while it continues to shield Naypyitaw from international pressure and deepens ties with a military regime now found guilty of one of the world’s worst atrocities in recent decades.

China drawn deeper into Myanmar–Thai river pollution dispute

China has promised to dispatch experts to help investigate river pollution affecting Mekong tributaries in Thailand due to unregulated Chinese-invested mining across the border in Myanmar.

The announcement came after a meeting in Bangkok on Tuesday where Thailand urged China to help halt mining operations in Shan State for at least six months as the Kok, Sai, Ruak and Mekong rivers flowing into northern Thailand are contaminated, threatening human health and livelihoods.

Thailand’s Pollution Control Department has repeatedly found arsenic, lead, cadmium and other heavy metals above safety limits in the rivers, tracing the pollution to unregulated gold and rare-earth mines in Shan State. Most of them are run by Chinese people in areas controlled by China-linked armed groups like the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Thailand and Myanmar agreed to conduct their first joint testing of the Kok and Sai next month. But while pledging to participate in the investigation, Beijing stopped short of agreeing to the proposed shutdown and cautioned against drawing “premature conclusions.”

Instead, the Foreign Ministry spokesman claimed Chinese companies operating overseas are required to comply with local laws and environmental regulations—except that these are non-existent in the lawless borderlands of Myanmar.

Still, China seems to feel it can no longer completely dodge the issue as Thailand has brought it up at every high-level meeting, no matter how amiable, in recent weeks amid growing outrage and protests at home.

Chinese scammers move with the times

Shaken up by major crackdowns on Myanmar’s border scam hubs, online fraud networks now infest other parts of the country, from upscale condominiums in the commercial capital Yangon to remote corners of Shan State.

Since mid-November, the military regime has reported a series of raids that netted more than 570 suspected online scammers and gambling operators, over 400 of them Chinese.

In Yangon, the raids in Yankin, Mayangone and Thaketa townships resulted in nearly 230 arrests. Nearly half of them were Myanmar nationals who reportedly worked voluntarily for their Chinese bosses. In Thaketa, arrests included a Chinese ringleader wanted by China’s Public Security Ministry, but in Yankin the boss escaped, throwing his workers under the bus.

In southern Shan around the same time, some 330 Chinese scammers and around 20 Myanmar women were arrested in Kyethi and Mong Kung townships. In Kyethi, they were nabbed with a cache of rifles and pistols.

Now some major border scam centers have been dismantled under pressure from Beijing, operators appear to have dispersed across the country, running smaller, more mobile operations. But in Myawaddy near the Thai border, big compounds still thrive under the protection of regime-aligned ethnic militias.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Garment Sector Braces for EU Bombshell After Genocide Verdict
World.content:
International labor unions’ calls for the European Union to strip Myanmar of its duty-free trade privileges after the International Court of Justice’s genocide ruling have sent shockwaves through local export industry. Operators warn that withdrawing benefits would have severe impacts on the country’s garment industry and hundreds of thousands of workers.

In a Nov. 24 letter to EU leaders, IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union called on Brussels to withdraw Myanmar’s Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preferences and terminate the EU-funded MADE in Myanmar program.

IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union represent over 50 million industrial and garment workers in more than 140 countries. Both have pressed for stronger action against Myanmar’s military regime over labor rights abuses since the 2021 coup.

The EBA grants tariff-free entry to European markets for all exports — barring weapons and ammunition — from least-developed countries, including Myanmar. The scheme underpins Myanmar’s US$ 3-billion annual garment export trade with Europe. MADE in Myanmar, meanwhile, is an EU-backed initiative aimed at improving labor standards and working conditions in the country’s garment industry.

Local garment manufacturers said international labor groups have pushed for withdrawal of Myanmar’s EBA privileges for years, but warned the move could devastate an industry on which hundreds of thousands depend.

“If the EU decides to suspend the scheme, we will have to find alternative markets. We can no longer rely on a single export destination,” one garment operator told The Irrawaddy.

Labor organizations argue that EBA and MADE in Myanmar help channel revenue into the coffers of an illegitimate military regime and should therefore be withdrawn. The EU has yet to respond their calls.

Local factory owners, however, say the industry’s difficulties stem more from domestic challenges since the coup — including foreign-exchange controls, rising production costs, shortages of raw materials, and financial transaction difficulties after Myanmar’s inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist.

The garment industry targeted $5 billion in export earnings for the 2026-27 fiscal year ending March, but industry sources say that goal is increasingly out of reach.

“With just a few months left, we have barely achieved half the target ,” said a Yangon-based garment business owner in Yangon.

Myanmar’s garment sector employs 450,000 to 500,000 workers, mostly women, and relies heavily on the Cut-Make-Pack (CMP) model, under which foreign brands pay factories to process their raw materials. Most exports go to Japan and the EU.

Before the 2021 coup, more than 70 percent of Myanmar’s garment exports went to the EU. That share has since fallen to around 50 percent after manufacturers began shifting production to other countries.

Industry sources say more than 20 manufacturers, including suppliers for major international brands such as H&M, have either closed or plan to leave Myanmar this year.

The Myanmar Garment Manufacturers Association (MGMA) has urged the EU to consider the potential impact on workers before making any decision, warning that broader trade restrictions could further weaken the export sector and threaten jobs across the industry.

World.title: Thailand Tests Find High Lead, Arsenic in River Shellfish
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other species in rivers contaminated by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.

The findings, from nearly two years of testing, prompted authorities to urge residents to avoid eating 10 species including shellfish and river snails.

The warning came earlier this week, but with no details of the contamination levels found or the testing processes.

An official from Thailand’s Fisheries Department, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to talk to media, told AFP that over 500 samples were taken from five rivers, and 18 had heavy metals at levels over safety limits.

The details came as Thai officials held talks in Bangkok to try to address growing public fears about river contamination from mining operations in war-torn Myanmar.

Heavy metals including mercury, lead, cadmium and arsenic were found at levels exceeding safety standards in 10 species, the Fisheries Department official said.

In some, arsenic was detected at nearly four times the permitted limit and lead at nearly six times the limit.

The affected species include freshwater shrimp, river snails, freshwater mussels and horse mussels, as well as local fish that feed on them, the official said.

The official said the tests involved samples from the Mekong and Salween rivers, which flow through Thailand and Myanmar, and three other rivers in Thailand’s north, the Sai, Kok and Ruak.

No contamination was found in farmed aquatic species, the official added.

Local residents in Thailand’s north and northeast have for months complained about river contamination from mines in Myanmar, but the issue has gathered growing public attention in recent weeks.

Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times higher than safe limits.

Campaigners, experts and politicians trace the pollution back to mining in Myanmar, where the long-running civil war has led to unregulated exploitation of natural resources.

In a bid to spur action, residents this week prepared traditional dishes with locally caught food from affected areas and invited politicians, attempting to highlight the risks they now face.

There are fears contamination could spread further down the Mekong, which supports millions of people across several countries.

“Fish are harder to find and even if you find, people won’t buy it,” said Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Chiang Mai, who joined a protest in Bangkok this week.

World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.

“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.

Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair next year, attended the stakeholders’ dialogue as an observer. Delegations from both the Philippines and Singapore received the SCEF’s policy paper on Myanmar during the meeting.

Also in attendance were representatives from Chin resistance forces, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), elected lawmakers and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on the military situation, obstacles to delivery of humanitarian aid, implications of the Rohingya genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and the regime’s escalating airstrikes against civilians.

SCEF said last week’s genocide ruling should spur stronger efforts to enforce accountability for the regime’s past atrocities and ongoing crimes in Myanmar. It urged the international community not to shield military leaders from responsibility or enable further violence.

Then-military chief Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the 2017 “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine that the World Court said amounted to genocide.

The regime rejected the ICJ ruling as “unfair” and stated its repatriation of Rohingya refugees would continue on its own terms, ignoring UN calls to grant them citizenship rights.

The democratic opposition’s appeal comes amid growing debate over ASEAN’s approach to Myanmar. While the bloc continues to exclude Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership from top-level meetings, members including Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia have expanded bilateral engagement with the regime in recent months.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Kazakhstan Votes for Local Councils: What Maslikhat Elections are All About
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan votes on Nov. 29 to replace every local council in the country, more than a year ahead of schedule, marking the final step in rebuilding the political system from the ground up after this year’s constitutional overhaul.

Nearly 11,000 candidates are running for 3,447 seats in 228 maslikhats, the elected assemblies that work alongside regional, city and district governments. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dissolved the maslikhats on Oct. 12.

The maslikhats approve the budgets that pay for roads, heating, schools and water pipes, and they can vote no confidence in akims, the appointed governors and mayors. Whether Sunday produces livelier councils or simply relabels the old ones will shape how much say people have over that money.

What a maslikhat does

A maslikhat is the elected council of a region, city or district, and the main voice voters have in local government. While the akims run the administration, the maslikhats are the elected check on them.

There are three tiers: 20 regional councils, 38 city councils and 170 district councils.

Their core powers include approving local budgets, proposing amendments, approving plans for a region, city or district, which decide, for example, where schools are built and which roads and utility networks get fixed. In cases set by law, deputies can start a no-confidence vote against an akim.

How the vote works

Deputies are elected for five years by secret ballot. Vote for maslikhats in the capital, the regions and cities of national significance, which are Astana, Almaty and Shymkent, mix party lists with constituency races, while districts and towns elect only individual candidates.

Of the 3,447 seats, 334 will be filled from party lists and 3,113 in single-member districts.

“In 20 regions, 97 party slates have been registered for 334 seats. These slates include 1,160 candidates. Thus, there are an average of three to four candidates per seat,” said Azamat Aimanakumov, a member of the Central Election Commission, at a Nov. 27 briefing in Astana.

Candidates are nominated by parties, in some cases by public associations, or by themselves in single-member races.

Seven parties are on the ballot: Auyl, the National Social Democratic Party, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Respublica, Aq Jol, the Baytaq Green Party and Adilet. Each party may register only one list per region, and women and young people together must make up at least 30% of it.

In single-member districts, 9,422 candidates are on the ballot. Any citizen aged 20 or older can run, except people a court has declared legally incapable, those serving prison sentences, and those with a criminal record or a corruption conviction. No one may run in more than one district.

“The fiercest competition is in the Turkistan Region, where there are up to five candidates vying for a single seat. In another 121 districts, four candidates are running for each seat. This represents the highest level of competition,” said Aimanakumov. “There are also regions with the least competition, where two candidates are vying for a single seat. Specifically, in 11 regions across 44 districts, two people are vying for a single seat,” he added.

Overall, 12,679,459 people are on the voter list. On Nov. 29, 10,338 polling stations will open: 101 at 6 a.m. and the rest at 7 a.m. Voting ends at 8 p.m. People with no permanent registration who were never on a voter list can register on the day at 218 designated polling stations.

Alongside digital outreach, precinct commission members went door to door with personal invitations to vote, said Mukhtar Yerman, the CEC’s deputy chairman.

“We see the task not just as reaching people with information, but as creating conditions in which every voter can easily get what they need to know and exercise their constitutional right on Nov. 29,” he said.

Some 258 public associations and nonprofit groups have accredited observers, 13 with the CEC and 245 with territorial commissions. O

Why now?

The maslikhats elected in March 2023 were not due to face voters until 2028. Their early end follows a year of rapid change at the national level. In March, a referendum approved a new Constitution that replaced the two-chamber parliament, the Senate and Mazhilis, with a single chamber, the Kurultai. It took effect July 1.

In June, Amanat, the former Nur Otan party built by first president Nursultan Nazarbayev, voted to merge itself into Adilet, a pro-presidential party registered in June. In August, Adilet won 71.17% of the parliamentary vote and 110 of Kurultai’s 145 seats. Its leader Aibek Dadebay, a former head of the presidential administration, became the chamber’s chairman.

In October, after consulting Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Kurultai Chairman Aibek Dadebay, as the Constitution requires, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the decree ending all maslikhat mandates.

World.title: Kazakhstan Brings Together Global Sports Leaders to Strengthen Anti-Doping Efforts
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan hosted a meeting of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Foundation Board on Nov. 26 in Astana, bringing together representatives of more than 50 countries to discuss global anti-doping policies, athlete protection and international cooperation.

The meeting was attended by WADA President Witold Bańka, Director General Olivier Niggli, Kazakh Tourism and Sports Minister Yerbol Myrzabossynov, representatives of the International Olympic Committee and International Paralympic Committee, and heads of national anti-doping organizations, the ministry reported.

Discussions focused on implementing the World Anti-Doping Code, strengthening safeguards for clean sport, expanding educational and scientific programs, and improving international cooperation.

Kazakhstan highlights clean sport priorities

Addressing the meeting, Myrzabossynov said Kazakhstan views clean sport as a matter of fairness and equal opportunities, emphasizing that athletes should win through honest effort.

He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to strengthening its national anti-doping system, aligning it with international standards and promoting anti-doping awareness among young athletes.

“Every athlete should achieve victory through honest work. Our common goal is to protect athletes’ rights, create equal conditions for everyone and preserve trust in sport,” he said.

Expanding cooperation with WADA

Cooperation between Kazakhstan and WADA gained momentum following Bańka’s visit to Kazakhstan in October 2025.

Earlier this year, Myrzabossynov and Bańka signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation in anti-doping education, prevention of anti-doping rule violations, scientific research and international knowledge-sharing.

The WADA Foundation Board is the agency’s highest governing body, comprising representatives of the international sports movement and governments. It plays a central role in shaping global anti-doping policy.

World.title: Hong Kong Sees Kazakhstan as Promising Tourism Market Ahead of Direct Flight Launch
World.content:
ALMATY – Hong Kong is looking to strengthen tourism ties with Kazakhstan and expand its presence in Central Asia ahead of the launch of direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong in January 2027, Hong Kong Tourism Board (HKTB) Executive Director Anthony Lau said at the travel mission presentation in Almaty on Nov. 27.

“The future has never looked brighter for tourism between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan,” Lau said in his welcoming remarks at the event.

Cathay Pacific plans to launch direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong on Jan. 9, 2027 with flights departing every Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday from Almaty.

The new route is expected to facilitate not only leisure travel but business exchanges. Forty representatives from Hong Kong’s tourism industry traveled to Kazakhstan to discuss opportunities for cooperation with local companies and industries.

“This enhanced connectivity will bring our cities closer than ever before and open up exciting new opportunities for tourism exchange and business cooperation in the years ahead,” Lau told The Astana Times.

Lau said the HKTB seeks to build long-term partnerships in Central Asia as part of their strategy. Tourism is not an exchange of residence, it is about exchange of culture, and friendship, and long-term business partnerships.

The mission also included a meeting between Lau and Galiya Tokseitova, Department of Tourism of Almaty City, to strengthen tourism exchanges.

“The world has changed, and for us, those developed markets are developed,” Lau said.

“We are looking for new sources of tourism growth. Our next phase of growth will be very much along the Belt and Road countries. We are picking different Belt and Road countries which we believe have potential for tourism growth. One factor in facilitating tourism exchange between two destinations would be air connectivity. There is really no point if there is no connection between one place and another. We think it is the right time for us to come to Almaty, to come to Kazakhstan, to understand the market,” he explained.

One of the main benefits is that Hong Kong offers 14-day visa-free entry for Kazakhstan passport holders, making it easier to plan visits.

“As of this moment, it is only three flights a week. Hopefully, if the business comes along, the number of flights will expand to daily, or even twice daily. We are also looking at possible connections with Chinese airlines. For example, from Almaty to Guangzhou or Shenzhen, you can take a fast 45-minute train ride to Hong Kong. You can spend a couple of days in Guangzhou, come to Hong Kong, and then return to Almaty,” said Lau.

Lau highlighted Hong Kong’s combination of urban attractions, natural landscapes, gastronomy and cultural experiences as part of its appeal to visitors. Visitors can travel from the city’s iconic skyline to its beaches in around 20 minutes. Its culinary scene ranges from Michelin-starred restaurants to local specialties, alongside a growing selection of halal-certified dining options.

Lau described Hong Kong as both a destination and a gateway to wider journeys across mainland China.

Cathay Pacific offers a 10% discount on the base fare for bookings made by Dec. 31, 2026, for travel to Hong Kong by March 31, 2027, and other options available on the company’s website.

“As Cathay Pacific’s very first destination in Central Asia, we look forward to welcoming customers onboard our non-stop flights connecting Almaty and Hong Kong. Whether traveling for business or leisure, customers can enjoy our signature hospitality, from our award-winning cabin crew services and lounges, Asia Pacific’s largest inflight entertainment selection, to Hong Kong-inspired dining and international flavors,” said Cathay Chief Customer and Commercial Officer Lavinia Lau.

World.title: Enjoy Final Days of Fall With Music and More
World.content:
ASTANA – As November comes to a close, the cities offer plenty of ways to enjoy the weekend. From ballet and classical music to theater performance and concerts, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events to explore with friends and family.

Astana

“Golden Centaurs” excursion, Nov. 28

Discover the military traditions of the Golden Horde through a guided museum tour featuring historical weapons, armour and interactive displays. Visitors can learn about the equipment used by medieval warriors and explore the history of nomadic military art.

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; 54 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Freedom Festival, Nov. 29

The internationally renowned London City Ballet will perform as part of the Freedom Festival, bringing together dancers from leading ballet companies. The programme features works by celebrated choreographers, including John Neumeier, Kenneth MacMillan and Ashley Page, offering audiences an evening of classical and contemporary ballet.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Symphony concert, Nov. 28

South Korean violinist Lim Ji-young will perform a classical music program. Enjoy beautiful melodies and experience the magic of live music.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Musical Heritage of Western Kazakhstan” concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate the musical traditions of western Kazakhstan through an evening of traditional songs and kuis. The program features works by renowned Kazakh composers and performers, including Mukhit Meraliuly and Garifolla Kurmangaliyev, highlighting the region’s rich musical heritage.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Dürer. Metamorphoses of Alchemy” exhibition, Nov. 27 – Jan. 24

Explore the artistic and intellectual world of the Renaissance through an exhibition dedicated to German artist Albrecht Dürer. The collection brings together engravings, historical books, geometric studies and alchemical texts, offering a closer look at the connection between art, science and philosophy.

Venue: LM Lulanshi Art; 22A Amanzholov Street. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Oyu gala concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate five years of Oyu live with a concert bringing together popular performers.
