World.title: Emergency warning after landslide on the Mornington Peninsula
World.content:
An emergency warning is in place after a landslide at McCrae on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula that is believed to have damaged a house.

The alert from authorities has urged people in the area to stay away from the landslide.

Road closures are in place on Point Nepean Road and The Eyrie.

Mornington Peninsula Shire Mayor Stephen Batty said the council was working closely with other authorities to establish the extent of the incident.

"Our immediate priority is the safety and wellbeing of those in the area, and the shire will exercise whatever regulatory powers are necessary to protect the community," he said.

"We ask that people avoid the area to ensure emergency services and authorised personnel can safely access the site and undertake their work.

"We acknowledge how distressing this will be for the McCrae community, particularly given the events of the past two years.

"The situation is still unfolding and we will provide further information as it becomes available."

The area has a history of landslides, with such events causing damage to properties in 2025 and 2022.

More to come.

World.title: Police link substance release at concert to robbery attempts
World.content:
The release of an unknown substance during a concert by rapper Don Toliver in Manchester is linked to attempts to commit robberies on the night of the event, British police say.

"We suspect that a small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night," Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said on Friday.

Greater Manchester Police did not provide any evidence and did not identify the substance released at Manchester's Co-op Live arena on Sunday night.

The 12,000 people present were evacuated soon after the incident, with 89 requiring medical checks for eye and respiratory irritation, and one person taken to hospital.

Concertgoers were evacuated after an "unknown substance" was released. (X: @BehrouzIX, via Reuters)

Constable Harding said a similar incident had occurred at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe, and that police are in contact with authorities involved in those investigations.

No arrests have been made, but Constable Harding said detectives are sifting through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV and that police are looking to find more than 100 people at the concert to help with enquiries.

Police were called to the venue about 10pm on Sunday, after reports people had been affected by a substance initially believed to be tear gas.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.

Co-op Live, which opened in 2024, is about 3.2 kilometres from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in a suicide bombing at an Ariana Grande concert in 2017.

"What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017," Constable Harding said.

Toliver, whose music blends trap and R&B, is nominated in five categories, including best new artist, for this year's Grammy Awards.

He also features on the soundtrack to the new "Grand Theft Auto" game.

AP

World.title: A bomb scare ignites 'terrorist' talk in the Territory, but was it justified?
World.content:
In the early hours of Thursday morning, an encrypted email lobbed into the inboxes of government officials in the Northern Territory.

It was a strange and garbled mix of criticism over political policy that crescendoed with a threat to kill people with bombs to be detonated in public places over the Christmas period.

All in all, it marked a troubling end to the NT's political calendar, dropping as it did on the final day of NT parliamentary sittings for 2026.

Lia Finocchiaro addressed NT parliament about the threats. (ABC News)

The NT government took it seriously and a senior communications advisor forwarded the email on to the Territory's media outlets, before police held a press conference later that morning.

As News Corp's Darwin tabloid dubbed it on the next day's front page: "IT'S A BLACK DAY".

"Territory families, along with politicians, are under threat of bomb attacks by fanatics opposed to the NT's new child protection laws," the NT News front page copy blared.

Well, maybe. Maybe not.

Flash forward to 24 hours after the email and NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole had stepped out to allay the public's fears, saying there was "no credible or imminent risk" over the threat.

Martin Dole spoke at a press conference on Friday, where he told the media there was "no credible or imminent risk". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The same encrypted email account has been used to send similar threats to organisations and individuals in several Australian jurisdictions, with messages tailored to local targets," he said.

We live in strange times, and despite its distance from Australia's major population centres, the NT has proven it is not immune from the spectre of terror faced elsewhere.

As Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro told parliament: "The threat contained in this email is disturbing and designed to strike terror into not only this parliament but the community."

Expert brands reaction 'irresponsible'

In spite of the threat, the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government didn't let it dampen its week, stepping out to meet constituents on Darwin's Smith Street Mall just hours later on Thursday.

"I hope that us being out on the mall reinforces to Territorians that it is their safety that is our number one priority," Ms Finocchiaro told the ABC.

Loading...

"We won't be letting the terrorists win."

Police say 'no credible or imminent threat' over bomb scare The NT Police Commissioner says joint counter terrorism officers have deemed there to be no "credible or imminent threat" from a bomb threat targeting NT politicians.

So, was the scale of the NT government and the media's (ABC included) reaction to this possible threat appropriate, considering they broadcast it before any firm warning of danger from police?

Well, maybe. Maybe not.

Commissioner Dole said yesterday that police often received similar reports of threats and that their usual practice would be "first to examine the credibility and the threat level to the community before we would give that information out publicly".

"The reason we've come out publicly and given information in the Territory is because of the wide release of that information publicly," he said.

Prominent Macquarie University criminologist Professor Vincent Hurley said he believed it "was irresponsible of the government to actually publicly put this out there" before police.

Vincent Hurley says it was "irresponsible" of the government to release the threat to the media before police had time to investigate. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

"I thought that it was irresponsible to actually declare this in public to [potentially] jeopardise what could be a really important criminal investigation that could possibly have implications Australia-wide," he said.

Shadow NT Attorney-General Chansey Paech echoed Professor Hurley's remarks.

"I think it is completely irresponsible and inappropriate that the CLP government were referring this matter on to the media before the police had the chance to stand up, talk to and inform the community about what was going on," he said.

Threat ends week of political landmines

The bomb threat also came at the end of a week when the NT government was trying to navigate its own political landmines.

Gosling's lawyer flags 'unequivocal evidence' of 'political interference' Luke Gosling's lawyer says there was "political interference" in the lead up to the prosecution of their client.

Those included controversial water law changes, child protection revelations and an explosive courtroom allegation of political interference involving the chief minister's office.

In a twist of fate for the CLP, the bomb threat did have the effect of defusing attention from some of those issues — take for example the NT News front page devoted to the scare.

In another example, the NT government declined an ABC interview request with Child Protection Minister Robyn Cahill about controversial new changes, citing the threat of the email.

Several hours later, Ms Cahill was out at the Darwin mall as well.

CLP politicians were in Darwin's Smith Street Mall meeting with constituents hours after the bomb threat. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Nobody can argue that in the wake of the Bondi Beach massacre and the horrific attack on MP Helen Haines, the public, government and media shouldn't be wary of lurking threats.

But maybe we all just need to take a minute to think about it before we light the fuse.

World.title: Farmers do not miss dusty old days as they embrace harvest technology
World.content:
For farmers across western New South Wales, harvest once meant long days in open-air cabins, swatting flies and battling sweltering heat and clouds of dust.

Now, air-conditioned harvesters fitted with sophisticated technology can strip vast paddocks in a fraction of the time.

It is a transformation Narromine region farmer Rob McCutcheon has witnessed firsthand.

His family has farmed in the region for more than a century, and he has worked on the land since 1969.

Before: Harvesting machinery in 2010. . . After: Harvesting machinery in 2026. (Supplied: Rob McCutcheon/Three Rivers Machinery) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Harvesting machinery in 2010. / Harvesting machinery in 2026. (Supplied: Rob McCutcheon/Three Rivers Machinery)

When he started, harvesting 5 or 6 tonnes of grain an hour was considered a major achievement.

Today, some of the largest machines can harvest more than 100 tonnes in the same time.

"There's certainly been some big changes in the way the crop's harvested and the way the crop's been delivered," Mr McCutcheon said.

Rob McCutcheon has witnessed more than five decades of change in harvesting and grain storage across western NSW. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

From bags to bulk grain

As a child, Mr McCutcheon would accompany his father to grain silos, when wheat was transported in bags on small trucks.

Workers would empty the bags before they were returned to the paddock to be refilled.

The introduction of bulk grain bins and unloading augers during the 1960s reduced much of the manual labour.

"It was hard work. [You] needed strong people with plenty of go to keep the harvest progressing," Mr McCutcheon said.

Allan McCutcheon and farm machinery dealer Roy Carr pictured with a harvester and chaser bin in 1974. (Supplied: Rob McCutcheon)

Headers also evolved from horse-drawn and tractor-towed machines to self-propelled harvesters.

Early machines had cutting fronts just 3 or 4 metres wide, compared with up to 20 metres on modern harvesters.

They also had open-air cabs, leaving farmers exposed to dust, soot and chaff.

"It was hot, it was dusty, it was dirty, but it was still a good job," Mr McCutcheon said.

" Your eyes would be full of soot; we'd have to wear goggles. Inside your elbow would get all chafed from the chaff. "

Enclosed cabins arrived in the early 1970s, although they initially lacked air conditioning.

Mr McCutcheon said grain delivery queues once stretched 10 blocks through Narromine, with farmers sometimes waiting an entire day to unload just one load.

The introduction of air-conditioned cabins improved working conditions for farmers during harvest. (Supplied: Rob McCutcheon)

He said some would pass the time at the pub, leaving others to move their trucks forward.

Larger vehicles, on-farm storage and faster delivery systems have largely made those queues a thing of the past.

"The wheat line as it used to be traditionally, where people shared gossip and told stories about their crops and all these things, they're gone today because you're straight in and straight out," Mr McCutcheon said.

Harvester with an 18.6-metre cutting front. (Supplied: Three Rivers Machinery)

Bigger machines, fewer workers

John Plunkett has sold harvest machinery for 25 years and has seen dramatic changes in their size and technology in that time.

John Plunkett says advances in harvesting technology have improved efficiency and reduced the requirement for labour. (Supplied: Three Rivers Machinery)

He said in the early 2000s, harvesters had about 280 horsepower and could harvest between 20 and 35 tonnes of grain an hour.

"We've put [harvesters] in the paddock this year that are over 700 or 775 horsepower," he said.

"They're harvesting 100 tonnes an hour."

Loading...

Mr Plunkett said the increased capacity allowed farmers to harvest crops faster and reduce the risk of rain damaging grain quality and value.

"If you get too much rain on a crop and the grain shoots ... it can get downgraded to pig feed basically and decimate your price by more than 50 per cent," he said.

Beyond their size and speed, the computers in modern harvesters automatically adjust machinery settings every 20 seconds to minimise grain losses.

"It'll make a dozen, 15 adjustments automatically to improve the crop sample," Mr Plunkett said.

"It's quite remarkable."

Mr Plunkett said advances in technology had reduced labour requirements, citing one customer who recently replaced four older harvesters with two larger machines.

Modern harvesters can strip vast paddocks in a fraction of the time it took earlier generations of farming machinery. (Supplied: Three Rivers Machinery)

"I think what you'll see is more automation, as in the combine basically driving itself down the track," he said.

For Mr McCutcheon, the scale of change was difficult to comprehend.

"My father probably would have had those thoughts when he was sitting on a tractor towing a header along," he said.

"I don't think he would possibly have imagined how far it's come."

World.title: High-heel skipping and handbag throwing: Perth's queer sports history uncovered
World.content:
Competitive handbag throwing and high-heel skipping were once acts of political defiance in Perth.

Both disciplines featured in what was originally known as the city's 'Gay Olympics', which ran annually from 1979 to 1999 to raise money for gay and lesbian charities.

They event also pushed for law reform at a time when consensual homosexual sex between men was still illegal in Western Australia; the decriminalisation of which only began in 1990.

The games were a colourful way of bringing the LGBTQIA+ community together. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Volunteers at the West Pride Archives have been sifting the event's history ahead of Perth hosting the 2030 International Gay Games.

Jo Darbyshire, co-convenor of West Pride Archives said Perth's original games had a strong political edge.

"Being visible out in the community and not being shamed was a huge element to (them)," she said.

Australia's longest-running gay nightclub, Connections, had a team base at the games. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"We were still fighting for gay law reform, for gay men in particular to be able to have sex with other men without being harassed by the police or charged or considered dirty and deviant."

Marches and colourful floats were part of the parade. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

The games galvanised the community, but fundraising was also a key part with money going towards things including the telephone bill for the Gay Lesbian Counselling Service.

The games were held in Perth from 1979 until 1999. (Supplied: Tim Grant/ State Library of WA)

"That sort of power over helping our own communities enabled us to have the courage to really push for gay law reform and equality in the law," she said.

" We refused to just roll over and die. "

'Winners with Muscles' receiving an award from Holly Wood at the McGillivray Oval in1983. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Tim Grant photographed the event in the 1980s, and said it was a unique chance to document his community, as it was forbidden to take photos inside bars and clubs at the time.

"It was safe and one the few large-scale spectaculars that my local community could ever have at the time," he said.

Costumes and fashion played a big role in the games and the community. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"I felt I had no restraints on what I could photograph on the day, as I was a known face and just a part of the scenery."

The Girls of Head Office Women’s Team #2 at the Opening Parade in 1982. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

International Gay Games

Ray Currell, 78, said the local event was "very important" for the community.

"It was great, we had high-heel skip, the handbag throw and then there were some serious events," he said,

" [The games] meant freedom. I've always been gay, I've never hidden the fact. "

West Pride Archives volunteer Sophie Herbert and Ray Currell hold his badges from international Gay Games. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Currell also helped organise the first Perth team of around 30 members to participate in the New York Gay Games in 1994, which coincided with the 25th anniversary of the Stonewall Riots.

Team Perth went to New York for the Gay Games in the 1990s. (Supplied: West Pride Archives)

The Gay Games do not require any qualifications for participants.

"As long as you could afford to get there and compete, they let you," Currell said.

Held every four years, Currell competed in five Gay Games and said he would still compete if his body allowed him.

Team Perth participated at the Sydney Gay Games in 2002. (Supplied: Adrian Lily and Ray Currell)

Perth to hold 2030 Gay Games

Perth will host the international Gay Games for the first time in 2030, which is expected to attract thousands of people.

At the 2026 Valencia Gay Games, more than 50 Western Australia participants formed the Australian contingent.

It is expected to be far larger when it's Perth's turn to host.

Ray Currell participated in five international Gay Games for bowling. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Sophie Herbert, volunteer at West Pride Archives, said it was "heartwarming and inspiring" to discover the light side of Perth's LGBTQIA+ history.

"They were very brave in the way that it was just people existing and going out and having fun — but just by doing that was an act of protest in itself," she said.

"Although there was so much awful stuff happening at that time, people were resisting in their own way and that's really inspiring."

She said she hopes the Gay Games sparks the local event to be resurrected and encouraged people to donate their photos and medals to the West Pride Archives ahead of the 2030 Games.

World.title: Nathan Lyon axed as Australia names Test squad
World.content:
Corey Rocchiccioli has ended Nathan Lyon's 13-year reign as Australia's first-choice spinner, with the veteran tweaker one of three players axed for the Test series against New Zealand.

Selectors on Saturday unveiled a 13-man squad for the home summer, with spinner Rocchiccioli and Queensland batter Jack Clayton named in their first Test squads.

Lyon, Cooper Connolly and Marnus Labuschagne are all gone from the team that lost a series decider to South Africa in Cape Town just four weeks ago.

Steve Smith is fit again and will return.

Australia Test squad vs New Zealand Pat Cummins (captain), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Jack Clayton, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Corey Rocchiccioli, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc

Beau Webster's future also appears clouded, missing out on the squad entirely after being dropped for the Cape Town loss after playing Australia's previous five Tests.

The omission of Connolly and Webster means Clayton is every chance of debuting in a reconfigured top seven, after averaging 74.83 in the Sheffield Shield this season.

Selectors have left the door open for another player to come into the group, with Cricket Australia confirming a 14th man will be added after next weekend's Sheffield Shield round.

There is also nothing stopping selectors changing their squad between Tests, given it is a home summer.

But still the most seismic decision of all comes with Rocchiccioli's selection ahead of Lyon, the nation's second leading wicket-taker of all time.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner since being recalled to the Test side midway through the 2013 Ashes, after briefly being dropped for Ashton Agar.

He has also formed part of every Australian Test squad since his debut tour of Sri Lanka midway through 2011.

At age 39, there are now serious questions over his future in the Test side.

Jack Clayton drawing on AFL experience Jack Clayton says missing out on the AFL draft has taught him how to deal with the pressure of chasing a Test cricket debut for Australia.

Lyon has made clear he wants to play in next year's tours of India and England, and as it stands he remains determined to fight back into the side.

He took six wickets at an average of 43.67 in Australia's most recent series loss to South Africa, where he was left out for the second Test in Gqeberha.

The 145-Test veteran has since returned to the Sheffield Shield and taken seven wickets 43.28 for NSW across two matches.

"Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches," chief selector George Bailey said.

"We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward."

Lyon's axing also calls into question whether Test cricket's most successful bowling quartet in history will take to the field together again, alongside Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Rocchiccioli, meanwhile, has been on the fringe of Australia's squads in recent years.

The 29-year-old has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 for Western Australia this summer, and showed his all-round ability with a century against Tasmania last week.

Whether he debuts in Perth remains to be seen, with Australia every chance of playing Scott Boland as one of four quicks.

"Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions," Bailey said.

AAP

World.title: Aboriginal community captured in ‘timeless, beautiful’ tintype portraits
World.content:
When Joan Lamont looks at the greyscale portraits of her Kaurna mob placed side by side, she sees the eyes of her ancestors looking back at her.

"How they look … is like looking back and seeing the old people come back to them," the Kaurna Narungga elder said.

The tintype portraits of her living community members have just finished developing and are drying out on a table next to a makeshift darkroom in a bathroom.

Members of the Kaurna community sat for tintype portraits in October. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The 83-year-old has just sat for her own tintype portrait taken by Kaurna artists James Tylor and Damien Shen in the Art Gallery of South Australia's courtyard.

Tylor and Shen spent a week in October with a vintage Linhof camera capturing their community in the analogue format.

The photo shoot is part of an international project the Critical Indigenous Photo Exchange (CIPX), started by Navajo man Will Wilson when he began using the tintype photography — popular during colonial era — to take striking portraits of his contemporary community.

Kaurna and Narungga man Michael O'Brien took part in the first CIPX Kaurna photo shoot. (ABC News)

Tylor and Shen's photos taken in this shoot in Adelaide will be blown up and displayed on the walls of SA's art gallery in coming weeks.

"It makes me very emotional that we will live on, you know," Ms Lamont said.

"We may die off, I don't think so, but we could.

"But we'll be up there, looking down on everyone and everyone will know who we are."

A camera with a colonial past

The tintype camera was developed in the mid-19th century and uses the wet plate photography process.

Travellers and anthropologists across the world often towed around a tintype camera, and photographed many First Nations people as subjects.

The Linhof camera used by James Tylor and Damien Shen. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In South Australia, Damien Shen has photos taken of his own great grandparents in 1939 at Raukkan (Point McLeay Mission) by anthropologist Norman Tindale.

"When I look at that and consider what was happening in that time, it's hard to know what type of consent was given by my family in terms of being captured in the way they were, if they really understood what was happening," Shen said.

"I try to interrogate that and retell that through some of my practice now."

Shen has seen the way Aboriginal people were portrayed in historical photography by settlers in colonial Australia.

"What I have looked at is the way there's like an anthropological or an ethnographic gaze on Aboriginal people since like the 19th century and how those images have been captured, essentially portraying Aboriginal people as like the 'other'," he said.

"Looking into that aspect of it has always fascinated me and I guess that's a little bit evident in some of the practice of mine over the years, and how I've then used photography to sort of retell that story."

Damien Shen transforms a bathroom into a pop-up darkroom to prep and develop the plates. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Tylor and Shen's subjects for the project get to choose what they wear and how they are portrayed.

Once the physical tin has been digitally captured, the Kaurna community member keeps the original plate and choose exactly how the digital photograph can be stored and shared, including if it will be part of Tylor and Shen's exhibition.

Damien Shen called the solution a "magic bath", where the photo can be seen appearing on the tin as it develops. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The photos are captured on a small sheet of black aluminium. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The week-long photo shoot had a daily run sheet of prominent members in the Kaurna community, of the Adelaide Plains in South Australia, who took turns in front of the vintage lens.

The wet plate photography process involves brushing a formula called collodion on black metal plate, placing it in a tank of silver nitrate for a few minutes before loading it in a light-safe camera cartridge and then into a tintype camera itself.

Once the photo is taken, the cartridge is taken to a dark room, developer solution is poured over for 10 to 15 seconds before it is submerged in a stop bath of water for several minutes and eventually placed into a fixing solution.

For Shen, the shoot is not just about capturing portraits, but also what happens on the sidelines.

"We're talking about family while we're doing it and other members of community are coming in and sitting down and chatting," he said.

"It's been quite a communal and a beautiful process."

James Tylor operates the Linhof tintype camera. (ABC News)

With an exposure time of 7 seconds and many variables in the tintype process, reshoots are often required and there may be several sheets of tin used before the perfect portrait is taken.

While the format may be a fickle one, the final products capture striking imagery of the Kaurna community in a way that not only refers back to a previous era, but reshapes it in a modern context.

AGSA says the photos from the second Kaurna photo shoot will be exhibited early next year. (ABC News)

Ms Lamont said she felt pride and joy in taking part in the project, which will be exhibited at the art gallery until the end of March.

"It's a real connection of us coming together and doing this wonderful, beautiful thing that will have us there looking at people," she said.

"It is timeless, beautiful; and we are working together as one to show who we are.

"We're the oldest people in the universe and we should be more appreciated as survivors."

World.title: Walker wins Australia's first medal of World Cup season
World.content:
Bree Walker has won bronze in the opening women's monobob event in Germany, securing Australia's first World Cup medal of the 2026-27 season.

In her first race since off-season knee surgery limited her preparation, the two-time Olympian delivered an impressive performance in Altenberg on Friday.

Walker posted the third-fastest time in heat one at 1:00.29, then went even faster in heat two with 59.87 seconds to secure third place overall with a combined time of 2:00.16.

The 34-year-old Queenslander's performance placed her just 0.54 seconds behind event winner Laura Nolte of Germany (1:59.62), and within striking distance of second-placed Lisa Buckwitz, also of Germany (1:59.87).

The medal marks Walker's 18th World Cup podium and her third at the Altenberg track.

"I wasn't too sure after this off-season with my knee rehab what shape I was going to be in, so [I'm] very happy to start the season off with a third place in Altenberg," Walker wrote on social media.

Sarah Blizzard also competed for Australia, finishing 11th.

Walker will be back in action again on Sunday evening (Monday AEDT), competing in the two-woman event at Altenberg, where she will be joined by newly arrived brakewoman Eden Wilson, who has transferred from Canada.

AAP

World.title: Victorian election 2026 LIVE updates: Jess Wilson, Ben Carroll cast votes as both go head-to-head; Labor on track for historic loss as half of Victorians cast ballots early
World.content:
The woman who pollsters predict will lead the Victorian Liberals out of the political wilderness made a fast but efficient stop to a school in her eectorate of Kew to cast her ballot.

With her young son Patrick in her arms, and her husband and sister in tow, Jess Wilson made a beeline for the cake stall and democracy sausages right after voting.

Loading

“I’m just here to look after Pat,” joked husband Aaron Lane as Wilson was mobbed by voters, her hands loaded up with treats and snags but still finding a way to dole out plenty of handshakes and hugs.

“There’s a long way to go between now and 6pm,” she told reporters but said the state faced an important and exciting choice.

She joined Patrick for a quick jaunt on the playground before disappearing into the leafy streets of Kew again as quickly as she appeared.

Ever the multi-tasker.

World.title: Caught between killers: An epidemic on one side, terrorists on the other
World.content:
Ismail Mbafumoja, a cacao farmer and gold miner, visits a new cemetery for Ebola victims on the edge of Biakato in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The initial Ebola outbreak has morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe. If that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Biakato, DR Congo: Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo. When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province. It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hotspots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests. Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain. Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. A relative mourns as Red Cross volunteers buried Mose Kalindera, a Biakato shopkeeper. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times “We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads the country’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.” And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State militant group. Ebola was already swamping Biakato when I got to the town in mid-October with photographer Daniel Berehulak. Exhausted health workers reported 300 cases in the span of a month, up from 20 the month before. But there were only two doctors; they had not been paid in months, and they felt utterly abandoned. The aid workers who would normally pour in and set up an Ebola treatment centre were being scared off by rebel fighters who have been terrorising the region for years.



In recent days, their fears were tragically realised when the rebels, who are affiliated with Islamic State, killed 106 people in a series of attacks across the region, United Nations officials said. One of the deadliest episodes occurred 40 kilometres south of Biakato, where militants torched homes, shops and health facilities, forcing Ebola patients to flee their beds. Thousands of residents also fled in an exodus likely to further spread the disease. Even by the standards of eastern DR Congo, where conflict has raged for three decades, the fighters – from a group called the Allied Democratic Forces, or ADF – are considered especially brutal. They roam the sprawling forests, periodically springing from their hiding places to mount attacks. Civilians are beheaded, mutilated and abducted. Children are forced to fight with the group. Mass killings have taken place at funerals and churches. In 2019, the group pledged allegiance to Islamic State, and by one recent estimate, it is the world’s second-deadliest group for civilians. Now, its terror tactics are hobbling the fight against Ebola. A casket holding an Ebola victim is transported by motorbike for burial in Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times A tentative effort to rescue Biakato is under way. Aid groups are using helicopters to fly over the perilous forests and have begun to build a treatment centre. Even so, the volunteers battling to hold back the tide of infections say they are in an impossible bind. “We’ve got the ADF on one side and Ebola on the other,” said Jean-Lefranc Sakara, head of a Red Cross team that collects the Ebola dead from their houses. “We are well and truly caught in the middle.” Loading



Since May, more than 5500 people have died in this outbreak, and experts fear the number is growing so fast that it may surpass the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014-16, the largest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people. As recently as September, experts thought they were getting a handle on this one, but in recent weeks the transmission rate has risen again, according to official figures, meaning it is still out of control. Until recently, violence was the most pressing concern in Biakato. In May, fighters with the Islamic State affiliate stormed into the town, killing 21 people. Soldiers from nearby Uganda began patrolling the streets, under an agreement with the DR Congolese government, to ward off attacks. But the upheaval continues just outside town. Germain Kanyungu (right) is helped at a makeshift treatment centre. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times At first, it seemed that Ebola might bypass Biakato, said Job Bakwata, the town’s chief medical officer. The first recorded case was a gold miner who returned from the town of Mongbwalu in June, then died. But in the following months, as the virus ravaged other areas, Biakato had only a dribble of cases: one more in June, 14 in July, 20 in August. Then in mid-September, infections surged, overwhelming the battered town. Sakara threw himself into the response. A one-time seminarian, he had moved to Biakato four years earlier seeking safety. The rebels had attacked his home in the mountains of North Kivu, killing a sister and three brothers. “My grandfather told me to get out,” he said. “We came here to start over.” After Ebola hit, he dropped everything to lead a small team that collects and disinfects the bodies of Ebola victims. Working that close to the virus was daunting, he said. The volunteers had protective suits but little training, and he felt terrified in the homes of Ebola victims who had just died.



His team also faced hostility from the people they were trying to save. Mourners hurled stones as they tried to bury the dead, showering them with insults and accusing them of somehow profiting from the outbreak. “They call it ‘Ebola business’,” he said. The World Health Organisation, which is leading the effort to get help to Biakato, has its own painful history in the town. During the last outbreak in this area, in 2019, armed men attacked its guesthouse in Biakato, killing three Ebola responders. Officials blamed the violence on the Mai-Mai, a term for local militias. A Sunday mass in Biakato. The town now accounts for as many as one-quarter of the DR Congo’s new Ebola cases. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times Ugandan soldiers help patrol Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times That leaves health officials walking a tightrope. Proceed too slowly, and Biakato could become a deep reservoir of Ebola, spreading infection across the region. Move too quickly, and they risk an attack, like a killing or a kidnapping of aid workers, that could collapse the entire effort. Mistrust among residents is also a problem. After decades of war, faith in the government had collapsed, officials said. The same Congolese soldiers who are supposed to protect the community also prey on it, seeking bribes or profiting from gold. “They don’t trust outsiders,” said Julien Harneis, the UN Ebola co-ordinator in DR Congo. “Experience has taught them not to.”



As infections began to rise in September, a WHO team returned to Biakato to see how they might help. The health workers woke one morning to find a headless sheep dumped outside their hotel – a sign they were not welcome, said Dr Steve Ahuka, the head of the country’s Ebola response. But within weeks, Ebola had become so overwhelming that Biakato’s distrustful leaders were pleading for help. Jean-Lefranc Sakara, a onetime seminarian who now leads a volunteer Red Cross team trying to cope with Ebola victim burials in Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times On October 12, Ahuka and Catherine Smallwood, a senior WHO official, returned to Biakato to a very different reception. Town leaders formed a circle around Smallwood and, after apologising for the 2019 killings, implored her to send help. “They asked me to put the past in the past,” she recalled. “It was an extremely touching moment.” Since then, the WHO has deployed officials and revamped the chaotic health centre. The DR Congolese government set up a lab to test patients. Medair, a Swiss aid organisation, has sent medics. And yet, even that may not be enough. To stamp out the virus, health workers need to trace every known contact of an infected person. That kind of investigative work is impossible in the countryside while the ADF still threatens it.

World.title: The Wallabies have less than a year to sort themselves out for the World Cup. It can be done
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion The Wallabies have less than a year to sort themselves out for the World Cup. It can be done Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author November 28, 2026 — 9:45am

November 28, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Could we do it? At the end of a long season of mixed results, could the Wallabies snatch a brilliant win against the second-ranked team in the world, Ireland, in this finals round of the Nations Championship at Twickenham? The Wallabies tried hard, but couldn’t prevail against Ireland in London. AP We certainly looked like they could, early. Up against a full-strength Ireland side, the Wallabies looked menacing! Our forwards more than held their own, our backs sniped through regularly, only to be brought down in extremis. The forwards were picking off line-outs – with great work by Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams – the backs were probing and picking on every weak point they could find.



If it were a boxing match, we’d have been way ahead on points. As it was rugby, the only points we actually could find were from lock Williams driving so low from the base of the ruck that his nose dinkum ploughed a furrow in the Twickenham turf, his ears leaving snail-trails on the evening dew. Unstoppable. Try! Wallaby Jeremy Williams crashes over to score a try against Ireland in London. Getty Images Converted, the Wallabies led 7-0 and all seemed right with the world, if only we could hold on until the half to regroup. We couldn’t.



When Max Jorgensen went off at the 30th minute mark for a head injury assessment, it saw Kurtley Beale come on for the vaunted “fairy-tale” return after five years out, at the age of 37. The problem was, he looked 37. Veteran Kurtley Beale had a go in his 96th cap for the Wallabies, but he looked his age. Getty Images The ball went awry from his first touch, and try as hard as he did, the magic seemed gone. Carter Gordon, who had started to seriously struggle, passed to no-one and kicked out on the full.



Ireland immediately started to dominate territory, camping in our 22 to pick off two quick converted tries, with a bonus penalty goal thrown in to lead 17-7 at the break. Surely however, after such a strong start, we could restore order in the second-half? We could not. Out of reach: Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii of Australia challenges Hugo Keenan of Ireland. Getty Images Again, with the athletically gifted Wallaby outside-centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii one of the most lethal men in the world from the kick-off at a range of anything up to 20 metres, we kicked off – ONCE AGAIN – 25 metres, just beyond his reach, and I must pause.



(WHY? WHY? WHY??? How hard is this? How obvious that you either do a kick-off within Suaalii’s possible grasp, or kick it to billy-o, to the corner. Give the bloke a freaking chance! Sorry, as you were. I shall calm myself) Straining to get to the ball, Suaalii got to the man in the air instead, gave away a penalty, and they scored shortly afterwards to lead 24-7. James Ramm challenges Ireland. Getty Images In just over 15 minutes of play, we’d gone from dominating the second-best team in the world, to the dominated. We’d shown what we could do, only to crumble like a Sao in a blender through careless and injudicious play. Yes, the extremely promising Wallabies half-back Kalani Thomas went over after great work by Taniela Tupou to bring it back to 24-14, but at this point it was all over bar the shouting of you and me at the TV screen.



Another perspective Australian rugby He was named after Allan Border. During a tsunami alert, this Wallaby lived up to the name Another clinically lethal Irish try from reserve forward James McNabney saw them lead 31-14, a feat he doubled up with a minute to go, to make it 38-14. All up, it was frustrating, did I mention? Our blokes are good enough to menace a top-ranked side like Ireland. A huge upset was not out of the question. In the end though, it is just us supporters who finished upset. This can be done. They can do it. They have less than a year to sort themselves out before the home World Cup. We have some outstanding players. All three back-rowers Carlo Tizzano, Tom Hooper and Rob Valetini had strong games. Len Ikitau had his moments, as did Jorgensen and Suaalii.



It came together in spots, but that was all. Related Article Live

Wallabies All ball, no bite: Wallabies end season with heavy defeat to Ireland The challenge will be to come up with the right halves combination, stick to it, and have the side as a whole learn how to sustain for 80 minutes. Ok. That’s it, youse blokes. Hit the surf. Think about it. The hard work starts on New Year’s Day. It can be done. The first 20 minutes against Ireland showed it. World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Lyon’s replacement revealed as bolter gets nod for Tests against New Zealand Tom Decent November 28, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Western Australian off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli has been confirmed as Nathan Lyon’s replacement in Australia’s Test squad for this summer’s series against New Zealand, with Queensland batter Jack Clayton the other potential debutant in a 13-man squad. Cricket Australia on Saturday confirmed this masthead’s report on Friday that Lyon, Australia’s second-most prolific wicket-taker in Test cricket, had been axed for the summer. WA spinner Corey Rocchiccioli is poised for a call-up to the Test squad. Getty Images In one of the most significant selection decisions in years, Lyon may have played his last Test on Australian soil, potentially depriving one of the country’s greatest bowlers of a farewell in front of family, friends and home crowds. While selectors have the flexibility to change the squad throughout the four-Test series, beginning in Perth on December 9, the decision to overlook Lyon for the summer represents a changing of the guard in Australia’s spin-bowling ranks. However, Lyon is likely to come into calculations for Australia’s five-Test tour of India in January and February.



“Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches,” Australia’s chairman of selectors George Bailey said in a statement. “We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward.” Lyon is among a host of casualties from last month’s tour of South Africa, with all-rounders Cooper Connolly and Beau Webster also overlooked. However, selectors have left one spot open in the squad, to be filled following the sixth round of the Sheffield Shield. Rocchiccioli has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 from five Shield matches this season and is in line to make his Test debut on home turf. Australia’s 13-man Test squad for New Zealand series Pat Cummins (NSW/Penrith Cricket Club) (c)

Scott Boland (VIC/Frankston Peninsula Cricket Club)

Alex Carey (SA/Glenelg Cricket Club)

Jack Clayton (QLD/University of Queensland Cricket Club)

Cameron Green (WA/Subiaco-Floreat Cricket Club)

Josh Hazlewood (NSW/St George Cricket Club)

Travis Head (SA/Tea Tree Gully Cricket Club)

Josh Inglis (WA/Joondalup Cricket Club)

Michael Neser (QLD/Gold Coast Cricket Club)

Matthew Renshaw (QLD/Toombul Cricket Club)

Corey Rocchiccioli (WA/University Cricket Club)

Steve Smith (NSW/Sutherland Cricket Club)

Mitchell Starc (NSW/Manly Warringah Cricket Club) *One player will be added after round six of the Sheffield Shield The 29-year-old’s ability to extract bounce and his familiarity with Perth conditions will be assets should selectors opt to play a frontline spinner in the opener.



“Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions,” Bailey said. Related Article Opinion

Test cricket It won’t be Sandpapergate that ends Cummins’ captaincy. It will be his form Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Queensland leg-spinner Mitch Swepson could consider himself unlucky to miss out, having taken a competition-leading 24 wickets at 16.91 from the same number of Shield appearances as Rocchiccioli this season. Meanwhile, Clayton’s selection is a reward for a prolific start to the domestic summer and puts the Queenslander on the cusp of a Test debut. The left-hander’s 449 runs at 74.83 were enough to earn him a call-up ahead of NSW’s Sam Konstas (479 runs at 68.43) and South Australia’s Jake Weatherald (509 at 56.56), both of whom have made compelling cases for Test returns through their domestic performances.



“Jack [Clayton] is a well-organised player who has performed consistently for an extended period,” Bailey said. “His game is well suited to complement the rest of the batting order.” There was also no room in the squad for Matthew Kuhnemann, Nic Maddinson or Sam Harper, while selectors had already announced Marnus Labuschagne would not be picked. World.title: Harry Styles is back in Melbourne. Does his show live up to the hype?
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews Harry Styles is back in Melbourne. Does his show live up to the hype? Nell Geraets November 28, 2026 — 9:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

MUSIC

Harry Styles | Together, Together Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 27 Dance, sweat and sing. This, Harry Styles says midway through his first show back in Melbourne in nearly four years, is all he wants to see from the crowd. With the roof of Marvel Stadium closed on a muggy, rain-soaked day, the sweat certainly comes in waves. But no one seems to notice the heat – they’re too busy watching the cavernous venue transform into a pulsing nightclub. Harry Styles transforms Marvel Stadium into a pulsing nightclub. Pham Styles transports the 50,000-something crowd to Berghain, Berlin’s renowned techno nightclub that partly inspired his latest album Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally. Lasers, multicoloured strobe lights and psychedelic on-screen animations send you into a trance, enraptured by both the sensory dream around you and the endlessly charismatic man leading the reverie. During Taste Back, some in the crowd close their eyes and swing their bodies wildly from side-to-side, almost as if having a religious experience.



Given the rapturous response to every move Styles makes, you’d think he actually were some kind of prophet. He removes his bright pink jacket, people lose it. He takes a sip of water, the crowd goes wild. He shimmies his hips on one of the catwalks extending into the audience, it’s game over – the fans’ brains have short-circuited. This close attention, however, is reciprocated. The degree to which Styles focuses on the crowd is practically unparalleled. Given the rapturous response to every move Styles makes, you’d think he actually were some kind of prophet. Pham He covers every inch of the stage, especially during higher-octane numbers like American Girls and Adore You, waving and blowing kisses to each side. A portion of the show is dedicated to Styles reading some of the fans’ handmade signs, one of which reveals they’d skipped their grandmother’s funeral to be there (whether you agree with that or not, it undeniably captures the hold Styles has over his “Harries”). Twice during the concert, Styles stops the show entirely, requesting the house lights be turned on so that dehydrated people on the floor could be helped out of the scrum.



Unlike a nightclub, however, Styles is backed by a bumping live band, including a large string section. During newer, admittedly flatter numbers – those like Pop and Season 2 Weight Loss – when even the pop star’s charm isn’t quite enough to electrify the room, the horns blast us away, and the keyboard breathes new life into tracks not yet iconic. Harry Styles wants the crowd to dance, sweat and sing Pham If there were any doubts over Styles’ ability to teleport us to a sweaty Berlin nightclub, those are put to rest during Ready, Steady, Go!, a propulsive electronic number that brings the star and his band to the centre of the stadium. Styles, with his distorted megaphone-like mic, gets the entire arena on its feet, jumping so wildly that the ground rumbles beneath us. But Styles ultimately puts it best when singing Dance No More: “It’s feelin’ like the music has been Heaven sent / And that there’s no difference in between the tears and the sweat”. On a muggy day like this, the sweat was always guaranteed. The tears, however, were all thanks to Styles.

Reviewed by Nell Geraets The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Apocalypse hangs over Sydney in new sci-fi film commissioned by the Powerhouse
World.content:
CultureMoviesAustralian film Apocalypse hangs over Sydney in new sci-fi film commissioned by the Powerhouse Garry Maddox November 28, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Shall we rehearse one?” Four floors up in the city council’s building, Neil Sharma is directing what he calls the “smoking gun scene” for the Australian sci-fi film 2 Moons in the centre of Parramatta. After a second moon has emerged in the sky, news is about to spread across the city that an ex-NASA physicist is predicting it will collide with the original moon. Neil Sharma (left) directs Fayssal Bazzi in the western Sydney sci-fi film 2 Moons. Wolter Peeters For five people – an anxious office worker, a pregnant free-spirited woman, a landscaper who is fa’afafine (Samoan third gender), an ambitious property developer and a matriarch with a secret – life will never be the same. Fayssal Bazzi (The Correspondent, The Twelve) is the best-known member of a cast that includes Nicoletta Dimas, Nicole Nabout, Peter Thurnwald and Ioane Sa’ula.





Nicoletta Dimas and Alex Burriel in 2 Moons. John Platt Sharma, 40, has taken a long arc to directing his first film since his youth in Parramatta – going from a humble runner on set to an assistant director, assistant to Jeffrey Walker on Dance Academy: The Movie and Taika Waititi on Thor: Love and Thunder, then directing TV dramas such as Heartbreak High, Critical Incident and Strife. With a Fiji-Indian heritage, he grew up selling The Sydney Morning Herald and Daily Telegraph in his parents’ newsagency just a short walk away in Westfield Parramatta. “In my youth, it was taboo to live out this way,” Sharma says. “But now it’s incredibly cool and if you look around you can understand why … This whole place has just morphed into this amazing new beast and I’m so excited to showcase it in a cinematic way on screen.” Lisa Havilah, the Powerhouse Parramatta chief executive who stepped aside in August pending the outcome of a departmental investigation into governance and procurement practices, commissioned 2 Moons after watching another western Sydney film, the Blacktown-based Here Out West, open the Sydney Film Festival in 2021.



Sharma at work on set. Wolter Peeters Havilah “loved it and came to [screen and theatre production company] Co-Curious and said ‘we’d be really interested to do something like this that might coincide-ish with our opening program’,” producer Sheila Jayadev (Here Out West, Stateless) says. As it turned out, “our first week of filming was the week that they opened”. The Powerhouse’s undisclosed funding joins federal and state government agencies and other investors backing what Jayadev calls “a low-budget arthouse” film that is creatively bold. “Unlike other low-budget films, we have five protagonists, five story worlds to establish and a sci-fi premise, so it’s hugely ambitious,” she says. “And two moons.”



Fellow producer Kali Reid says the five writers wanted to use sci-fi, rather than the anthology drama model of Here Out West, to address deep existential questions. Related Article Visual art Sydney’s newest museum is expensive, ambitious and controversial. But is it worth it? “It elevates what people might expect of a story that comes from this region,” she says. “The sci-fi premise is the hook of the film. It’s what we hope will get audiences to want to see it because it’s not just your standard offering of a multi-protagonist story. “Yes, the stories are grounded in drama but hanging over them is ‘will the world end or not?’” Even in a parallel city, the Lebanese-Australian property developer Bazzi plays has a typically Sydney eye for a dollar.



“Once the second moon appears in the atmosphere, he turns his attention to building bunkers,” he says. “It’s a lucrative pivot for him. “At the start of the film, he believes that everyone is blowing it out of proportion. As the movie progresses, he starts to take it more seriously when he sees a few changes in the skies.” Bazzi says the film tells a beautiful story. “We’re watching five different stories play out at once, mainly set in the final week before these moons either collide or pass each other by,” he says. The producers are aiming to give 2 Moons a festival run next year before opening in cinemas.

World.content:
The woman who pollsters predict will lead the Victorian Liberals out of the political wilderness made a fast but efficient stop to a school in her electorate of Kew to cast her ballot.

With her young son Patrick in her arms, and her husband and sister in tow, Jess Wilson made a beeline for the cake stall and democracy sausages right after voting.

Loading

“I’m just here to look after Pat,” joked husband Aaron Lane as Wilson was mobbed by voters, her hands loaded up with treats and snags but still finding a way to dole out plenty of handshakes and hugs.

“There’s a long way to go between now and 6pm,” she told reporters but said the state faced an important and exciting choice.

She joined Patrick for a quick jaunt on the playground before disappearing into the leafy streets of Kew again as quickly as she appeared.

Ever the multi-tasker.

World.title: Caught between killers: An epidemic on one side, terrorists on the other
World.content:
Ismail Mbafumoja, a cacao farmer and gold miner, visits a new cemetery for Ebola victims on the edge of Biakato in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The initial Ebola outbreak has morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe. If that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Biakato, DR Congo: Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo. When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province. It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hotspots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests. Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain. Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. A relative mourns as Red Cross volunteers buried Mose Kalindera, a Biakato shopkeeper. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times “We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads the country’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.” And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State militant group. Ebola was already swamping Biakato when I got to the town in mid-October with photographer Daniel Berehulak. Exhausted health workers reported 300 cases in the span of a month, up from 20 the month before. But there were only two doctors; they had not been paid in months, and they felt utterly abandoned. The aid workers who would normally pour in and set up an Ebola treatment centre were being scared off by rebel fighters who have been terrorising the region for years.



In recent days, their fears were tragically realised when the rebels, who are affiliated with Islamic State, killed 106 people in a series of attacks across the region, United Nations officials said. One of the deadliest episodes occurred 40 kilometres south of Biakato, where militants torched homes, shops and health facilities, forcing Ebola patients to flee their beds. Thousands of residents also fled in an exodus likely to further spread the disease. Even by the standards of eastern DR Congo, where conflict has raged for three decades, the fighters – from a group called the Allied Democratic Forces, or ADF – are considered especially brutal. They roam the sprawling forests, periodically springing from their hiding places to mount attacks. Civilians are beheaded, mutilated and abducted. Children are forced to fight with the group. Mass killings have taken place at funerals and churches. In 2019, the group pledged allegiance to Islamic State, and by one recent estimate, it is the world’s second-deadliest group for civilians. Now, its terror tactics are hobbling the fight against Ebola. A casket holding an Ebola victim is transported by motorbike for burial in Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times A tentative effort to rescue Biakato is under way. Aid groups are using helicopters to fly over the perilous forests and have begun to build a treatment centre. Even so, the volunteers battling to hold back the tide of infections say they are in an impossible bind. “We’ve got the ADF on one side and Ebola on the other,” said Jean-Lefranc Sakara, head of a Red Cross team that collects the Ebola dead from their houses. “We are well and truly caught in the middle.” Loading



Since May, more than 5500 people have died in this outbreak, and experts fear the number is growing so fast that it may surpass the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014-16, the largest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people. As recently as September, experts thought they were getting a handle on this one, but in recent weeks the transmission rate has risen again, according to official figures, meaning it is still out of control. Until recently, violence was the most pressing concern in Biakato. In May, fighters with the Islamic State affiliate stormed into the town, killing 21 people. Soldiers from nearby Uganda began patrolling the streets, under an agreement with the DR Congolese government, to ward off attacks. But the upheaval continues just outside town. Germain Kanyungu (right) is helped at a makeshift treatment centre. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times At first, it seemed that Ebola might bypass Biakato, said Job Bakwata, the town’s chief medical officer. The first recorded case was a gold miner who returned from the town of Mongbwalu in June, then died. But in the following months, as the virus ravaged other areas, Biakato had only a dribble of cases: one more in June, 14 in July, 20 in August. Then in mid-September, infections surged, overwhelming the battered town. Sakara threw himself into the response. A one-time seminarian, he had moved to Biakato four years earlier seeking safety. The rebels had attacked his home in the mountains of North Kivu, killing a sister and three brothers. “My grandfather told me to get out,” he said. “We came here to start over.” After Ebola hit, he dropped everything to lead a small team that collects and disinfects the bodies of Ebola victims. Working that close to the virus was daunting, he said. The volunteers had protective suits but little training, and he felt terrified in the homes of Ebola victims who had just died.



His team also faced hostility from the people they were trying to save. Mourners hurled stones as they tried to bury the dead, showering them with insults and accusing them of somehow profiting from the outbreak. “They call it ‘Ebola business’,” he said. The World Health Organisation, which is leading the effort to get help to Biakato, has its own painful history in the town. During the last outbreak in this area, in 2019, armed men attacked its guesthouse in Biakato, killing three Ebola responders. Officials blamed the violence on the Mai-Mai, a term for local militias. A Sunday mass in Biakato. The town now accounts for as many as one-quarter of the DR Congo’s new Ebola cases. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times Ugandan soldiers help patrol Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times That leaves health officials walking a tightrope. Proceed too slowly, and Biakato could become a deep reservoir of Ebola, spreading infection across the region. Move too quickly, and they risk an attack, like a killing or a kidnapping of aid workers, that could collapse the entire effort. Mistrust among residents is also a problem. After decades of war, faith in the government had collapsed, officials said. The same Congolese soldiers who are supposed to protect the community also prey on it, seeking bribes or profiting from gold. “They don’t trust outsiders,” said Julien Harneis, the UN Ebola co-ordinator in DR Congo. “Experience has taught them not to.”



As infections began to rise in September, a WHO team returned to Biakato to see how they might help. The health workers woke one morning to find a headless sheep dumped outside their hotel – a sign they were not welcome, said Dr Steve Ahuka, the head of the country’s Ebola response. But within weeks, Ebola had become so overwhelming that Biakato’s distrustful leaders were pleading for help. Jean-Lefranc Sakara, a onetime seminarian who now leads a volunteer Red Cross team trying to cope with Ebola victim burials in Biakato. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times On October 12, Ahuka and Catherine Smallwood, a senior WHO official, returned to Biakato to a very different reception. Town leaders formed a circle around Smallwood and, after apologising for the 2019 killings, implored her to send help. “They asked me to put the past in the past,” she recalled. “It was an extremely touching moment.” Since then, the WHO has deployed officials and revamped the chaotic health centre. The DR Congolese government set up a lab to test patients. Medair, a Swiss aid organisation, has sent medics. And yet, even that may not be enough. To stamp out the virus, health workers need to trace every known contact of an infected person. That kind of investigative work is impossible in the countryside while the ADF still threatens it.

World.title: The Wallabies have less than a year to sort themselves out for the World Cup. It can be done
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion The Wallabies have less than a year to sort themselves out for the World Cup. It can be done Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author November 28, 2026 — 9:45am

November 28, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Could we do it? At the end of a long season of mixed results, could the Wallabies snatch a brilliant win against the second-ranked team in the world, Ireland, in this finals round of the Nations Championship at Twickenham? The Wallabies tried hard, but couldn’t prevail against Ireland in London. AP We certainly looked like they could, early. Up against a full-strength Ireland side, the Wallabies looked menacing! Our forwards more than held their own, our backs sniped through regularly, only to be brought down in extremis. The forwards were picking off line-outs – with great work by Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams – the backs were probing and picking on every weak point they could find.



If it were a boxing match, we’d have been way ahead on points. As it was rugby, the only points we actually could find were from lock Williams driving so low from the base of the ruck that his nose dinkum ploughed a furrow in the Twickenham turf, his ears leaving snail-trails on the evening dew. Unstoppable. Try! Wallaby Jeremy Williams crashes over to score a try against Ireland in London. Getty Images Converted, the Wallabies led 7-0 and all seemed right with the world, if only we could hold on until the half to regroup. We couldn’t.



When Max Jorgensen went off at the 30th minute mark for a head injury assessment, it saw Kurtley Beale come on for the vaunted “fairy-tale” return after five years out, at the age of 37. The problem was, he looked 37. Veteran Kurtley Beale had a go in his 96th cap for the Wallabies, but he looked his age. Getty Images The ball went awry from his first touch, and try as hard as he did, the magic seemed gone. Carter Gordon, who had started to seriously struggle, passed to no-one and kicked out on the full.



Ireland immediately started to dominate territory, camping in our 22 to pick off two quick converted tries, with a bonus penalty goal thrown in to lead 17-7 at the break. Surely however, after such a strong start, we could restore order in the second-half? We could not. Out of reach: Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii of Australia challenges Hugo Keenan of Ireland. Getty Images Again, with the athletically gifted Wallaby outside-centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii one of the most lethal men in the world from the kick-off at a range of anything up to 20 metres, we kicked off – ONCE AGAIN – 25 metres, just beyond his reach, and I must pause.



(WHY? WHY? WHY??? How hard is this? How obvious that you either do a kick-off within Suaalii’s possible grasp, or kick it to billy-o, to the corner. Give the bloke a freaking chance! Sorry, as you were. I shall calm myself) Straining to get to the ball, Suaalii got to the man in the air instead, gave away a penalty, and they scored shortly afterwards to lead 24-7. James Ramm challenges Ireland. Getty Images In just over 15 minutes of play, we’d gone from dominating the second-best team in the world, to the dominated. We’d shown what we could do, only to crumble like a Sao in a blender through careless and injudicious play. Yes, the extremely promising Wallabies half-back Kalani Thomas went over after great work by Taniela Tupou to bring it back to 24-14, but at this point it was all over bar the shouting of you and me at the TV screen.



Another perspective Australian rugby He was named after Allan Border. During a tsunami alert, this Wallaby lived up to the name Another clinically lethal Irish try from reserve forward James McNabney saw them lead 31-14, a feat he doubled up with a minute to go, to make it 38-14. All up, it was frustrating, did I mention? Our blokes are good enough to menace a top-ranked side like Ireland. A huge upset was not out of the question. In the end though, it is just us supporters who finished upset. This can be done. They can do it. They have less than a year to sort themselves out before the home World Cup. We have some outstanding players. All three back-rowers Carlo Tizzano, Tom Hooper and Rob Valetini had strong games. Len Ikitau had his moments, as did Jorgensen and Suaalii.



It came together in spots, but that was all. Related Article Live

Wallabies All ball, no bite: Wallabies end season with heavy defeat to Ireland The challenge will be to come up with the right halves combination, stick to it, and have the side as a whole learn how to sustain for 80 minutes. Ok. That’s it, youse blokes. Hit the surf. Think about it. The hard work starts on New Year’s Day. It can be done. The first 20 minutes against Ireland showed it. Western Australian off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli has been confirmed as Nathan Lyon’s replacement in Australia’s Test squad for this summer’s series against New Zealand, with Queensland batter Jack Clayton the other potential debutant in a 13-man squad. Cricket Australia on Saturday confirmed this masthead’s report on Friday that Lyon, Australia’s second-most prolific wicket-taker in Test cricket, had been axed for the summer. WA spinner Corey Rocchiccioli is poised for a call-up to the Test squad. Getty Images In one of the most significant selection decisions in years, Lyon may have played his last Test on Australian soil, potentially depriving one of the country’s greatest bowlers of a farewell in front of family, friends and home crowds. While selectors have the flexibility to change the squad throughout the four-Test series, beginning in Perth on December 9, the decision to overlook Lyon for the summer represents a changing of the guard in Australia’s spin-bowling ranks. However, Lyon is likely to come into calculations for Australia’s five-Test tour of India in January and February.



“Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches,” Australia’s chairman of selectors George Bailey said in a statement. “We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward.” Lyon is among a host of casualties from last month’s tour of South Africa, with all-rounders Cooper Connolly and Beau Webster also overlooked. However, selectors have left one spot open in the squad, to be filled following the sixth round of the Sheffield Shield. Rocchiccioli has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 from five Shield matches this season and is in line to make his Test debut on home turf. Australia’s 13-man Test squad for New Zealand series Pat Cummins (NSW/Penrith Cricket Club) (c)

Scott Boland (VIC/Frankston Peninsula Cricket Club)

Alex Carey (SA/Glenelg Cricket Club)

Jack Clayton (QLD/University of Queensland Cricket Club)

Cameron Green (WA/Subiaco-Floreat Cricket Club)

Josh Hazlewood (NSW/St George Cricket Club)

Travis Head (SA/Tea Tree Gully Cricket Club)

Josh Inglis (WA/Joondalup Cricket Club)

Michael Neser (QLD/Gold Coast Cricket Club)

Matthew Renshaw (QLD/Toombul Cricket Club)

Corey Rocchiccioli (WA/University Cricket Club)

Steve Smith (NSW/Sutherland Cricket Club)

Mitchell Starc (NSW/Manly Warringah Cricket Club) *One player will be added after round six of the Sheffield Shield The 29-year-old’s ability to extract bounce and his familiarity with Perth conditions will be assets should selectors opt to play a frontline spinner in the opener.



“Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions,” Bailey said. Related Article Opinion

Test cricket It won’t be Sandpapergate that ends Cummins’ captaincy. It will be his form Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Queensland leg-spinner Mitch Swepson could consider himself unlucky to miss out, having taken a competition-leading 24 wickets at 16.91 from the same number of Shield appearances as Rocchiccioli this season. Meanwhile, Clayton’s selection is a reward for a prolific start to the domestic summer and puts the Queenslander on the cusp of a Test debut. The left-hander’s 449 runs at 74.83 were enough to earn him a call-up ahead of NSW’s Sam Konstas (479 runs at 68.43) and South Australia’s Jake Weatherald (509 at 56.56), both of whom have made compelling cases for Test returns through their domestic performances.



“Jack [Clayton] is a well-organised player who has performed consistently for an extended period,” Bailey said. “His game is well suited to complement the rest of the batting order.” There was also no room in the squad for Matthew Kuhnemann, Nic Maddinson or Sam Harper, while selectors had already announced Marnus Labuschagne would not be picked.
