World.title: Harry Styles is back in Melbourne. Does his show live up to the hype?
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews Harry Styles is back in Melbourne. Does his show live up to the hype? Nell Geraets November 28, 2026 — 9:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

MUSIC

Harry Styles | Together, Together Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 27 Dance, sweat and sing. This, Harry Styles says midway through his first show back in Melbourne in nearly four years, is all he wants to see from the crowd. With the roof of Marvel Stadium closed on a muggy, rain-soaked day, the sweat certainly comes in waves. But no one seems to notice the heat – they’re too busy watching the cavernous venue transform into a pulsing nightclub. Harry Styles transforms Marvel Stadium into a pulsing nightclub. Pham Styles transports the 50,000-something crowd to Berghain, Berlin’s renowned techno nightclub that partly inspired his latest album Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally. Lasers, multicoloured strobe lights and psychedelic on-screen animations send you into a trance, enraptured by both the sensory dream around you and the endlessly charismatic man leading the reverie. During Taste Back, some in the crowd close their eyes and swing their bodies wildly from side-to-side, almost as if having a religious experience.



Given the rapturous response to every move Styles makes, you’d think he actually were some kind of prophet. He removes his bright pink jacket, people lose it. He takes a sip of water, the crowd goes wild. He shimmies his hips on one of the catwalks extending into the audience, it’s game over – the fans’ brains have short-circuited. This close attention, however, is reciprocated. The degree to which Styles focuses on the crowd is practically unparalleled. Given the rapturous response to every move Styles makes, you’d think he actually were some kind of prophet. Pham He covers every inch of the stage, especially during higher-octane numbers like American Girls and Adore You, waving and blowing kisses to each side. A portion of the show is dedicated to Styles reading some of the fans’ handmade signs, one of which reveals they’d skipped their grandmother’s funeral to be there (whether you agree with that or not, it undeniably captures the hold Styles has over his “Harries”). Twice during the concert, Styles stops the show entirely, requesting the house lights be turned on so that dehydrated people on the floor could be helped out of the scrum.



Unlike a nightclub, however, Styles is backed by a bumping live band, including a large string section. During newer, admittedly flatter numbers – those like Pop and Season 2 Weight Loss – when even the pop star’s charm isn’t quite enough to electrify the room, the horns blast us away, and the keyboard breathes new life into tracks not yet iconic. Harry Styles wants the crowd to dance, sweat and sing Pham If there were any doubts over Styles’ ability to teleport us to a sweaty Berlin nightclub, those are put to rest during Ready, Steady, Go!, a propulsive electronic number that brings the star and his band to the centre of the stadium. Styles, with his distorted megaphone-like mic, gets the entire arena on its feet, jumping so wildly that the ground rumbles beneath us. But Styles ultimately puts it best when singing Dance No More: “It’s feelin’ like the music has been Heaven sent / And that there’s no difference in between the tears and the sweat”. On a muggy day like this, the sweat was always guaranteed. The tears, however, were all thanks to Styles.

World.title: Apocalypse hangs over Sydney in new sci-fi film commissioned by the Powerhouse
World.content:
CultureMoviesAustralian film Apocalypse hangs over Sydney in new sci-fi film commissioned by the Powerhouse Garry Maddox November 28, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Shall we rehearse one?” Four floors up in the city council’s building, Neil Sharma is directing what he calls the “smoking gun scene” for the Australian sci-fi film 2 Moons in the centre of Parramatta. After a second moon has emerged in the sky, news is about to spread across the city that an ex-NASA physicist is predicting it will collide with the original moon. Neil Sharma (left) directs Fayssal Bazzi in the western Sydney sci-fi film 2 Moons. Wolter Peeters For five people – an anxious office worker, a pregnant free-spirited woman, a landscaper who is fa’afafine (Samoan third gender), an ambitious property developer and a matriarch with a secret – life will never be the same. Fayssal Bazzi (The Correspondent, The Twelve) is the best-known member of a cast that includes Nicoletta Dimas, Nicole Nabout, Peter Thurnwald and Ioane Sa’ula.





Nicoletta Dimas and Alex Burriel in 2 Moons. John Platt Sharma, 40, has taken a long arc to directing his first film since his youth in Parramatta – going from a humble runner on set to an assistant director, assistant to Jeffrey Walker on Dance Academy: The Movie and Taika Waititi on Thor: Love and Thunder, then directing TV dramas such as Heartbreak High, Critical Incident and Strife. With a Fiji-Indian heritage, he grew up selling The Sydney Morning Herald and Daily Telegraph in his parents’ newsagency just a short walk away in Westfield Parramatta. “In my youth, it was taboo to live out this way,” Sharma says. “But now it’s incredibly cool and if you look around you can understand why … This whole place has just morphed into this amazing new beast and I’m so excited to showcase it in a cinematic way on screen.” Lisa Havilah, the Powerhouse Parramatta chief executive who stepped aside in August pending the outcome of a departmental investigation into governance and procurement practices, commissioned 2 Moons after watching another western Sydney film, the Blacktown-based Here Out West, open the Sydney Film Festival in 2021.



Sharma at work on set. Wolter Peeters Havilah “loved it and came to [screen and theatre production company] Co-Curious and said ‘we’d be really interested to do something like this that might coincide-ish with our opening program’,” producer Sheila Jayadev (Here Out West, Stateless) says. As it turned out, “our first week of filming was the week that they opened”. The Powerhouse’s undisclosed funding joins federal and state government agencies and other investors backing what Jayadev calls “a low-budget arthouse” film that is creatively bold. “Unlike other low-budget films, we have five protagonists, five story worlds to establish and a sci-fi premise, so it’s hugely ambitious,” she says. “And two moons.”



Fellow producer Kali Reid says the five writers wanted to use sci-fi, rather than the anthology drama model of Here Out West, to address deep existential questions. Related Article Visual art Sydney’s newest museum is expensive, ambitious and controversial. But is it worth it? “It elevates what people might expect of a story that comes from this region,” she says. “The sci-fi premise is the hook of the film. It’s what we hope will get audiences to want to see it because it’s not just your standard offering of a multi-protagonist story. “Yes, the stories are grounded in drama but hanging over them is ‘will the world end or not?’” Even in a parallel city, the Lebanese-Australian property developer Bazzi plays has a typically Sydney eye for a dollar.



“Once the second moon appears in the atmosphere, he turns his attention to building bunkers,” he says. “It’s a lucrative pivot for him. “At the start of the film, he believes that everyone is blowing it out of proportion. As the movie progresses, he starts to take it more seriously when he sees a few changes in the skies.” Bazzi says the film tells a beautiful story. “We’re watching five different stories play out at once, mainly set in the final week before these moons either collide or pass each other by,” he says. The producers are aiming to give 2 Moons a festival run next year before opening in cinemas.

World.title: Italy pip Fiji 23-21 in London
World.content:
In the first Nations Championship rugby play-off game of the weekend Italy beat Fiji 23-21.

The win pushes Fiji to the wooden spoon and gives Italy its first win in the series.

It also meant the Italians were able to avenge their 21-16 loss to the Flying Fijians last weekend.

Italy can thank full-back Tommaso Allan, who made the difference with his boots, kicking two conversions and three penalties for a personal tally of 13 points.

Fiji scored three tries to Italy's second and were in the hunt for the winning try in the last 10 minutes but a knock-on and a ripped ball by the Italian defence meant the islanders were unable to get their second consecutive win they were looking for.

Italian captain Niccolò Cannone said the match was a tough one but was happy with the team's performance.

"We were under pressure, but we continue to work, and we are so happy and we continue to work."

Italy led 17-7 at halftime, with two converted tries and a penalty.

Federico Mori (9') and Giacomo Nicotera (18') got their names on the scoresheet in the first 40 minutes spell.

Allan converted two tires and added a penalty.

The Fijians hit back with a try to Ponipate Loganimasi, which was converted by Caleb Muntz.

Italy took control of the game early in the first half, winning two of Fiji's lineout throws, showed composure on attack and won the aerial kick battles as well.

They also came off their lines on defence quickly, compared to Fiji's slow off the mark defensive runs.

Fiji changed their front row with seven minutes to go to halftime, with Vilikesa Nairau, Peniami Nasali Narisia and Inoke Ravuiwasa taken off, replaced by the experienced trio of Peni Ravai, Tevita Ikanivere and Luke Tagi.

Not enough for Fiji

Mesake Vocevoce, with the ball, takes on the Italians in London in the team's Nations Championship match. Italy won 23-21 Fiji Rugby

Fiji scored two tries in the second spell of 40 minutes.

But that did not count in the end as Italy hung on to claim a famous victory.

A lineout move saw Peniasi Dakuwaqa run in from wide out after the ball travelled the backline, before Jiuta Wainiqolo stepped through two defenders to release Dakuwaqa to run in for the Italian line.

Muntz converted as Fiji trailed 14-17 as the second half resumed.

But a 51st minute penalty gave Allan another chance to kick for goal, extending Italy's lead to 20-14.

Fiji kept the ball for a number of phase, with offloads involving the forwards and backs, before Dakuwaqa put in a grubber that was collected by Wainiqolo who fed Kitione Salawa.

Salawa went over flying through to score, with Muntz's conversion giving them a 21-20 lead in the 53rd minute.

Italy reclaimed the lead in the 67th minute from another Allan kick, after Fiji's front row was penalised for collapsing a scrum just outside the Fijian's 22 metre zone.

Fiji attacked hard again in the last quarter of the game, but knock-ons spoiled their chance of claiming a fourth try.

Replacement hooker Tevita Ikanivere lost the ball in a tackle five metres from the Italian's tryline and Joseva Tamani was penalised for side entry into a ruck, three steps from the tryline as well.

In the end the Italians held on to win the match.

Sevens

Samoa Sevens team in Dubai Manu Samoa Sevens

Meanwhile, in the SVNS 3 tournament in Dubai, the Samoan men's sevens rugby team recorded two wins from their two pool matches on Friday night.

They beat Hong Kong 17-14 in their opening game before beating Italy 33-12.

But the women's team won one and lost one.

A 24-5 win over Mexico kicked off their campaign, before they were thrashed 59-0 by China.

The Samoa men's team have another pool game against Chile at 10.28pm NZT tonight, while the women's side will meet Colombia.

World.title: Green Party tells 'authentic' new MP Tania Waikato to stay focused after 'squish my booty' post
World.content:
The Green Party has spoken to incoming MP Tania Waikato regarding her social media post about Education Minister Erica Stanford, but one of the co-leaders has also defended her as being "authentic and creative".

In a since-deleted post, the incoming MP, who came second in Waiariki but entered Parliament through being 13th on the Green Party list, said she was allocated Stanford's seat in the debating chamber during her parliamentary induction.

"Oh no, it's that 'frankly disgusting' list and map maker sitting in your chair Ewicaaaaaaaa!"

Stanford had previously criticised Waikato's campaign to create lists and maps of schools that pledged to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

"I think it's frankly disgusting the behaviour, creating maps around the country and lists that people feel that they have to be on otherwise, you know, they'll be maligned," Stanford said in 2025.

Waikato's post went on to say while she was in Stanford's chair she "took my shoes off and made sure to touch EVERYTHING and squish my booty all up in there real good to imprint my wairua deep in that tūru."

Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Speaking to media on Friday, Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said the party had spoken to Waikato about "how to ensure that the focus stays on the commitments and the priorities" of the party.

"It's part of who Tania has been, is, you know, being authentic in herself and being creative. It's not something that I would do, and you know she realises that this is now coming into a mainstream platform, and that's going to require some change around keeping the focus of the Green Party kaupapa."

Davidson said the conversation was around Waikato understanding she now had a broader and "privileged" platform and audience, but that the reason she is an MP is because she had "incredible support from our members, from her communities, to be authentic, to reach in a way that no other politician has been able to."

World.title: The giant turtles travelling 12,000km to New Zealand need our help
World.content:
There's a lot to love about leatherback turtles - they can weigh up to 1000kg and grow up to two metres long, and can dive more than a kilometre to feast on the jellyfish that make up their diet.

And now, community-led conservation efforts tracking Western Pacific leatherback turtles, known to visit New Zealand waters, are kick-starting a recovery of the critically endangered species.

Audio player for " Conservation work helping leatherback turtle population " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2852566%2Fthe-giant-turtles-travelling-12-000km-to-new-zealand-need-our-help

Conservation work helping leatherback turtle population Nine To Noon Download MP3 11m

A study from The Nature Conservancy using satellites shows the giant turtle's population has increased about 10 percent each year in the last decade.

That comes after efforts to save one of the world's most threatened sea turtle populations began at Haevo, in Solomon Islands.

Western Pacific leatherback turtles swim around 12,000km on migrations from the east coast of California all the way across the Pacific Ocean to breeding grounds in the islands north of New Zealand.

One of their biggest fans is senior conservation and science advisor with The Nature Conservancy Richard J Hamilton.

He told Nine to Noon that among the turtles' "really cool behaviours" is being a "superstar of free diving".

"We had a turtle we were tracking a number of years ago which broke the world record for a leatherback. It dove down to 1344 metres, I think, when it was tracking back towards New Zealand from its nesting grounds in the Solomons."

Another fun fact: they feed on jellyfish, and they have to eat a lot of them - sometimes 70 percent of their body weight in a day.

"But unfortunately, for a whole range of reasons, the Western Pacific leatherback … is critically endangered. So we've been working a lot with communities in the Solomons for the past couple of decades to … give [the turtles] a better chance of making it into the next century," Hamilton said.

"You'd think of them being in the ICU and we're trying to get them into the main water of the hospital.

"The scary thing is … the Malaysian leatherback nesting population used to be one of the largest in the world. It went functionally extinct in the 1980s and is now completely extinct as far as we can tell.

"So these crashes can happen quite quickly ... I would say we've probably got 20 years max to turn that around or it's very likely that that species will go extinct in our lifetime."

Complicating the conservation battle is that leatherbacks bounce between different countries because of their long-distance migrations, exposing them to a range of threats.

"The leatherbacks which come into New Zealand waters are threatened by accidental bycatch in your shallow-set longline fisheries," Hamilton said.

"And there's been a lot of focus on that in the past decade, I'd say, because there's been an increased realisation about just how many turtles are being caught in New Zealand waters."

He quoted a report from last year that said 44 leatherbacks were caught in the New Zealand fisheries, of which 16 were injured and potentially 10 of those may have died after release.

"So there's a problem with bycatch in New Zealand and then there's a problem with protecting them at their nesting beaches in countries like the Solomon Islands.

"So in the Solomon Islands, there's still a lot of harvesting for subsistence purposes. They've been culturally important there and from a nutritional point of view for probably thousands of years. But as [human] populations have increased, that's become unsustainable."

(ALL RIGHTS, BU permission required) Local ranger Rodney Heinz takes a DNA sample from the leatherback Princess Beauty in the Solomon Islands. © Justine E. Hausheer/TNC

Plastics are another problem, with the turtles ingesting them. Also, climate impacts are leading to a lot of beach erosion and inundation of nests.

"A leatherback nest will take about two months to incubate. If it gets covered by a high sea-level event, those eggs will rot."

To counter that, community rangers in areas targeted for conservation efforts will relocate nests to higher ground.

If they survive all that and make it to New Zealand waters on their migrations, the leatherbacks face a threat from shallow-set longline fishing.

"They're not getting hooked as such, they're just getting tangled up. So the same sort of eddies and convergent zones which attract commercial fishing also attract leatherbacks.

"They're just basically swimming through shallow-set long lines and getting entangled."

A bycatch of 44 leatherbacks in a commercial fishery may not sound like a lot, Hamilton said, but for a critically endangered population estimated to be down to about 1000 individuals, it means extinction by the end of the century without efforts to improve hatchling success rates at nesting beaches and reducing that bycatch.

The good news is that satellite tracking by The Nature Conservancy comparing long-term trends in nest numbers at two beaches in Solomons Islands has found some success in community-based conservation.

"The real success story and I guess the beacon of hope is the Haevo nesting beach in Isabel and the Solomon Islands," he said.

The group was approached about 15 years ago by community leaders there concerned about declining leatherback numbers. In response, The Nature Conservancy employs rangers to look after beaches where the leatherbacks come to nest.

"What we've seen there is basically since people stopped eating the leatherbacks and started conserving them, there's been quite a steady increase in nest numbers. So that's a really positive sign."

The study showed that the Solomon Islands was probably the second most important nesting grounds for the Western Pacific leatherback, and also that many were nesting in Solomons Islands and then heading into New Zealand waters.

World.title: Election: Recount deadline looms for tight seats
World.content:
The Electoral Commission is not aware if any application has been made for a recount, following some close results in the General Election.

The official results were released at 2pm on Friday.

They revealed National, ACT and New Zealand First would need the support of Opportunity to form a Government.

If not, Parliament would be hung, and another election would take place.

National's Mike Butterick was ahead by 139 votes for Wairarapa on election night, but a swing in the specials gave Labour's Kieran McAnulty a buffer of 81.

Labour also saw victory in Hamilton East, with Georgie Dansey pulling ahead of National's Ryan Hamilton by 172 votes.

The Electoral Commission said an application for a recount is made to the District Court, with the process led by a District Court judge.

It added that candidates had three working days to apply, meaning an application for a recount in the 2026 General Election would need to be made by Wednesday 2 December. Candidates must also include a $1000 deposit with an application.

World.title: Jamie Kaiwai: Grandparents waiting to bring their moko home
World.content:
The grandparents of missing East Coast mother Jamie Kaiwai are cautiously hopeful a new line of enquiry might finally bring their moko home.

Speaking to Mata Reports following Friday's revelations that police are preparing to visit a site identified in an anonymous letter, Eru and Elaine Kaiwai described the pain and uncertainty of seven years without answers.

Jamie was 27 when she disappeared from Tolaga Bay in October 2019, leaving behind a young child.

For Eru and Elaine, life in Tolaga Bay has carried on. They have attended numerous tangihanga, farewelling others in their community while still not knowing what happened to their granddaughter.

"Life just carries on, we been to so many tangi and meetings around Tolaga," Eru Kaiwai said.

Asked whether attending tangihanga was difficult when they still did not know where their granddaughter was, Eru Kaiwai said:

"It is, she's not here we don't know where she is and that's it."

The couple have relied on each other through seven years of uncertainty.

"We just look after each other.

"She's gone missing, we don't know what happened, it's awful not knowing the answers."

Jamie's grandparents, Eru and Elaine Kaiwai. Supplied

On Friday, Mata Reports revealed police were preparing to visit a location identified in a handwritten letter purporting to reveal where Jamie's body could be found.

The letter, addressed to Eru and Elaine, was delivered to the Tolaga Bay Post Office several years ago.

Asked about police investigating the contents of the letter, Eru Kaiwai said he thought "something probably turn up there."

"I suppose good if they can find something and come to a conclusion, it's been so many years now."

Seven years without answers

Police did not treat Jamie's disappearance as suspicious, but her whānau have long maintained otherwise.

Eru Kaiwai expressed frustration with the progress of the investigation over the years.

"It's been a long time, the police have been slack as far as I am concern. It's been stop, start, stop, start," he said.

"We don't hear anything so we just carry on."

The letter that has renewed hope

As revealed by Mata Reports on Friday, the handwritten letter contains details of where Jamie's body can purportedly be found, in an area where her whānau have long suspected she could be.

To Mr & Mrs Eru Kaiwai

c/o Post Office

Tolaga Bay

East Coast

Gisborne

The family of Jamie

She's 5 kms up the [road name withheld] Rd on the left - in a gully at the bottom of the hill - caught between 2 logs wrapped in a yellow or cream sheet.

Post office staff handed the letter to Eru and Elaine Kaiwai, who kept it in a box of papers alongside Jamie's belongings, hoping someone would eventually investigate its contents.

The letter is now with a team of investigators working with the whānau.

Police have confirmed to Mata Reports they are working with a member of the whānau's investigative team and are preparing to visit the site.

"We plan to visit the site soon and are working towards that," police said.

Mata Reports has seen the letter but is withholding details of the location ahead of the planned site visit.

Jonique Oli-Alainu'uese, Jamie’s cousin Supplied

Jamie's cousin, Jonique Oli-Alainu'uese, who has led the whānau's seven-year search for answers, told Mata Reports on Friday that the letter stands out from other information they have received.

"We've had thousands of messages about Jamie over the years. This letter is different. It's detailed and knowing."

Both police and the whānau are appealing directly to the person who wrote the letter to come forward.

"Our message to the person who wrote the letter is to make yourself known to police (in confidence if they like) so we can work together to corroborate the contents," police said.

Oli-Alainu'uese also has a message for the author.

"I want the author of the letter to know that I recognise the courage and bravery it took to send it, and I'm incredibly grateful.

"I hope they find the strength to come forward, knowing they will be supported and that their safety and protection will be our priority. Their voice could make a real difference in finally getting the justice Jamie deserves."

Asked about the status of the investigation in light of the new information, police said: "Jamie's disappearance is unexplained and it remains that way to date."

The contents of the letter have yet to be corroborated.

World.title: Partially treated wastewater discharged near Karori Stream
World.content:
A mechanical failure has caused the discharge of partially treated wastewater at Wellington's Western Wastewater Treatment Plant overnight, the second to occur in two days.

The capital's water authority, Tiaki Wai, says the failure occurred at about 3am on Saturday and the wastewater will emerge at Cook Strait near the mouth of Karori Stream.

Tiaki Wai said a failure at the Western UV Weir Gate on Friday afternoon led to a discharge of treated wastewater that also emerged near the mouth of Karori Stream.

People are being advised to stay out of the water for two to three days after heavy rain.

RNZ is seeking further information from Tiaki Wai.

World.title: 'Not just a name on a list': Remembering missing Kiwi in Nepal Shweta Mhatre
World.content:
Three months after the devastating flash floods in Nepal, a mentor and close family friend of Shweta Mhatre remembers the missing New Zealander for her warmth, generosity and love for life.

Mhatre was among five New Zealanders reportedly missing after flash floods tore through the Nepal-China border region on 26 August.

The massive flash flood, triggered by a collapse of ice and rock from a Himalayan glacier, sent a torrent of water, mud and debris through a river valley, burying villages and destroying critical infrastructure.

Mhatre was part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage group believed to have been caught in the disaster, and her disappearance has left family and friends facing months of uncertainty.

"Shweta is not just a name on a list of people missing in Nepal," hospitality business owner Sunny Kaushal said.

"I mean, she is a much-loved person who built a life, a career and friendship in New Zealand."

Kaushal has known Mhatre for more than 15 years, having first met her when she was a student in New Zealand.

"I remember her as a young woman who was enthusiastic, ambitious and keen to make something of the opportunities New Zealand offered," he said.

Kaushal said Mhatre had made the most of those opportunities in a relatively short time.

She quickly established herself in the hospitality industry and rose to a senior management role within a few years.

"She was exceptionally capable, intelligent and a very quick learner as I still remember," he said.

More than 6000 remain missing following the devastating flash floods on the Nepal-China border on 26 August, according to latest figures from Nepalese and Chinese authorities. AFP / Manan Vatsyayana

Kaushal said he was shocked to learn that Mhatre was among the New Zealanders missing after the floods.

"We have been hoping and praying for positive news [for] three months," he said.

"The uncertainty is particularly painful for everyone who knows her and above all, for her family."

Kaushal said Mhatre had invited him and his family to celebrate when she bought her first home in New Zealand.

He still remembers how delighted she was about the milestone.

"It was one of those occasions when you could genuinely see how proud and excited someone was about building their future in New Zealand," he said.

"These are the little memories that stay with you: the excitement, the laughter and the smile."

Four other New Zealanders - Dejan Kuzmic, Kinnari Patel, Mihir Patel and Suhasini Reddy - were also reported missing in the disaster, leaving families across New Zealand and overseas waiting for answers.

Latest figures from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said more than 1400 people were killed and more than 5700 remained missing following the disaster as of 21 September.

On the Tibetan side of the border, 43 people were reported dead, with more than 500 missing, according to figures reported by Chinese state media in September.

Nepal ended its active search-and-rescue operation in October, shifting its focus towards recovery and rehabilitation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade has previously confirmed that New Zealand Police are supporting the families of the five missing New Zealanders.

A spokesperson for the ministry told RNZ on Tuesday that New Zealand authorities were continuing to support the families.

"New Zealand's High Commission in New Delhi continues to engage with Nepalese authorities as they work through ongoing disaster response processes," the spokesperson said.

Kaushal said he continued to hope for answers.

"She was one of those people who walked into a room with a smile and brought positive energy with her," he said.

World.title: MotoGP world champion Marquez announces shock retirement
World.content:
Marc Marquez will take his final bow in Valencia after the eight-time MotoGP champion announced on Friday that he would retire following the 2026 season finale, ending one of motorcycle racing's greatest careers.

The Spaniard made the announcement days after wrapping up a record-equalling eighth premier-class title in Portugal, drawing him level with Giacomo Agostini.

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage.

Loading Instagram content

The announcement came as a surprise after Marquez, who won six MotoGP titles with Honda before joining Ducati, signed a contract extension with the Italian team earlier this year that was due to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old said he decided to retire at last month's Japanese Grand Prix after the physical and mental toll of repeated injuries and operations began to weigh heavily on him.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," Marquez said.

"When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder (in May)."

Marquez said he had begun to "feel the fear" despite remaining determined to compete and had also been troubled by brief recurrences of double vision after the Indonesian and French grands prix.

He recovered within days on both occasions but said the episodes made him more cautious.

"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he added.

Marquez had been expected to lead MotoGP into its new 850cc era, with compatriot Pedro Acosta's arrival at the factory Ducati team viewed as a symbolic passing of the torch.

There were tears in the Ducati garage and among the crowd when fans at the Circuit Ricardo Tormo were told the Spaniard would be competing in his final race this weekend.

Jorge Martin, his main rival for the 2026 title, appeared stunned, while Marquez's brother Alex, who had been told of the decision during the Japanese Grand Prix, watched with a sombre expression.

From rookie champion to all-time great

Marquez swept into MotoGP in 2013 and won the title at his first attempt, becoming the youngest premier-class world champion at the age of 20.

By 2019, he had amassed six championships with Honda and appeared virtually unbeatable, a blur of orange and red tearing through the field.

Everything changed at the opening race of the 2020 season in Jerez, where he crashed and broke his arm.

The injury began the darkest period of his career. Marquez underwent four operations, abandoned several comeback attempts and suffered blurred vision, all while trying to push an underperforming Honda bike far beyond its limits.

He later spoke of wondering whether continuing was worth the pain as speculation about his retirement intensified.

Instead, Marquez took the decision to leave Honda and make the switch to Gresini Racing, which was using year-old Ducati machinery.

He slowly rediscovered his belief, ending a 1,043-day wait for victory in Aragon before securing the factory Ducati seat that would change everything.

"I had my second life (after leaving Honda), and I enjoyed my second life in MotoGP," Marquez said.

In 2025, Marquez claimed his seventh MotoGP crown in Japan, a feat Acosta likened to basketball great Michael Jordan's return from baseball to lead the Chicago Bulls to another NBA title.

Erasing a 102-point deficit

What followed in 2026 was perhaps even more extraordinary as Marquez overturned a 102-point deficit to retain the championship.

After failing to win early in the season and then crashing in France, he underwent surgery on his shoulder and a fractured foot, missing his home grand prix while his rivals collected victories and points.

He sat eighth in the standings but won six of the next nine rounds, as Aprilia rivals Martin and Marco Bezzecchi faltered, before sealing the title in Portugal with a round to spare.

If his seventh championship was his most emotional, the eighth cemented his place among the sport's greats and was marked by a celebration rich in symbolism.

Marquez climbed a staircase as the silhouette of a goat, shorthand for "greatest of all time", appeared on a screen behind him before Agostini presented him with a commemorative golden helmet.

Reuters

World.title: Wallabies end 2026 with 38-14 loss to Ireland in London
World.content:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss admits his side has "work to do" after finishing their 2026 campaign with a 38-14 defeat to Ireland in the Nations Championship at Twickenham.

With the Rugby World Cup in Australia less than 12 months away, the result in London saw the Wallabies end the Test season with a 6-7-1 (win-loss-draw) record.

They finished sixth in the Nations Championship, one spot behind Ireland.

Trailing 17-7 at half-time, the Wallabies were made to pay for several wasted attacking opportunities when camped in Ireland's territory.

They earned repeated entries inside the Irish 22, but a Kalani Thomas try was all they could show for their efforts in the second half.

Ireland, on the other hand, crossed for three second-half tries, a tally which included a double to reserve forward James McNabney.

The Wallabies, ranked seventh in the world, lost five of their last six Tests for the year.

A win over world champions South Africa in September was a rare highlight for Kiss's troops.

"Every team above us [on the world rankings], bar one, we haven't been able to beat," Kiss told Stan Sport.

"We've got work to do."

Irish reserve James McNabney scored a late double in the win over the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Seb Daly)

The Wallabies opened the scoring against Ireland in the 21st minute following Jeremy Williams's converted try.

World number two Ireland, who was coming off a 20-17 win over the Springboks in Dublin, replied on the scoreboard with tries to Robbie Henshaw and Nick Timoney.

Sam Prendergast converted both and added a penalty goal on the stroke of half-time to establish Ireland's 10-point lead at the break.

Robert Baloucoune scored Ireland's third straight try early in the second half and following Prendergast's conversion, the Wallabies were trailing 24-7.

Thomas's try, and Carter Gordon's conversion, closed the gap, but McNabney's brace inside the final 10 minutes of the match helped ice Ireland's winning margin.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season
World.content:
All season the North Melbourne AFLW side was not allowed to use the word "three-peat".

The team came into the year as back-to-back premiers and outright favourites for the flag. They started the finals series as minor premiers, having lost just one game (to Hawthorn), their first defeat in three years.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

For the duration of the year, the AFLW world was talking about the Kangaroos' incoming third consecutive flag. But not the Roos themselves.

As Jasmine Garner said post-game, it's a cliche as old as football, but one that's tried and tested: treat the season as one game at a time.

Then the siren sounded. They had defeated Melbourne by 26 points under lights at Princes Park after beating Brisbane the two years prior.

And they let the emotions overrun them.

North Melbourne is the first side in AFLW history to claim three consecutive premierships. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

All Australian Erika O'Shea said it was one of "the best moments of my life, 100 per cent".

"Oh my god, it's the most surreal feeling,"O'Shea told ABC Sport.

"Nothing will ever feel like this. I started crying instantly when I heard that siren.

"I think a sigh of relief, but also just all the hard work that we've done during the year, and yeah … three-peat. I can't believe it.

"To finally be able to say it with a smile is the best thing ever."

Head coach Darren Crocker said it was up to the AFLW community and media to decide whether the side was a dynasty or not, but he was pretty sure the consecutive flags made for one.

He said the 2024 flag — the first AFLW cup for North Melbourne — meant a lot. The second broke new ground when the first side became the first to go back-to-back in AFLW history.

And the three-peat felt pretty good.

Even opposition captain Kate Hore said "we'll talking about this team forever".

Jasmine Garner won her second best-on-ground medal on Friday night. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Garner said this year was more difficult than last.

"I always had the belief that we were good enough to do it, but you know, this year, it hasn't been perfect," she said.

"We've lost one game in 42, but we've been challenged. We've had injuries. We've had different hurdles pop up along the way.

"But we felt this year we were kind of building slowly and we kept our best footy to the finals. I think that's what got us over, our experience and our calmness.

"I reckon this final series has been the best it's ever been, but it's just so good for women's footy. Just really proud of the group."

The players were finally able to let the emotions flow after a challenging but near flawless season. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Kangaroos forward Kate Shierlaw said this win made her the most emotional of the three.

"I'm very overwhelmed with emotions. Relief, excited," Shierlaw said.

"It's just like a lot of hard work over four or five years … just Kearns [Emma Kearney, North Melbourne stalwart defender and Shierlaw's partner] and I having a great time out here, living our dreams. Three in a row."

Shierlaw and Kearney hinted at possible retirement. Shierlaw said she would "talk to the club" and Kearney told the broadcast she may have played her last game.

World.title: Australia 'have to be better,' humbled by England at rain-soaked Gabba
World.content:
England has taken a 2-1 series lead in its T20I series against Australia with another dominant victory on a rainy Friday evening at the Gabba.

Australia was bowled out for just 108 in 16.5 overs, its lowest ever T20I score on home soil when batting first.

The 23,536 Gabba fans may have feared whether, after three superb Sheffield Shield games went down to the wire this week, they would see a second lopsided white-ball contest in as many matches following England's dominant victory at Carrara on Tuesday.

And although Riley Meredith (3-30) and Billy Stanlake (0-46) provided some jeopardy with their own vicious pace, the result was never in doubt.

"A very disappointing night. We have to own that," Mitch Marsh said.

"Some of our [shot] selection was not to up to it tonight, but I said to to this young group at the start of the series I don't want them to fear making mistakes.

"Probably tonight we needed to be more calculated and understand the conditions we were playing in.

"That was a belting wicket - as good as the Gabba can get - so no excuses. We have to be better."

England comfortably chased down a revised target of 93 with 43 balls to spare, sealing a seven-wicket victory.

Jamie Overton was irresistible, bowling with pace and ferocity that Australian bowlers have terrorised Englishmen with for decades at this ground, taking a career-best 5-12.

Jordan Cox scored an unbeaten 33. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

England has traditionally been carved up by Australian quicks at the Gabba, but this time the shoe was on the other foot.

England won the toss and bowled first, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann saying on ABC Radio that "Australia will be looking for 220, maybe more," and were on track early despite Mitch Marsh being caught at mid-on for 11 off Dawson's bowling.

Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper both hit out, smashing five sixes between them before both fell in consecutive overs; Harper for 26 off 14 balls and Fraser-McGurk becoming Overton's first victim after an 11-ball 22.

Nikhil Chaudhary, scorer of 66 and 45 in his last two innings for Australia, forwent the power displayed by his colleagues to deliver a range of delightful dabs with a delicacy and deftness at odds with the slogging shown elsewhere.

Overton wasn't having a bar of it, though.

The 32-year-old Devonian aimed a sharp bouncer that cracked into Chaudhary's helmet in one over, and thumped Tim David on the forearm with a 142km/h the next.

The next ball, David (6) was out, hooking a 145km/h snorter straight to Henry Crocombe at fine leg, with Overton claiming the wicket of Joel Davies (3) soon after.

Chaudhary literally hit back for Australia, smashing a fearsome drive straight back at Overton, who was smashed on the thumb in his follow-through.

Jamie Overton delivered some blows, and took one himself. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

After a short delay for treatment, Overton had Chaudhary (19) caught after he spooned a lofted drive straight down long-on's throat.

Overton still was not done. Ben Dwarshuis was beaten for pace and edged behind for a four-ball duck, a double-wicket maiden to finish, giving Overton the second-best figures by an England player in T20 international cricket.

Adam Zampa's dismissal was the first wicket Overton did not play a part in, when he edged Dawson behind for 3.

But Australia's malaise deepened when Mitchell Owen, Australia's last real batting hope, was catastrophically run out for 16 by Phil Salt trying to take a mad second run to cover.

Curran, who went for 16 in his first disastrous over, ended Australia's innings in his second, bowling Billy Stanlake for a duck as Australia were all out for 108.

England started well but lost Phil Salt (5), caught at cover off a rising Riley Meredith delivery, and Aneurin Donald, carrying on with his big-hitting ways by belting six boundaries in a 13-ball 32.

The first brief rain delay 3.5 overs into England's reply gave Australia time to regroup, with Stanlake underlining the hosts' renewed vigour by knocking Harry Brook off his feet with a spectacular bouncer first ball back.

Billy Stanlake felled Harry Brook with a brute of a bouncer after the first rain break. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Meredith then took two wickets in the next over as England stumbled from 1-45 to 3-49 in six deliveries.

After a further delay that wiped three overs from England's chase, a revised target of 98 set by DLS method, Meredith should have had another, Chaudhary dropping Jordan Cox when the wicketkeeper was on 1.

Dwarshuis then shelled a tough caught-and-bowled chance on Banton with the Englishman on 9.

Another rain delay, with England just seven runs short at that point, further reduced the target to 93 in 16 overs, with the tourists comfortably making it with 43 balls to spare as Jordan Cox (33) and Tom Banton (10) steered them home.

England is now two wins from two in T20 cricket at the Gabba, having beaten New Zealand by 20 runs en route to the 2022 T20 World Cup title.

Australia was beaten for just the second time in nine completed matches, its first T20I defeat since losing to the West Indies in 2013.

England can seal the five-match series on Sunday at the SCG, with the final game in Canberra on Wednesday.

World.title: Roos create AFLW history with three-peat after downing Dees in epic
World.content:
North Melbourne has become the first club to claim three straight AFLW premierships after downing Melbourne in a thrilling grand final.

The Kangaroos were pushed to the limit in wet conditions at Princes Park, but kicked the last three goals of the match inside the final five minutes to run out 6.8 (44) to 2.6 (18) winners.

Kangaroos skipper Jasmine Garner was named Best on Ground after finishing with 26 disposals and five clearances to go along with a goal.

North came out of the gates kicking the first three goals of the game, but were pegged back when the Dees kicked the next two to cut the margin to six points at half-time.

Tayla Harris was inspirational for Melbourne in the second quarter, kicking her team's first goal of the match after taking a towering contested mark inside 50.

With rain increasing after the main break, the second half turned into a dour slugfest as both teams held each other goalless in the third quarter.

The Kangaroos were forced to defend grimly for much of the final quarter as the Demons drew to within one goal with five minutes remaining, but proved to be too strong in the end, with Bella Eddey's final quarter goal proving to be the eventual backbreaker.

North forward Blaithin Bogue was the only multiple goalscorer of the match, kicking both of her goals in the final few minutes to seal the premiership win.

Follow the live blog below for a blow-by-blow recap of the AFLW grand final.

World.title: Matildas legend enters arena of greatness in milestone match
World.content:
It was almost imperceptible.

The slightest shake of her head as Steph Catley listened to Matildas coach Joe Montemurro describe her as one of the world's best footballers.

It was as if she disagreed with the label. But there is no disputing the veteran defender's standing in the game.

She is among the world's elite and one of Australia's greatest ever, as a player, leader, and humble champion.

Against Colombia in Canberra tomorrow night, she will become just the seventh Matilda to reach 150 caps; three other members of that club are in this squad.

"This team feels like my family. We've grown up together, and I'm honoured every single time I touch the pitch with these girls, and I wear that jersey," Catley said.

"So 150 times is massive, and I'm very, very proud of that."

Steph Catley says it's special to reach the milestone at home. (ABC News)

Catley has been at the heart of this generation that has driven women's football in Australia at full throttle, from the shadows into the spotlight.

"I think the work that the previous Matildas have put into this team and women's football has been incredible," she said.

"But this group has done so much for the game, for this team, for women's sport in general.

"There's still a long way to go, but what we've achieved so far has been incredible."

Catley is a fierce presence on the pitch, whether playing for the Matildas or Arsenal, and, at 32, is still very much in her prime.

Steph Catley has been a mainstay of the Matildas' defence for over a decade. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

But when she took the time to reflect on her career, the tears welled up in her eyes.

She said the emotion made it hard to talk about, but she regained her composure and did it anyway.

"I'll never take it for granted that I'm able to represent this team and play for my country," she said.

"And even representing Arsenal, it's everything that I dreamed of as a kid. It's everything I've worked my entire life for, and 150 caps is massive.

"And you do get to a point where every day gets a little bit harder on your body and mentally. But I think being around the girls and the fact that we are like a family … I want to be the best version of myself for them.

"That's what drives me, I think, and my family as well. They're all the way over here in Australia, and I've played overseas pretty much my entire adult life.

"So those sacrifices are big, and I think you want to make it worth it in the long run."

Steph Catley says her teammates and family drive her to keep going. (ABC News)

Montemurro has been a constant in the Catley journey, from coaching her in the A-League Women, to Arsenal, to the national side.

His affection for her as a player and person is clear.

"I've had the honour and the pleasure of working with what I think is one of the world's best footballers, but more importantly, as a person," he said.

"We should be proud as a country to have someone of the calibre of Steph Catley in our midst and growing up and hopefully still with us for a while.

"But what she's given on the field and off the field, I think, has been absolutely special and very unique in the world of football."

Steph Catley has captained the side for extended periods during Sam Kerr's various absences. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Catley, like so many members of this Matildas' golden generation, has achieved so much but is still missing a major international trophy.

Her tearful interview after losing the Women's Asian Cup final in March was filled with the feeling of a missed opportunity.

Time has helped reignite the fire to try again.

"We really could have won that tournament, so I think that was tough for us to take," she said.

"It just builds that hunger for the next chance that we get, another step to build towards what we want to achieve."

World.title: Sam Walker signs with PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL season
World.content:
Premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has signed with the Papua New Guinea Chiefs for the 2028 season.

Walker, whose relationship with the Sydney Roosters fell apart after the club's grand final victory, will head to Port Moresby on a two-year deal.

The Queenslander is coming off the best year of his career, making State of Origin and Australian Test debuts.

"Sam is undoubtedly a gifted footballer who has already shown that he has tremendous vision, an outstanding kicking game and an ability to create something out of nothing," PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said.

"He is also a very smart footballer who understands how to influence and control a game and has shown that he can perform on the biggest of stages across club, state and now international level.

"We're really excited about what he can bring to the team and his partnership alongside Jarome Luai allows us to have one of the game's most creative and influential halves combinations — something which I'm excited to see develop as we take to the field."

Walker made his Test and Origin debuts this season. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The 24-year old was the 2021 Dally M Rookie of the Year and has been the Tricolours starter ever since.

He also attracted interest from South Sydney and Canterbury.

PNG Chiefs General Manager of Football Michael Chammas said the team believed Walker's best football was still yet to come.

"Sam was someone we identified as a player who we believe could have a transformational impact on our team — both in how we play on the field but also on the way we build our side and the way other players excel around him," Chammas said.

"He is a premiership winner, an Origin star and a World Cup winner and he has shown that he can perform under pressure in the biggest moments of our game.

Walker is the latest star signing for the PNG Chiefs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He is also still young and we believe that his best years are ahead of him.

"We're thrilled that Sam has committed to what we are building and we look forward to seeing him play a key role in the bright future of the PNG Chiefs."

Walker is the latest star signing for the Chiefs, who have created shockwaves in the player market with their ability to offer tax-free contracts.

In the past week, they have signed Canberra and New South Wales backrower Hudson Young and North Queensland star Jeremiah Nanai.

Luai, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and Joseph Manu will also line up for the Chiefs in their inaugural season.

Walker is the ninth player they have signed with either Test or Origin experience.

World.title: Lyon's career in limbo as he faces Test axe
World.content:
Nathan Lyon is set to be axed from Australia's squad for the first Test in a move that raises questions over the 39-year-old's future in the team.

Australia will on Saturday name their squad for the December 9 series opener against New Zealand in Perth, but it is understood Lyon will not be included.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner when fit for more than 13 years, but selectors have shown a willingness to go without a specialist tweaker more often recently.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

He has three times been left out of Australia's team over the past 18 months, with selectors picking four quicks in Tests against West Indies, England and South Africa.

But the spinner's omission from the squad is even more notable, given previous such calls have been made on seeing the final wicket closer to the toss.

Lyon has made no secret of his desire to continue playing, with legacy-defining tours of India and England in the next nine months.

The sixth-leading wicket-taker of all time with 577 scalps, Lyon worked around the clock to recover from a hamstring injury last summer and return to the Test side.

His push has included giving up alcohol and spending more time in the gym, having previously described how he is trying to squeeze every last bit out of his career, with 145 Tests already to his name.

Nathan Lyon struggled to make a breakthrough in the latter stages of the third Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

Where that career goes from here is now in question.

Lyon took six wickets at 43.67 in Australia's most recent tour of South Africa, where he was overlooked for Scott Boland in a wet second Test in Gqeberha.

Included in that was Australia's inability to take wickets on the fourth day of the final Test in Cape Town, as South Africa recovered from a 100-run first-innings deficit.

South Africa spinner Simon Harmer then bagged 6-16 on the final day to bowl the Proteas to victory.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

Lyon has since taken seven Sheffield Shield wickets across two matches on return to Australia, but was out-bowled by Queensland leg spinner Mitchell Swepson in Sydney this week.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald had indicated after the loss in Cape Town that Lyon remained Australia's number one spinner, when asked if that would be reviewed.

"Review it?" McDonald responded at the time.

"I don't think it's something to review now. We'll sit back and we'll go through Shield cricket.

"Nathan will be preparing for the first Test match in Perth."

AAP

Tech.title: The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
Tech.content:
We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date.

The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game.

The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify.

It’s just the latest company, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, to suffer an outage in the last few weeks. As of Friday afternoon, access to accounts through the app and site appeared to still be down. When asked for comment, the company pointed us to a notice on its site reading:

Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees.

Opening the app pops up a notification saying the company is working to “restore access as soon as possible,” and encourages customers to contact the company by phone to file and manage claims. Users have flooded X and Reddit with complaints about the outage, some of whom have either been left waiting for roadside assistance or have been unable to insure new vehicles.

Allstate hasn’t publicly identified a cause for the outage.

Tech.title: My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware. My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins.

Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.

There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in.

For a look at some of the custom firmwares, effects, and other mods already available for the MPC Sample, check out this video from Loopop.

Tech.content:
If you’re tired of constantly scrounging around for your lost belongings, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for an all-time low of $18 at Amazon , Walmart , and Best Buy . The handy location trackers have a list price of $29 each, but have been consistently available for around $24 since Amazon Prime Day in late June.

The upgraded ultra-wideband chip and improved Bluetooth in the latest AirTag should provide more precise location tracking, with a range 1.5x wider than the first-gen model. The internal speaker is also 50 percent louder than the original, making it easier to find whatever item your AirTag is attached to, whether it’s buried deep in your couch cushions or at the bottom of your bag.
